sections.heading: What a Jumeirah 2 search for an IB maths tutor usually means
paragraphs: Parents in Jumeirah 2 type this phrase for one of three reasons, and they need different answers. The first group has a DP1 pupil who was comfortable in MYP Mathematics and is now below their predicted grade six weeks into Analysis and Approaches. The second has a DP2 pupil whose exploration deadline is close and whose draft has no mathematics in it above course level. The third has a Year 11 family choosing option blocks and trying to work out whether Analysis and Approaches or Applications and Interpretation is the honest choice.

None of those three is solved by the same weekly hour. The DP1 case is a fluency problem and responds to short, frequent, drilled sessions. The exploration case is a single piece of coaching plus feedback on a draft the student writes themselves. The route case needs one conversation with somebody who has read both syllabuses, and then nothing at all until September. A tutoring arrangement that treats all three as 'weekly maths help' wastes money on at least two of them.

The word 'in Jumeirah 2' in the search is about availability rather than geography. Parents want to know that somebody can teach their child's exact course at the hour their child is actually free, and that the arrangement does not depend on who happens to live within driving distance of a villa off Jumeirah Beach Road. Delivering lessons online answers that: the constraint becomes the timetable instead of the traffic, and a Higher Level specialist is reachable whether or not anybody with that specialism lives in Jumeirah.

sections.heading: The Jumeirah 2 school-day clock, and the slot that survives it
paragraphs: Dismissal times are published by each school and they move between phases and between years, so treat the table below as the shape of the problem rather than as your child's timetable. The pattern holds across the Jumeirah clusters: secondary pupils come out between a quarter to three and half past three, the roads around Al Wasl Road and Jumeirah Beach Road absorb every school in the district at once, and the honest start time for a lesson is between thirty and ninety minutes after the bell depending on where the school sits.

Two things make the picture worse than the raw drive time suggests. The first is split pick-ups: a family with a primary child in Jumeirah and a secondary child in Al Sufouh is making two journeys, and the second one ends after four o'clock. The second is activity scheduling. Swimming, football and music in this part of Dubai cluster between five and seven in the evening, which means the slot that looked free at 17:00 in September is gone by October.

The practical answer is to pick a slot that cannot be destroyed by either, and then defend it. For families inside the Jumeirah and Al Safa ring, that is usually 16:00 on a fixed weekday. For everyone else it is 19:30. Once chosen, the slot should stay put for the term: a pupil who is taught at a different hour every week never builds the habit of arriving with questions, and the first ten minutes of every session go on remembering where the last one stopped.

sections.heading: Analysis and Approaches or Applications and Interpretation: the choice that sets two years
paragraphs: This is the decision that most affects how much tutoring a Jumeirah 2 family ends up buying, and it is usually made on the wrong evidence. Pupils choose the route their friends chose, or the one their MYP teacher expects, or the one with the reputation for being easier. The correct test is narrower: read the entry requirements of the degree courses your child is plausibly applying to, and see which route is named. Engineering, mathematics, physics and many economics courses at research universities frequently specify Analysis and Approaches, often at Higher Level.

The two courses are not a hard version and an easy version of the same subject. Analysis and Approaches is a methods course: proof, algebraic manipulation, trigonometric identities, calculus done by hand, and a Paper 1 sat with no calculator at all. Applications and Interpretation is an applied course: modelling, regression, statistical inference, matrices and graph theory, with a graphic display calculator permitted in every paper. A pupil who is strong at structured calculation and weak at interpreting a messy context will find Analysis and Approaches easier, and the reverse is just as true.

Getting this wrong costs more than a bad fit. A pupil on Analysis and Approaches HL who cannot manipulate algebra at speed spends two years on remediation and still loses marks on Paper 1. A pupil on Applications and Interpretation who then applies for engineering discovers in Year 13 that the prerequisite is missing. Both are expensive, and both are avoidable with one honest conversation in Year 11 - which is a single consultation, not a tutoring contract.

sections.heading: How IB Mathematics is weighted, paper by paper
paragraphs: Weightings decide where revision time should go, and most pupils do not know them. Standard Level on either route is two written papers at forty per cent each plus the exploration at twenty. Higher Level is three written papers - thirty, thirty and twenty per cent - plus the same exploration at twenty. That means a Higher Level pupil who ignores Paper 3 until April has left a fifth of the grade untouched, which is exactly as much as the exploration they have been worrying about since DP1.

The calculator rule is the other structural fact worth internalising. On Analysis and Approaches, Paper 1 is sat without a calculator, so every piece of arithmetic, surd manipulation and exact trigonometric value has to be secure by hand. Pupils who have done all their practice with a graphic display calculator in front of them discover this in the first mock and lose marks that have nothing to do with understanding. On Applications and Interpretation the calculator is permitted throughout, and the failure mode flips: pupils lose marks on syntax, on rounding, and on not showing the method the mark scheme wants to see.

Confirm the current weightings and component structure with your child's Diploma coordinator before building a revision plan on them. The IB publishes and revises subject guides on its own site, and a tutoring page is not the right authority for an assessment detail that decides how a family spends four hundred hours. The structure below is the shape of the course as taught in Dubai schools this year; the coordinator holds the version that applies to your child's cohort.

sections.heading: Where IB maths marks actually leak
paragraphs: Almost nobody loses an IB maths grade because of a topic they have never met. Grades go on four recurring, diagnosable failures, and all four are visible in a marked past paper within twenty minutes. The first is arithmetic and algebraic slips under time pressure: a sign lost in a rearrangement, a bracket expanded wrongly, a surd left unsimplified. Each costs one or two marks, and across a full paper they are the difference between a five and a six.

The second is method marks never claimed. The mark scheme rewards a stated method even where the final answer is wrong, and pupils who do their working on a separate sheet or in their head forfeit those marks silently. The third is command-word blindness: 'hence' means use the previous result, 'show that' means the answer is given and the working is the mark, and 'write down' means no working is expected. Pupils who treat all three the same way either waste minutes or leave marks on the table.

The fourth is pacing. Paper 1 and Paper 2 reward finishing, and a pupil who spends twelve minutes on a four-mark question has already lost more than that question is worth. Fixing pacing is not a teaching problem; it is a timed-practice problem, which is why the weekend block exists. A diagnostic session that marks one recent paper against these four categories tells a Jumeirah 2 family more about where the money should go than any amount of general revision.

sections.heading: The mathematical exploration, criterion by criterion
paragraphs: The exploration is worth a fifth of the grade, is marked by the class teacher against five criteria and is then externally moderated. The criteria total twenty marks and they are not evenly weighted, which matters enormously for how a pupil spends their time. Criterion E, use of mathematics, carries six of the twenty marks on its own: an exploration with a tidy structure, careful notation and no mathematics above course level cannot score well, however pleasant it is to read.

The commonest Dubai failure pattern is a topic chosen for interest rather than for mathematical depth. A survey of classmates analysed with a mean and a bar chart is a perfectly nice piece of work that cannot reach the top band of criterion E on a Higher Level course. The fix happens at topic stage, months before any writing: test the idea by asking which techniques from the syllabus it will force the student to use, and whether those techniques sit at or above the level of the course.

What a tutor may do here is bounded by IB academic-honesty rules, and the boundary is worth stating plainly because the search results around this query are not all honest about it. A tutor explains what each criterion rewards, teaches the mathematics the student has chosen to use, reads the student's own draft and says where the argument breaks. A tutor who contributes written content, supplies a topic ready-made, or edits prose into its final state has produced work that is not the candidate's, which is malpractice and puts the student's whole Diploma at risk. IB Gram does not supply exploration content, and no tutor on the platform is permitted to.

sections.heading: Arabic, Islamic Education and the timetable hours KHDA requires
paragraphs: Parents weighing up a maths slot often ask why their child's school day is already so full. Part of the answer is regulatory. Arabic, Islamic Education and social and moral studies are mandatory in all Dubai private schools whatever international curriculum the school is licensed to teach, and KHDA's published requirements had to be in place by the start of the 2025-26 academic year. Those lessons occupy real timetable space alongside the Diploma or IGCSE programme, which is one reason a Higher Level maths pupil in Jumeirah has fewer free periods than their cousin in London.

The rules are specific. KHDA calculates mandatory-subject instructional time on a forty-minute lesson unit, allows schools to vary lesson length provided the weekly total is met, and advises that no mandatory-subject lesson should run shorter than twenty-five minutes. Schools must organise separate classes for Arabs and non-Arabs in Arabic as a first language, Islamic Education and social studies, and combined classes for the two groups are prohibited because the curriculum expectations and the language of instruction differ. Teachers of Arabic and Islamic Education must hold the appropriate KHDA approval to teach those subjects.

For a tutoring plan, two consequences follow. First, the week has less slack in it than the published finishing time suggests, so a realistic plan books one defended slot rather than three hopeful ones. Second, mandatory-subject content is tightly controlled: KHDA states that using different or additional content without prior permission from the Ministry of Education is prohibited, so a family wanting Arabic support should work from the school's own materials. IB Gram is not a party to any of this and holds no approval from KHDA or the Ministry of Education; the rules are described here because they shape your child's week.

sections.heading: Counting backwards from the May session in a Jumeirah diary
paragraphs: UAE schools sit the May Diploma session, and the single most useful planning habit is to count backwards from it rather than forwards from today. The IB publishes session and results dates on its own site and revises them, so confirm every date with your child's Diploma coordinator; no tutoring website should be the authority on when an examination falls. What can be planned without a date is the order of work, and that order is remarkably stable from cohort to cohort.

Eighteen months out, at the start of DP1, the jobs are structural: route confirmed, calculator bought and learned, notation habits established, one defended weekly slot in the diary. Twelve to fourteen months out, the exploration topic should be shortlisted and tested for mathematical depth against criterion E - the single highest-value hour of coaching in the whole two years. Eight to ten months out, a first draft exists and gets one round of feedback. From four to six months out, the work becomes timed papers and an error log, and in the final six to eight weeks it becomes Paper 1 without a calculator, Paper 3 technique for Higher Level, and nothing new at all.

For a Jumeirah 2 family the practical point is that the shape of the week changes across those phases. DP1 runs comfortably on a 16:00 weekday hour. DP2 does not: it needs the 19:30 slot or a weekend block, because a full Paper 2 cannot be sat in sixty minutes after a school run. Families who plan for that in advance keep the same tutor through both phases; families who do not tend to change tutor in January of DP2, which is the worst possible month to start again.

process.title: Tell us the course route and the clock
process.description: The enquiry form asks for two things most tutoring forms do not: which maths course your child is sitting, including level and route, and what time they are realistically free on a school day. Those two answers determine which tutors can be offered at all, so getting them right saves a wasted trial lesson.

process.title: A free trial lesson in the slot you actually want
process.description: One trial lesson per student, at no charge, booked before any fee is discussed. It runs in the slot you intend to keep rather than whenever a tutor happens to be free, because a trial at 15:30 tells you nothing about how your child works at 19:30 after the drive home from Al Sufouh.

process.title: A written plan against your school's deadlines
process.description: After the trial the tutor writes a short plan: the topics to repair in order, the internal exploration deadline from your child's school, which papers get timed and when. It is a page, not a brochure, and it is the thing to hold the arrangement against in six weeks' time.

process.title: Weekly notes, and a different tutor if the match is wrong
process.description: Each session ends with a note on what was covered, what was set and what is still weak. If the match is not working, say so and a different tutor is arranged; a pupil who does not want to talk to their tutor will not ask the questions that make a session worth paying for.

process.title: A change of shape when DP2 starts
process.description: The arrangement is reviewed when the pupil moves into the second Diploma year, because the sixty-minute weekday hour that suited DP1 cannot hold a full timed paper. Most Jumeirah 2 families move to a 19:30 session or a weekend block at that point and keep the same tutor.

whyPoints.title: Matching starts with the route, not the postcode
whyPoints.description: Analysis and Approaches and Applications and Interpretation are different courses with different papers and different calculator rules. A tutor is proposed for your child only if they teach that route at that level, which is a narrower filter than 'maths tutor in Dubai' and the reason the first lesson is usually productive.

whyPoints.title: The tutor pool is not limited by driving distance
whyPoints.description: Because every UAE lesson runs online, the question is never whether a Higher Level specialist happens to live near Jumeirah Beach Road. It is whether one is free at your slot. A family in Jumeirah 2 gets the same choice of Analysis and Approaches HL teachers as a family anywhere else.

whyPoints.title: Academic honesty stated in writing, not implied
whyPoints.description: The exploration is the student's work. Tutors teach the mathematics, explain the criteria and give feedback on drafts the student has written. Nobody on this platform supplies exploration content, and the limit is written into the plan you receive after the trial so there is no ambiguity later.

whyPoints.title: Sessions built around the Jumeirah school run
whyPoints.description: Slots are offered at 16:00, 16:30, 19:30 and weekend mornings on Gulf Standard Time, and they move after iftar during Ramadan without changing tutor. Nobody is asked to be ready at a time that assumes an empty Al Wasl Road.

whyPoints.title: Market rates published, our own fee quoted after the trial

faqs.question: What time can an IB maths lesson start if my child finishes school at 3pm?
faqs.answer: Later than most families expect. A 15:00 finish in Al Sufouh or Umm Suqeim means a fifteen to twenty-five minute drive back to Jumeirah 2 at the busiest hour of the school day, so the pupil is at a desk around 15:45 at the earliest and is not ready to think until 16:15. Booking 15:30 buys a session that starts with an arrival. For families inside the Jumeirah and Al Safa ring, 16:00 works. For everyone else, 19:30 after food is the slot that holds all term.

faqs.question: Is Analysis and Approaches or Applications and Interpretation the right route for my child?
faqs.answer: Check the degree before you check the child. Engineering, mathematics, physics and many quantitative economics courses at research universities name Analysis and Approaches, frequently at Higher Level, and a pupil without it finds out in Year 13 when the prerequisite is missing. If the destination is open, the deciding question is whether your child is stronger at structured algebraic method or at reading a messy real context. Both courses are demanding. Neither is the easy one, and the choice is set by school option blocks months before the Diploma starts.

faqs.question: How many IB maths sessions a week do Jumeirah 2 families usually book?
faqs.answer: One in the first Diploma year and two in the second is the common pattern, but the pattern should follow the problem rather than the calendar. A fluency gap in algebra responds to short frequent sessions, so two half-hours can beat one full hour. An exploration needs a handful of sessions clustered around topic choice and the first draft, then nothing. Timed paper practice in the final term needs a block long enough to sit a complete paper, which rules out a sixty-minute weekday slot after the school run.

faqs.question: Can a tutor help with my child's mathematical exploration without breaking IB rules?
faqs.answer: Yes, within a clear boundary. A tutor may explain what each of the five criteria rewards, teach the mathematics your child has chosen to use, question a topic until its mathematical depth is clear, and give feedback on a draft your child has written. A tutor may not contribute written content, hand over a ready-made topic, or edit prose into a finished state. That boundary is an IB academic-honesty requirement, not a house style, and crossing it puts the whole Diploma at risk for the student rather than for the tutor.

faqs.question: My child cannot finish Paper 1 in the time allowed - what actually fixes that?
faqs.answer: Pacing is a practice problem rather than a teaching problem, so the fix is timed work with a stopwatch and a marked script, not more explanation. The usual diagnosis is that twelve minutes went on a four-mark question early in the paper. The repair is a rule the pupil applies under pressure: allocate roughly a minute and a half per mark, abandon a question that has overrun, and come back if time allows. On Analysis and Approaches add daily non-calculator arithmetic drill, because hesitation on surds and exact values is what eats the clock.

faqs.question: Do you cover both Standard Level and Higher Level IB Mathematics for Jumeirah pupils?
faqs.answer: Yes, on both routes. Standard Level on either route is two papers at forty per cent each plus the exploration at twenty. Higher Level adds Paper 3, worth a fifth of the grade on its own, and extends the syllabus substantially. Matching is done at that level of detail: a tutor is offered for Analysis and Approaches HL only if they teach Analysis and Approaches HL, because Paper 3 technique and the non-calculator demands of Paper 1 are not things a generalist picks up from the Standard Level course.

faqs.question: What do IB maths tutors charge per hour in Dubai at the moment?
faqs.answer: The Dubai market splits into bands. Budget online tutoring, often by university students, is advertised from roughly AED 45 to AED 150 an hour. Qualified subject tutors working online sit around AED 150 to AED 300, with one agency publishing IB rates from AED 200 in October 2026. Diploma and IGCSE specialists run AED 200 to AED 450 and above, and named or examiner-led tutors are advertised at AED 500 to AED 650. In-home visits add travel and are quoted at AED 180 to AED 500. Those are market figures, not IB Gram's; ours is quoted after the free trial.

faqs.question: Does a tutor come to our villa in Jumeirah 2, or is the lesson online?
faqs.answer: Online, always. IB Gram does not send anyone to a UAE address, and home visits are not a service offered anywhere in the Emirates; they exist only in our India operation. A lesson runs live and one to one over video on Gulf Standard Time, with a shared whiteboard your child writes on and the board work kept afterwards. The practical gain is specialist access: the tutor is chosen for teaching Analysis and Approaches HL rather than for living within a twenty-minute drive of Jumeirah Beach Road.

faqs.question: How do maths sessions work during Ramadan when the school day is shortened?
faqs.answer: Timings move and the arrangement does not. School hours are reduced during Ramadan and official working hours change, so the afternoon slot that worked in February is usually too early and too tiring. Most Jumeirah families shift to a post-iftar session, often around 21:00, and some drop from two sessions to one for the month and add a weekend block instead. The tutor stays the same, which matters more than the hour: continuity through a disrupted month is worth more than squeezing in the usual timetable.

faqs.question: My child moved from MYP Mathematics into Analysis and Approaches SL and is drowning - what now?
faqs.answer: This is the most common Jumeirah enquiry of the autumn term and it is usually one specific gap rather than general weakness. MYP Mathematics is marked on four criteria out of eight and rewards investigation and communication; Analysis and Approaches rewards fast, accurate algebraic manipulation and formal notation. A pupil who came through standard rather than extended MYP Mathematics has often never been drilled on surds, indices, rearrangement or exact trigonometric values. Six to eight weeks of short, frequent sessions on those mechanics usually closes it, which is a different purchase from a two-year arrangement.

faqs.question: Which calculator does my child need, and when is it not allowed?
faqs.answer: Both IB maths routes assume a graphic display calculator, and schools publish the models they permit, so buy from the school's list rather than from a general recommendation. The rule that catches pupils out is Paper 1 on Analysis and Approaches, which is sat with no calculator at Standard and Higher Level. Pupils who practise exclusively with the device in front of them lose marks on arithmetic, surds and exact values that have nothing to do with their understanding. On Applications and Interpretation the calculator is permitted throughout and the risk shifts to syntax and rounding.

faqs.question: Is it too late to start maths tutoring eight weeks before the May session?
faqs.answer: It is late for syllabus repair and perfectly timed for technique. Eight weeks is not enough to rebuild two years of calculus, but it is enough to mark three past papers against a fixed set of failure categories, close an error log, drill Paper 1 without a calculator, and teach Paper 3 technique to a Higher Level pupil who has been ignoring it. The honest version of the answer is that the gain comes from marks currently being dropped on method and pacing rather than from new content, and that should be said before any money changes hands.

faqs.question: Does a private tutor in the UAE need a permit to teach my child?
faqs.answer: Yes. Private tuition in the UAE runs on a work permit introduced by Ministerial Resolution No. 710 of 2023 and issued through the Ministry of Human Resources and Emiratisation. The permit is granted free of charge for two years, and eligible applicants include teachers in government and private schools, government and private-sector employees, unemployed residents, university students and school students aged fifteen to eighteen. Anyone tutoring without one is subject to fines and penalties under the applicable laws; no fine schedule is published, so treat any specific figure you read with suspicion. Applications go through MoHRE's own service.

faqs.question: What happens in the first lesson, and is anything payable before it?
faqs.answer: Nothing is payable before the trial lesson, which is free, one per student, and booked through the enquiry form. The lesson itself is mostly diagnostic: the tutor works through a recent piece of your child's own school work or a section of a past paper, watches how your child sets out working, and identifies which of the four standard failure categories is costing marks. You receive a short written plan afterwards naming the topics to repair in order and the school deadlines it is built around, and only then is a fee discussed.

faqs.question: Can one tutor cover IB Maths and Physics for the same student?
faqs.answer: Often, and it is worth asking for. Diploma Physics leans heavily on the same skills as Analysis and Approaches: rearranging formulae, resolving vectors, reading gradients and areas off graphs, and handling exponentials. A tutor who teaches both can treat a mechanics problem as the algebra exercise it usually is, which saves a session a fortnight. Where the physics need is specialised - an investigation write-up, or the Higher Level fields and quantum content - a second specialist is the better answer, and we will say so rather than stretch one tutor across both.

dubai/ib-maths-tutor-in-jumeirah-2.closingHeading: Book the slot that survives the school run
dubai/ib-maths-tutor-in-jumeirah-2.closingBody: The hardest part of arranging an IB maths tutor in Jumeirah 2 is not finding somebody who knows the syllabus. It is finding an hour that still exists after the drive back along Al Wasl Road, the second pick-up and the 17:30 swimming session. Tell us the course route, the level and the time your child is genuinely free, and the free trial lesson runs in that slot rather than in whatever gap a timetable happens to show. If the match is wrong you get a different tutor, and if the honest answer is that eight weeks of technique work is all you need, we will say that too.

intro.heading: The cost question, answered before anybody pitches you
paragraphs: Most Lakes parents arrive at this search after a DP1 report that says "working below potential in Mathematics" and a WhatsApp group that has produced four numbers between AED 120 and AED 650 an hour. The spread is real, and it is not random. It tracks three things: whether the tutor teaches the exact course your child sits, whether the rate carries somebody's car across Dubai, and how close the May session is. Understanding those three variables is worth more than any list of tutor photographs, because it tells you which number on your shortlist is a fair price and which is a markup on convenience.

Start with the published market. Dubai providers who show their rates put a budget or university-student tutor between AED 45 and AED 150 an hour online, a qualified subject tutor between AED 150 and AED 300, an IB or IGCSE specialist between AED 200 and AED 450, and a premium named tutor at AED 500 to AED 650. In-home visits sit higher again, roughly AED 180 to AED 500 depending on distance and subject, because an hour of teaching inside a villa in Emirates Living costs the tutor two hours of their evening. None of those figures is our price list; they are what the market says, each attributable to the provider that published it, and they are the benchmark any quote you receive should be measured against.

The expensive mistake is not paying AED 300 an hour. It is paying AED 300 an hour for the wrong hour. A student who cannot reliably differentiate a quotient does not need three hours a week; they need four targeted hours on the chain and quotient rules, then a return to school homework. A student sitting Analysis and Approaches HL who has never seen a Paper 3 investigation under timed conditions is not helped by more Paper 2 practice, however cheap. Every dirham that goes into generic revision when the loss is diagnosable is a dirham that buys nothing, and in a two-year Diploma that compounds into five figures.

The second expensive mistake is the package bought before the diagnostic. Monthly bundles advertised in Dubai run around AED 799 a month for eight online sessions and AED 1,599 to AED 1,799 a month for four two-hour in-home visits. A bundle is excellent value once the tutor is right and the plan is agreed. Bought in week one, it locks a family into a pairing nobody has tested, and the cancellation terms are where the goodwill goes. Pay for one or two diagnostic hours, read the written outcome, then commit.

The third is geography. Searching for a maths tutor within driving distance of The Lakes limits the pool to whoever happens to live between Al Barsha, The Greens and Emirates Hills and happens to be free at 17:00. IB Gram does not offer home visits in Dubai - tutors travelling to homes is a service we run only in India - so the pool for a Lakes family is every available IB Mathematics specialist on Gulf Standard Time instead of everyone inside a twenty-minute drive. That is the practical argument for online delivery here, and the rate table further down shows what it saves.

dubai/ib-maths-tutor-in-the-lakes.programmesIntro: Mathematics in an IB school is a twelve-year sequence, and a Lakes family usually meets it at three points: a PYP child who has stopped enjoying number work, an MYP student hitting the criterion-based mark scheme, and a DP student choosing between two courses that cost different amounts to support.

programmes.name: Diploma Programme Mathematics
programmes.description: Two separate courses, each at Higher and Standard Level. Analysis and Approaches is the algebra, calculus and proof route; Applications and Interpretation is the modelling, statistics and technology route. Standard Level is assessed by Paper 1 at 40%, Paper 2 at 40% and the exploration at 20%. Higher Level adds Paper 3, a two-part investigation, and the split becomes 30%, 30%, 20% and 20%.
programmes.countryNote: In Dubai the route choice is frequently made on timetable availability rather than on the degree the student wants, because not every IB school in the Emirates Living catchment can run four maths courses at once. One paid hour spent on AA versus AI before DP1 begins is the highest-value money in this entire price list.

programmes.name: Middle Years Programme Mathematics
programmes.description: Standard and Extended mathematics, assessed against four criteria each marked out of eight: knowing and understanding, investigating patterns, communicating, and applying mathematics in real-life contexts. A student can be fluent in technique and still sit on a 4, because two of the four criteria reward explanation and investigation rather than answers.
programmes.countryNote: MYP mathematics is where Lakes families most often overpay, because the obvious fix - more practice questions - targets criterion A while the marks are being lost in B and C. A tutor who has read the criteria and marks against them is worth the qualified-tutor band; a tutor who sets worksheets is not.

programmes.name: Primary Years Programme Mathematics
programmes.description: Number, pattern and function, measurement, shape and space, and data handling, taught through transdisciplinary units rather than as a separate subject. Assessment is continuous and teacher-designed, so there is no paper to revise for and no mark scheme to drill.
programmes.countryNote: Primary maths support for a Lakes child is usually a short, cheap engagement - six to eight sessions on place value, fractions or times tables - and should be priced at the lower market band. Paying a Diploma specialist rate for a Year 4 number gap is the clearest waste in the Dubai tutoring market.

programmes.name: The IGCSE to Diploma maths bridge
programmes.description: Many students in the Emirates Living catchment sit Cambridge or Pearson IGCSE mathematics at 16 and then enter the Diploma. The gap is not content coverage; it is the jump from a mark scheme that rewards method to one that rewards reasoning, plus unfamiliar notation and a far heavier algebraic load in the first term of Analysis and Approaches.
programmes.countryNote: A six-session summer bridge between Year 11 and DP1 is the single cheapest intervention on this page. Bought in August at the mid band it costs roughly what two months of panic tutoring costs in DP2, and it removes the term-one confidence collapse that generates most of the emergency calls we take from Dubai in October.

dubai/ib-maths-tutor-in-the-lakes.subjectsIntro: Maths tutoring is sold by subject name and bought by component. The list below is organised the way a quote should be written: the course, the level, and the specific thing the hours are for.

subjects.name: Mathematics: Analysis and Approaches HL
subjects.description: Proof by induction, complex numbers in Cartesian and polar form, integration by substitution and parts, differential equations, Maclaurin series. Marks go missing in the algebra of a correct method rather than in the method itself, which is why timed non-calculator practice matters more than new content.

subjects.name: Mathematics: Analysis and Approaches SL
subjects.description: Functions and transformations, sequences and series, trigonometry, differentiation and integration, probability and statistics. Paper 1 is sat without a calculator, so students who have done every exercise with technology are often a grade below their understanding.

subjects.name: Mathematics: Applications and Interpretation HL
subjects.description: Matrices, graph theory, Voronoi diagrams, non-linear regression, chi-squared and t-tests, and modelling with differential equations. The hardest marks are interpretive: stating whether a test's conditions are met, and what a coefficient means in the context given.

subjects.name: Mathematics: Applications and Interpretation SL
subjects.description: Descriptive statistics, correlation and regression, probability distributions, financial mathematics, and modelling with technology. Students lose marks by reporting output without interpreting it, and by rounding at intermediate steps instead of at the end.

subjects.name: Paper 3 investigations
subjects.description: Two extended problems, each building from a guided start to an open generalisation. This component rewards stamina and structured conjecture rather than recall, and it is the one place where a block of four or five tutored hours reliably changes a grade.

subjects.name: The Mathematics exploration
subjects.description: A twelve to twenty page individual piece of mathematics worth twenty per cent of the grade, marked against five criteria. The student chooses the topic and writes every line; a tutor's role is questions, deadlines and feedback on one draft within the school's internal policy.

subjects.name: Graphic display calculator skills
subjects.description: Regression, numerical solving, distributions, and sketching from a table of values. Calculator fluency is worth whole marks in Applications and Interpretation and in Analysis and Approaches Paper 2, and it is cheap to teach in two focused sessions.

subjects.name: MYP Extended Mathematics
subjects.description: The route into Analysis and Approaches HL, covering function families, algebraic manipulation and proof-shaped reasoning earlier than Standard mathematics does. Criterion B investigations are the usual mark loss: students find the pattern but do not justify the general rule.

subjects.name: MYP Standard Mathematics
subjects.description: Number, algebra, geometry and trigonometry, statistics and probability, assessed against four criteria out of eight each. The practical tutoring task is translating a 5 in criterion C into clearer written explanation, which is a writing problem wearing a maths hat.

subjects.name: Year 11 to DP1 maths bridge
subjects.description: Surds and indices without a calculator, function notation, the factor and remainder theorems, radian measure, and the early differentiation that DP1 assumes in week three. Six sessions over a Dubai summer, priced at the mid band, is the standard shape.

sections.heading: What an IB maths tutor in The Lakes actually costs
paragraphs: An IB maths tutor working with a family in The Lakes costs between roughly AED 150 and AED 450 an hour online in the Dubai market as of October 2026, with university-student help below that and named premium tutors above it. In-home visiting rates run higher, roughly AED 180 to AED 500, because the hour you pay for carries the travel either side of it. Those are market figures published by providers in this city, not an IB Gram price list; our own rate is quoted after a trial lesson and depends on course, level and frequency.

The reason the bands exist is specificity. A tutor who can teach GCSE maths accurately is not automatically able to teach Analysis and Approaches HL, where the content includes complex numbers, Maclaurin series and proof by induction and where Paper 1 is sat without a calculator. The pool of people who can teach that course well in any city is small, and small supply is what the specialist band is paying for. Applications and Interpretation HL has the same effect from the other direction: the statistics is genuinely university-level in places, and a tutor who has never run a chi-squared test on real data cannot teach the interpretation marks.

Read the table below as a benchmark rather than a menu. If a quote sits in the premium band, ask what in your child's situation requires it - a specific HL component, a six-week deadline - and if the answer is vague, the band is wrong for you. If a quote sits in the budget band for HL work, ask which course and which papers the tutor has taught, and ask it in those words. The gap between the honest answer and the confident answer is where most of Dubai's wasted tutoring money sits.

sections.heading: Four ways Emirates Living families overpay for maths
paragraphs: The first is buying hours instead of buying a diagnosis. A family forwards us a quote for twenty sessions and no written statement of what the student cannot currently do. Twenty sessions of unfocused support at the mid band is AED 3,000 to AED 6,000, and a two-hour diagnostic that produces a ranked list of recoverable topics costs a fraction of that and changes what the twenty sessions are for. Ask for the diagnosis in writing before you agree to the block.

The second is paying the specialist band for primary and lower-MYP work. A Year 5 child who has not secured place value, or an MYP 2 student stuck on negative indices, needs careful, patient teaching at the qualified band. The Diploma specialist whose value is Paper 3 and exploration supervision is not better at times tables; they are simply more expensive. Match the band to the problem.

The third is paying twice for the same hour through travel. An in-home tutor crossing Dubai to reach the Emirates Living gates at 17:00 has to recover that time, and it appears either as a higher rate or as a quiet surcharge nobody itemises. The fourth is the automatic renewal: a monthly bundle that made sense in November and is still running in March after the original gap closed. Diary a review date when you start, and treat the bundle as something that ends by default rather than continues by default.
None of these is a reason not to spend money on maths. They are reasons to know what each dirham is for, which is the difference between a tutoring budget and a tutoring habit.

sections.heading: Tutoring cost in context: fees, hours and a two-year plan
paragraphs: Tutoring never arrives as a standalone line in a household budget; it lands next to school fees, buses, activities and exam entries. The useful question is not whether AED 250 an hour is expensive in the abstract, but what a year of it looks like beside everything else a Lakes family already pays for a Diploma student. KHDA's announcement of 22 May 2026 that private school fees in Dubai would not rise for the 2026-27 academic year, made under the emirate's second economic incentives package, is the right anchor: for most families the fee line is flat this year, which is precisely when a maths plan can be funded deliberately rather than in a panic.

The table below converts hourly bands into the periods families actually budget in. The two-year figures are the ones worth sitting with. One session a week for the whole Diploma at the mid band is a serious commitment, and a family who sees that total up front usually makes a better decision than one discovering it a month at a time. Frequently the better plan is a lighter year in DP1 with a bridge in the summer, then a heavier final term - the same total money, spent where it converts.

Exam entry costs are worth a note of their own. A student entered through their school pays through the school; a private candidate pays the centre directly and the figure varies by centre, so no single number belongs on a page like this. Ask the school's examinations officer for the written schedule rather than relying on a tutoring site.

sections.heading: Analysis and Approaches or Applications and Interpretation: the choice that sets the bill
paragraphs: No decision in a Lakes family's Diploma affects the tutoring budget more than which maths course the student takes, and very few are made with less information. The two courses are not harder and easier versions of each other. Analysis and Approaches is algebraic: proof, calculus, trigonometric identities, and a Paper 1 sat with no calculator at all. Applications and Interpretation is interpretive and technological: modelling, statistics, graph theory, and a calculator in every paper. A student who thinks numerically but dislikes abstraction will spend fewer tutored hours on the second course than the first, and vice versa.

The university dimension matters and is often overstated by both sides. Engineering, physics, mathematics and many economics courses in the United Kingdom and the United States list Analysis and Approaches, usually at Higher Level, in their published entry requirements. Business, psychology, design and several life-science routes accept Applications and Interpretation comfortably. The honest position is that the requirement belongs to the specific university and the specific course, in writing, on that institution's own admissions page - and that a tutoring site is the wrong place to learn it.

What this page can tell you is the cost consequence. A student placed in Analysis and Approaches HL against their grain is the most expensive configuration in Dubai tutoring: they need weekly support for two years, then an intensive before the session, and the total runs well into five figures. The same student in Applications and Interpretation HL frequently needs a short block each term. One consultation before DP1 subject selection, paid at the specialist band, is the cheapest hour on this entire page.

sections.heading: The exploration: twenty per cent of the grade, and the strict limits on help
paragraphs: The Mathematics exploration is worth twenty per cent of the final grade in every DP maths course, at both levels, and it is marked against five criteria totalling twenty marks. It is also the component where parents most often ask what a tutor is allowed to do, and where the wrong answer ends a Diploma. The boundary is not subtle: the student chooses the topic, does the mathematics and writes every word. A tutor teaches technique, asks questions, holds deadlines and gives feedback on a draft within the school's own internal policy. Anybody offering to supply finished text is offering the student an academic-honesty investigation.

Within that boundary the gains are real and cheap. Most explorations lose marks in presentation and communication rather than in mathematics: undefined variables, graphs without axis labels, a twenty-eight page document where twelve focused pages would score higher, and a reflection section that summarises rather than evaluates. Those are coachable in three or four sessions, and because criteria A, B, C and D account for fourteen of the twenty marks, they are better value than another pass through the content.

Timing is the other lever. A student who starts the exploration in the spring of DP1 has time for one proper draft and one round of feedback. A student who starts in the final term is paying specialist rates for crisis management while also revising for papers. The cheapest exploration is the early one, and the table below shows where the marks sit.

sections.heading: Online versus a tutor at the gate: the Emirates Living arithmetic
paragraphs: This comparison is usually presented as a question about learning style. In The Lakes it is mostly a question about time and supply. The community is a gated villa estate off Sheikh Zayed Road with internal cluster roads, and a tutor arriving for a 17:00 session from Al Barsha or the Marina is committing ninety minutes of driving to deliver sixty minutes of teaching. That cost is in the rate whether it is itemised or not, and it also decides who is available: only tutors who live close enough and are free in that window.

IB Gram delivers to The Lakes as one-to-one live video, and the reason is not cost alone. A Lakes family wanting Analysis and Approaches HL with strong Paper 3 teaching should be choosing from every available specialist on Gulf Standard Time, not from the subset who can reach Emirates Living before dinner. Home visits are not something IB Gram sells anywhere in the UAE - that is an India-only service - and the page would be dishonest if it implied otherwise. The trade is real: a parent cannot sit in the next room and overhear the lesson. What replaces it is a written note after each session, a shared screen the student can revisit, and a recording policy agreed in advance.

For maths specifically, online delivery has a technical advantage worth naming. Mathematics is written, not spoken, and a shared whiteboard with both parties writing keeps the working visible in a way a notebook on a dining table does not. Calculator teaching is easier too: the tutor can display the same model the student is holding, which is awkward across a kitchen table and trivial on screen.

sections.heading: The May session counted backwards from a Lakes kitchen table
paragraphs: Dubai IB schools sit the May session, and the budgeting mistake families make is treating May as the deadline. It is not; it is the last in a chain of deadlines that start in the previous calendar year, and the expensive tutoring is always the tutoring bought after one of the earlier ones has passed. Working backwards from the papers rather than forwards from today changes what a given month's money should buy.

A DP2 student's internal deadlines - exploration drafts, the Extended Essay, Theory of Knowledge - are set by the school, not by the IB, and they cluster in the autumn and early winter term. That clustering is why November and December are the months when Lakes families most often double their tutoring spend: three internal deadlines and a mock series land inside six weeks. A plan that funds exploration coaching in DP1's summer term removes most of that collision for the price of four sessions.

We do not publish IB session or results dates on these pages. The IB's own site is the only acceptable source for them and it cannot be checked reliably by an automated process, so a specific date here would be a guess dressed up as a fact. Ask your child's Diploma coordinator for the school's dated internal calendar and the official session timetable, and build the plan on that document. Cambridge and Pearson publish their International GCSE timetables openly, which is why those dates appear on our IGCSE pages and IB dates do not.

Nine months out: exploration topic agreed and the first mathematics attempted
Six months out: mock series marked against published criteria, weak topics ranked
Three months out: timed papers under exam conditions, one per fortnight minimum
Six weeks out: nothing new taught; recoverable marks only, ranked by yield

sections.heading: Paying a maths tutor legally in Dubai, and what to ask for
paragraphs: Private tutoring in the UAE is permitted and regulated, which is useful information when you are comparing quotes. Individuals giving private lessons need a private tuition work permit from the Ministry of Human Resources and Emiratisation, introduced by Ministerial Resolution No. 710 of 2023. The permit is granted free of charge for two years, and the eligible categories are broad: teachers registered in government or private schools, government and private-sector employees, unemployed residents, university students, and school students aged fifteen to eighteen. MoHRE's own service page, 'Issuance of a New Work Permit - Private Tutor Licensing', lists a two working-day completion time and is applied for through the MoHRE app, website and e-services system.

Two consequences for a Lakes family. First, a tutor who tells you no permit exists or that it is optional is wrong: individuals offering private tutoring without a permit from MoHRE are subject to fines and penalties under the applicable laws, and no fine schedule is published, so treat any specific figure you are quoted as unverified. Second, the code of conduct attached to the permit, and Abu Dhabi's professional-ethics rules for school staff, bar a teacher from tutoring students enrolled at their own school. If the plan under discussion is your child's own classroom teacher, privately, that is the arrangement to decline.

A tutoring business with premises and staff in Dubai is a different legal animal again: it needs a KHDA Educational Services Permit for a training institute. IB Gram is an online matching platform, not a licensed Dubai training institute, and holds no KHDA, ADEK, SPEA, MoE, IB or Cambridge accreditation. Any page telling you its tutors are regulator-approved is telling you something that cannot be true of an online platform.

sections.heading: What a trial lesson should tell you before you spend anything
paragraphs: The first lesson is a diagnostic, and it should be treated as the cheapest piece of market research available. IB Gram offers one trial lesson at no charge - thirty minutes, one per family, no card details taken and nothing to cancel - and the point is not to be charmed. The point is to find out whether this tutor can name, by the end of the session, the two or three specific things standing between your child and the next grade. A tutor who finishes a trial with 'we will build confidence' has not done the job. A tutor who finishes with 'she can integrate but she cannot choose a substitution, and her Paper 1 algebra breaks under time pressure' has.

Ask three questions in the trial. Which papers have you taught for this exact course, and in which years? What is the first topic you would work on with my child, and why that one? What will I receive in writing after each session? The answers tell you whether you are buying a specialist or a generalist, and whether the band you are being quoted matches what you are getting.

Then decide on a short commitment. Four sessions is enough to see whether the diagnosis was right and whether the student turns up willingly. If it works, extend; if it does not, change tutor without having prepaid a term. A family in The Lakes who spends two trial lessons and four paid sessions choosing carefully will usually spend less across a Diploma than one who commits to twenty sessions in October on a recommendation from a neighbour.

process.description: The last report, a marked mock paper, or a photograph of a piece of homework that went wrong. A marked paper is worth more than any description of the problem, because it shows where the method held and where the algebra collapsed.

faqs.question: How much should an IB maths tutor for a family in The Lakes cost per hour in 2026?
faqs.answer: Published Dubai rates put a qualified online maths tutor at AED 150-300 an hour and an IB specialist at AED 200-450 or more; university-student help starts around AED 45-65 and named premium tutors reach AED 650. In-home visiting rates run roughly AED 180-500 because travel is inside the hour. Those are market figures from providers in this city as of October 2026, not an IB Gram price list. Our rate is quoted after the trial lesson and depends on the course, the level and how often you want sessions. Judge any quote by asking what in your child's situation justifies the band.

faqs.question: Is an online maths tutor genuinely cheaper than a home tutor for Emirates Living?
faqs.answer: On published market bands, yes, and the gap is mostly travel rather than teaching quality. Online one-to-one in Dubai runs AED 150-450 an hour; in-home one-to-one runs AED 180-500 for the same level of tutor, because a visit to a gated villa community costs the tutor roughly ninety minutes to deliver sixty. The second difference is supply: online you choose from every specialist on Gulf Standard Time rather than those who can reach The Lakes by 17:00. IB Gram does not offer home visits in the UAE, so for a Lakes family the comparison is between our online delivery and a local in-home provider.

faqs.question: Why do IB maths rates sit above IGCSE maths rates in the Dubai market?
faqs.answer: Supply. Unitors publishes IGCSE tutoring from AED 150 an hour and IB from AED 200, and the pattern holds across providers. The content is the reason: Analysis and Approaches HL includes proof by induction, complex numbers and Maclaurin series, Paper 1 is sat with no calculator, and Paper 3 is an open investigation. Far fewer tutors can teach that reliably than can teach IGCSE Extended maths, and scarcity sets the band. If a quote prices HL Diploma work at IGCSE rates, ask which papers the tutor has taught and in which years before taking it as good value.

faqs.question: How many sessions a week does an Analysis and Approaches HL student actually need?
faqs.answer: One a week through DP1 is the usual shape, rising to two in the final term if the mock series shows several unrecovered topics. That maps onto Bestimate's Dubai monthly estimates of AED 600-1,200 for a weekly hour and AED 1,000-2,000 or more for specialist exam-year support. More than two is rarely productive, because the student also needs time to attempt problems alone. The exception is a short component block, four to six sessions on Paper 3 or on non-calculator algebra, run at higher intensity over a fortnight and then stopped.

faqs.question: Should we buy a package of ten or twenty sessions up front?
faqs.answer: Not before a diagnostic. Bundles advertised in Dubai run around AED 799 a month for eight online sessions and AED 1,599-1,799 for four two-hour in-home visits, and they are good value once the tutor is right and the plan is agreed. Bought in week one they commit you to a pairing nobody has tested, and the cancellation terms are where families lose money. Take the trial, agree a block of four to six sessions with a stated end date, and only then consider a bundle. Diary a review date on the first invoice so the arrangement ends by default rather than continuing by default.

faqs.question: Is the rate in The Lakes quoted per hour or per lesson, and does it include VAT?
faqs.answer: Ask both questions in writing before the first paid session, of us or of anybody else. A rate quoted per hour against a ninety-minute lesson is a different number from a rate quoted per session, and the two are mixed up constantly in this market. On tax, the only thing a tutoring page should state is whether its own quoted figure is inclusive; the VAT treatment of tuition in the UAE is a matter for the Federal Tax Authority and not something to take from a tutoring site. Our quotes state the session length, the figure and whether tax is included.

faqs.question: Do we keep paying through Dubai school holidays and the summer break?
faqs.answer: Only if you want sessions. Billing per session rather than per term means a pause costs nothing, and for most students a genuine break is more useful than continuity for its own sake. The exception is the summer between Year 11 and DP1, where six sessions on surds, indices, function notation and early differentiation is the cheapest intervention available - it prevents the term-one collapse that generates most of the emergency calls we take from Dubai families in October. Short summer work before a transition year is worth funding; holiday cover for its own sake usually is not.

faqs.question: Can one tutor cover both Maths AA and Physics to save money?
faqs.answer: Sometimes, and it is worth asking. Analysis and Approaches and Diploma Physics overlap in calculus, vectors and graph interpretation, and a tutor strong in both can cut scheduling and sometimes the effective rate. The caution is depth: a physics teacher who is comfortable with SL maths is not automatically able to teach Paper 3 at Higher Level, and a maths specialist may not know the current physics assessment structure. Ask which of the two they have taught to examination and in which years. If the answer is one of them, use two tutors for the component that matters most.

faqs.question: Is the Mathematics exploration worth paying a specialist to support?
faqs.answer: For most students, yes, and in a small number of sessions. The exploration is twenty per cent of the final grade, and fourteen of its twenty marks sit in presentation, communication, personal engagement and reflection rather than in the mathematics itself. Those are coachable: an undefined variable, an unlabelled graph, a reflection that summarises instead of evaluating. Three or four sessions in the spring of DP1 typically do more than the same hours spent on content. The limits are strict - the student chooses the topic, does the mathematics and writes every line, and a tutor gives feedback on one draft within the school's policy.

faqs.question: Does a private maths tutor working with Dubai families need a MoHRE permit?
faqs.answer: Yes. Individuals giving private lessons in the UAE need a private tuition work permit from the Ministry of Human Resources and Emiratisation, introduced by Ministerial Resolution No. 710 of 2023. It is granted free of charge for two years and covers registered school teachers, government and private-sector employees, unemployed residents, university students and school students aged fifteen to eighteen. Applications go through the MoHRE app, website or e-services system, and MoHRE's service page lists a two working-day completion. Anyone tutoring without one is subject to fines and penalties under the applicable laws; no fine schedule is published, so treat quoted amounts as unverified.

faqs.question: What is the cheapest honest route from a 4 to a 5 in Applications and Interpretation SL?
faqs.answer: A diagnostic, a ranked list, and four to six sessions on the top two items. At Standard Level in this course the recurring losses are predictable: reporting calculator output without interpreting it, rounding at intermediate steps, missing the conditions for a chi-squared test, and losing marks on financial mathematics through unit errors. Those are fixable in a short block rather than a term-long engagement. Add one session on calculator fluency, which is worth whole marks in both papers. The expensive route is open-ended weekly support that never names a target; the cheap route starts with a written diagnosis.

faqs.question: Do tutoring rates in Dubai rise as the May session gets closer?
faqs.answer: Effective prices do, for two reasons. Specialist availability thins through the final term, so the tutors still free are often the ones at the higher bands, and families booking in March usually want two sessions a week rather than one. Bestimate's monthly estimates reflect that pattern, with specialist exam-year support at AED 1,000-2,000 or more a month against AED 600-1,200 for a weekly hour earlier in the year. The practical answer is to book the specialist you want in the autumn at the frequency you can sustain, rather than paying for intensity in April because nothing was done in November.

faqs.question: What should I send a tutoring provider to get an accurate quote rather than a range?
faqs.answer: Five things: the exact course and level, the school and year group, the most recent report with its grade or criteria scores, one marked piece of work that went badly, and the days and times that genuinely work around your school run. A marked paper is the most valuable of these, because it shows whether marks are lost in method, in algebra or under time pressure. With those five, a provider can name a band and a first target. Without them, any figure quoted is a guess, and guesses in this market drift upwards.

faqs.question: What happens to our money if the first tutor turns out to be the wrong match?
faqs.answer: With per-session billing, nothing beyond the sessions already taught. That is the practical reason to avoid prepaying a term: a mismatch in week two should cost you two sessions, not twenty. Tell us what did not work - pace, explanation style, the time slot, the subject depth - and we propose a different tutor from the same course specialism. Say it early rather than politely waiting. A student who has quietly disengaged for a month is a more expensive problem to solve than a swap made after the second lesson.

faqs.question: Is a small group class in The Lakes better value than one-to-one maths tutoring?
faqs.answer: It depends entirely on whether everyone in the group shares the same gap. Group rates in Dubai run roughly AED 60-200 an hour per student against AED 150-450 for one-to-one, so the saving is real. It evaporates when the group covers a topic your child already has and skips the one they do not, which is the common outcome with Diploma maths because the losses are individual. Groups work for broad revision and for younger students building fluency. For a diagnosed topic gap at Higher Level, four one-to-one sessions usually beat twelve group hours.

dubai/ib-maths-tutor-in-the-lakes.closingHeading: Start with one hour that tells you what the next ten are for
dubai/ib-maths-tutor-in-the-lakes.closingBody: If you are weighing quotes for an IB maths tutor in The Lakes, the useful next step is not another recommendation from the community group. It is thirty minutes with a tutor who teaches your child's exact course, followed by a written note naming the two or three specific gaps and what to do about them. That costs nothing, takes one per family, and needs no card details. From there you can price a block of four to six sessions honestly, against the market bands on this page, and decide with numbers rather than hope. Lessons run one-to-one over live video on Gulf Standard Time, around the Emirates Living school run.

dubai/ib-myp-arabic-home-tutor.tutorsIntro: The tutors listed here teach Arabic and measure it. Each one runs the same opening diagnostic, logs a timed reading check, and bands written work against the phase descriptors so a family can see movement without being able to read the script themselves.

intro.heading: You do not need to read Arabic to tell whether Arabic tutoring is working
paragraphs: This is the particular difficulty of paying for Arabic in Dubai. In maths a parent can look at a page and see whether the answers are right. In Arabic the page is unreadable to most of the people paying for it, which leaves a family relying entirely on a tutor's cheerful assurance and a report card that arrives months later. The result is that Arabic support gets renewed on faith and cancelled on frustration, often without either decision being informed.

The way out is to insist on measurements that do not require you to understand the language. Reading speed on the same passage, once with short vowels printed and once without, is a number. The count of letters confused in initial, medial and final position is a number. Words per minute on unseen vowelled text is a number. Two recordings of the same speaking prompt a fortnight apart is a comparison any parent can hear. None of it depends on knowing a word of Arabic.

Those measurements also happen to be diagnostic rather than decorative. A Dubai student who reads fluently with harakat and collapses without them does not need more vocabulary; they need a decoding block. A student whose medial letter forms are weak is guessing from context, which works until the text gets harder. A student using one verb pattern in every sentence has a range problem, not an effort problem. The right next step falls out of the measurement instead of being guessed at.

The home-tutor question deserves a plain answer. People do drive across Dubai to teach Arabic in villas, the market charges between AED 180 and 500 an hour for it according to Bestimate's 2026 rate table and independent listings, and monthly packages of AED 1,599 to 1,799 for four two-hour visits are widely advertised. IB Gram does not do it: in-home teaching is offered only in India. Dubai lessons are one-to-one over live video on Gulf Standard Time.

For Arabic script work specifically, that is less of a compromise than it sounds and in one respect it is an improvement. A tutor writing on a shared screen shows stroke order the right way up, rather than upside down across a dining table. Written work photographed and annotated comes back inside two days rather than at the next visit. And the timed checks get logged in a file rather than remembered, which is the whole point of measuring anything. The rest of this page is the detail behind those claims: what the opening diagnostic tests and why each task is there, the sequence that unvowelled reading follows and roughly how long each stage takes, what the in-home alternative in Dubai actually costs and contains, and the four documents a family should be holding by the end of a term. It also says, in plain terms, what the stopping condition is, because a provider who cannot name one is selling a subscription rather than a solution.

dubai/ib-myp-arabic-home-tutor.programmesIntro: Arabic is on the timetable from the earliest years in any Dubai private school, and what counts as evidence of progress changes as the reporting changes. Here is what is measurable at each stage, and what the school paperwork will and will not tell you.

programmes.name: Middle Years Programme
programmes.description: Arabic as an additional language is marked on four criteria, each on a band out of eight, against descriptors written for the student's phase. That is unusually helpful for evidence, because a band is a comparable number rather than a percentage of a particular test. Two scripts banded the same way three months apart is the cleanest proof of progress available in this subject.
programmes.countryNote: Dubai MYP reports often show the converted 1 to 7 grade without the four criterion bands behind it. Ask the subject teacher directly for the band numbers rather than going through the office; most schools release them on request, and without them you cannot tell whether a flat grade hides a reading problem or a writing one.

programmes.name: Primary Years Programme
programmes.description: Reporting is narrative, with no bands and nothing numerical to compare year on year. Evidence at this stage is behavioural and physical: can the child write the letters unprompted, do they recognise their own name in script, can they read a vowelled line aloud. Those are all observable at a kitchen table in two minutes.
programmes.countryNote: Dubai families are often surprised when MYP 1 placement puts a child who seemed comfortable in primary Arabic into an early phase. That is almost always a reading and writing measurement meeting a child whose Arabic was built from listening and speaking, which is the normal order, and it is worth saying so out loud to an eleven-year-old who has just been told they are a beginner.

programmes.name: Diploma Programme
programmes.description: Arabic continues as Language B, as ab initio for a genuine beginner, or as Language A where a school offers it. Evidence becomes mock components and marked papers, so the feedback loop tightens considerably and the consequences of a weak reading foundation become visible quickly rather than slowly.
programmes.countryNote: Predicted grades issued by Dubai schools go to universities, which makes the quality of the evidence behind them a practical matter rather than an academic one. Families who kept banded Arabic work through the MYP arrive able to read a mock script and ask a specific question about it, instead of only seeing the number written on the front page.

dubai/ib-myp-arabic-home-tutor.subjectsIntro: Arabic bookings on this page are made against a measurement rather than against a topic list. Each item below is something that can be tested at the start, worked on, and tested the same way again, which is what makes progress arguable rather than a matter of opinion.

subjects.name: Decoding speed on unvowelled text
subjects.description: The headline measurement for most non-Arab students in Dubai. The same passage read with and without harakat, timed, and compared month to month. A narrowing gap between the two times is the clearest single indicator that reading is genuinely developing.

subjects.name: Harakat awareness and when vowels are dropped
subjects.description: Understanding what short vowels do, where they sit, and why school texts stop printing them. Measured by reading a sentence vowelled, then unvowelled, then predicting the vowels on an unseen word built from a familiar pattern.

subjects.name: Letter-form and joining accuracy
subjects.description: Letters in initial, medial and final position, plus which letters never join forwards. Measured by a twelve-letter check with no context cues. Weak medial forms are the most common hidden fault and the cheapest one to repair.

subjects.name: Verb pattern recognition
subjects.description: Root and pattern awareness, so an unseen word becomes decodable rather than unknown. Measured by reading cold words built on taught patterns. This is the measurement that separates a student who is reading from one who is recalling.

subjects.name: Listening against a transcript
subjects.description: Short clips answered under time, then the transcript revealed. The useful output is a log of which question types keep failing, since numbers, negatives and speaker attitude fail for different reasons and need different work.

subjects.name: Recorded oral on a repeated prompt
subjects.description: The same speaking prompt revisited every fortnight, recorded with written consent. Evidence a parent can assess directly: fewer silences, longer turns, recovery after an error rather than a full stop. No Arabic needed to hear it.

subjects.name: Weekly banded written task
subjects.description: One piece of writing a week, banded against the phase descriptor, rewritten once by the student, then compared. The pair of scripts with bands on them is the document that makes a conversation with a subject teacher productive.

subjects.name: Islamic Education terminology in Arabic
subjects.description: Vocabulary and phrasing support working from the school's own scheme, since KHDA guidance prohibits different or additional content for the mandatory subjects without prior Ministry of Education permission. Measured on the school's own task wording.

subjects.name: One-page record for the Arabic teacher
subjects.description: The measurements and banded scripts written up on a single page a teacher can read in two minutes. It is what makes a request for a phase review or a change of set a documented conversation instead of a parental impression.

dubai/ib-myp-arabic-home-tutor.regionsIntro: Where a family lives in Dubai changes the realistic start time and very little else, because every lesson is over video. These are the communities Arabic bookings come from most often, with the timing or demand pattern that actually holds in each.

regions.name: Oud Metha and Al Karama
regions.note: Dense, central and close to several long-established schools, so arrival times are early and a 4pm slot is genuinely workable. Short script-drilling sessions suit that window better than a full hour does.

regions.name: Al Nahda and Al Twar
regions.note: High Arabic exposure in daily life, which usually means strong listening and speaking alongside slow unvowelled reading. The decoding block is the most frequent booking from these communities by a wide margin.

regions.name: Al Mizhar and Mirdif Hills
regions.note: Villa areas with awkward evening drives to the school clusters on the other side of the city. Slots after 5.30pm hold reliably, and the written tasks tend to get done at the weekend.

regions.name: Dubai Sports City
regions.note: Mixed school destinations and long bus runs, so sessions start late. Families here often prefer two thirty-minute slots because a single long evening session rarely survives a full term intact.

regions.name: Jumeirah Golf Estates
regions.note: Long runs in both directions and heavy weekend activity schedules. The reliable pattern is a fixed weekday evening slot with reading checks logged monthly rather than squeezed in whenever there is time.

regions.name: Al Barsha Heights and Tecom
regions.note: Apartment living, so the constraint is a quiet room rather than a commute. Headphones handle most of it, and short sessions work better than long ones in a flat with younger siblings.

regions.note: A newer community with children spread across several school systems, which produces unusually mixed Arabic starting points. The opening diagnostic matters more here than anywhere, because prior provision varies so widely.

schoolClusters.city: Emirates Hills, Al Wasl and the Al Khail corridor
schoolClusters.note: Students we support across these communities are predominantly non-Arab, sitting in the middle phases with speaking ahead of reading. Requests here are almost always for the decoding block first and written work second, which is the right order rather than the obvious one.

schoolClusters.city: The southern communities, Mirdif and Festival City
schoolClusters.note: Smaller Arabic cohorts and more mixed-phase classes, so a class rarely pitches at any one student's level and one-to-one measurement earns its keep. A higher proportion of requests from this cluster involve Islamic Education terminology alongside Arabic itself.

sections.heading: What families searching for an IB MYP Arabic home tutor in Dubai are really asking
paragraphs: Three different needs arrive under the same phrase. A few families genuinely require somebody in the room, usually because a younger child makes any other arrangement impossible or because a teenager will not sit down otherwise. Some want the reassurance of watching the hour happen. Most, though, are asking for private one-to-one Arabic outside a classroom and have never thought about the delivery format at all, because the word home is simply how the search gets typed.

What all three groups share is the underlying worry, and it is not about location. It is that Arabic feels unverifiable. A family can pay for eighteen months of lessons, hear that things are going well, and then read a report with a 4 on it. That experience is common enough in Dubai that parents arrive already slightly braced for it, which is why the question worth answering first is how progress will be shown rather than where the lesson happens.

IB Gram does not sell in-home visits anywhere in the UAE; it is a service offered only in India. Dubai lessons are one-to-one over live video on Gulf Standard Time. The reason to accept that trade in this subject is partly supply, since teachers who can band Arabic script against a phase descriptor are thin on the ground in any single community, and partly that the measurements this page is built around are easier to capture, log and compare on a screen than on a dining table.

sections.heading: The opening Arabic diagnostic and what each task reveals
paragraphs: The first session is six short tasks rather than a lesson, and it takes about forty minutes with a break. None of the tasks is designed to be passed. They exist to separate problems that look identical from the outside: a student who cannot read and a student who can only read with vowels printed look the same to a parent and need completely different work for completely different lengths of time.

The output is a short written note with numbers in it. Which letters were confused and in which position. The time taken on the vowelled sentence against the unvowelled one. Which of three listening questions failed and why. How many distinct verb patterns appeared in four self-written sentences. Those numbers are the baseline, and they are deliberately cheap to repeat, because a measurement nobody can afford to take twice is not a measurement.

Parents sometimes ask whether this is worth an hour that could have been teaching. It is, for the same reason a physiotherapist does not start with exercises. The single most expensive error in Arabic support is a term spent on vocabulary and conversation for a student whose actual problem is that they are decoding every word letter by letter. That diagnosis takes forty minutes to make and saves a term, and the note stays useful for a year. Teaching starts in the second session and does not stop again, and the diagnostic tasks themselves double as teaching once the numbers have been taken.
