sections.heading: Reading unvowelled text: the measurable thing almost nobody measures
paragraphs: Arabic is printed with short vowels in beginner material and without them in nearly everything else, including most of what a Dubai MYP student will be assessed on from the middle phases upwards. That transition is the single biggest cliff in the subject, and it arrives quietly. A student who was doing well suddenly is not, their confidence drops, and the explanation offered is usually that the work got harder. It did not get harder; it got unvowelled.

The reason this matters for anybody paying for lessons is that the cliff is measurable to the second. Give a student a phase-level passage with harakat and time them. Give them the equivalent passage without and time them again. The ratio between the two is the number that matters, and it moves in a predictable sequence as the underlying skills come in. A family can watch that ratio close over a term without reading a single Arabic word.

The milestones below are the sequence that ratio follows, with how each one is tested and roughly how long it takes. Treat the week ranges as planning figures for an average middle-phase student having two short sessions a week, not as promises; a student with secure letter forms moves through the early stages quickly, and one who is still guessing medial letters will not move at all until that is fixed. Order matters more than hours, and skipping a stage because it looks elementary is the most reliable way to spend a term standing still.

sections.heading: Letter forms, joining and the errors that cost marks silently
paragraphs: Handwriting is the part of Arabic that parents dismiss and markers do not. Arabic letters change shape according to position, six of them never join to what follows, and short vowels sit above or below the line rather than on it. A student who has absorbed those rules roughly rather than precisely produces writing that is readable to a sympathetic teacher and penalised by a careful one, and nobody ever tells them that is what is happening.

The errors are specific and repeatable, which makes them cheap to fix. Joining a letter that does not join forwards. Writing the medial form where the initial belongs. Spacing words so inconsistently that a reader cannot tell where one ends. Placing harakat ambiguously between two letters. Four short sessions of deliberate form work clears most of this, and the gain shows up in every written task afterwards rather than in the one being worked on.

The measurement here is a twelve-letter check with no surrounding words, because context lets a student guess and a guess is not knowledge. Repeat it fortnightly until all twelve are clean in all three positions. It takes three minutes and it is the only Arabic measurement a parent can administer themselves once a tutor has written out what the twelve letters are and what a correct answer looks like in each position. Three minutes a fortnight at a kitchen table, with the answer sheet in front of you, is the cheapest piece of quality control available in this subject.

sections.heading: Why a screen is not a handicap for Arabic script work
paragraphs: The instinctive objection to teaching script over video is that writing is physical and a screen is not. In practice the comparison runs the other way on most of the specifics. When a tutor demonstrates a letter on a shared screen, the student sees the strokes in the correct orientation; across a table they are watching an upside-down hand. Stroke order, which is what makes letter forms stick, is visible rather than inferred, and it can be replayed.

Written work still happens on paper, because handwriting is the skill being built. The student writes, photographs the page, and the tutor annotates the image in a shared file. That annotation comes back inside two days instead of waiting for the next visit, which matters because a correction read while the attempt is still fresh teaches a rule, whereas the same correction a fortnight later reads as a verdict on something already forgotten.

Right-to-left typing is worth sorting out early for a different reason. Some Dubai schools accept typed submissions for written tasks and others do not, and a student who has never set up an Arabic keyboard will lose time at exactly the wrong moment. Fifteen minutes in an early session on keyboard layout, direction handling and where the harakat keys live removes a recurring source of frustration that has nothing to do with language ability. The same fifteen minutes covers how to handle a document that mixes Arabic with English or numerals, which is where most students lose their place entirely.

sections.heading: What an in-home Arabic hour in Dubai contains, and what it costs
paragraphs: The in-home option is a real market with real strengths, and a comparison is more useful than an argument. Bestimate's Dubai 2026 rate table puts in-home one-to-one at AED 180 to 350 an hour, independent listings reach AED 500, and monthly packages of AED 1,599 to 1,799 for four two-hour visits circulate widely. Travel sits inside those figures, which is why the sessions are long: nobody drives across Dubai for thirty minutes.

Session length is where the economics and the teaching disagree. Script drilling stops paying back after about forty minutes because it is a concentration task, so a two-hour in-home visit spends most of its time on something other than the thing that needed fixing. The useful pattern for decoding is short and frequent, which the in-home model cannot deliver at a sensible price however good the individual teacher happens to be.

Where in-home genuinely wins is presence, and that is not a small thing for some students. If a child will not engage without somebody physically there, that fact outranks everything in this table, and the honest advice is to buy locally and accept the session shape that comes with it. For everybody else the trade is a shorter, more frequent, measured session with a tutor chosen for the phase rather than for the postcode. It is also worth separating the two decisions. Presence and measurement are not a package: a family can buy an in-home hour locally for a subject where one long weekly session genuinely suits the work, and keep Arabic script and reading on a screen where the sessions can be short, frequent and logged.

sections.heading: Proof over a term: four things to keep in one folder
paragraphs: By the end of a term a family paying for Arabic should hold four kinds of document, and they should be in one place rather than scattered through a messaging app. The first is the opening diagnostic note with its numbers. The second is the sequence of timed reading checks, dated. The third is the stack of banded written tasks with the criterion letter on each. The fourth is two or three oral recordings on the same prompt, if consent was given.

Those four together answer every question a parent can reasonably have. Did the reading gap narrow? The checks say so or they do not. Did the writing band move? The scripts are dated and banded. Is the student more fluent? Listen to the first recording and the last one. Was the original diagnosis right? Compare the note from week one with what actually turned out to be the problem, which is a question tutors should be willing to answer honestly.

The folder has a second use that families discover later. When something needs to be raised with the school, whether a phase review, a change of set or simply a disagreement about a grade, a one-page summary drawn from dated evidence changes the tone of the conversation completely. Teachers respond to evidence because it is what they work in. An impression, however strongly felt, gives a subject teacher nothing to act on. Keep the folder even after the lessons end; the next teacher inherits none of it.

sections.heading: What the school's own Arabic scheme covers, and what it does not
paragraphs: Before buying hours, find out what the school already provides and how it is arranged. KHDA calculates mandatory-subject instructional time from a 40-minute lesson unit, permits schools to vary lesson length provided the weekly total is met, and advises that no mandatory subject lesson runs shorter than 25 minutes. A school delivering its full weekly allocation well presents a top-up problem. One delivering it thinly presents a much larger and more expensive one.

There is also a constraint on material that catches providers out. KHDA guidance states that for the mandatory subjects the use of any different or additional content, without prior permission from the Ministry of Education, is strictly prohibited. Tutoring for mandatory Arabic therefore works from the school's own scheme and the student's own tasks. Anybody selling their own Arabic curriculum for this purpose is selling something a Dubai school cannot use as a substitute.

What a school scheme reliably does not cover is individual diagnosis. A class of twenty-five working through a shared unit cannot stop to time one student's unvowelled reading or repair one student's medial letter forms, and no teacher should be expected to. That gap is exactly where paid one-to-one time earns its place, which is also why it should be spent on measured, specific work rather than on going over the week's lesson again more slowly. Repeating a class lesson at half speed is the most common and least useful way to fill a paid hour.

sections.heading: When to stop paying for Arabic support, and how you would know
paragraphs: Good providers should be able to tell you when to stop, and most never do. For a decoding block the stopping point is concrete: the gap between vowelled and unvowelled reading times has closed to the point where unfamiliar words are being worked out rather than recognised, letter forms are clean in all three positions, and the student reads unseen phase-level text without stalling. At that point the expensive problem is solved and the remaining work is ordinary practice.

For written work the signal is different. When banded scripts sit consistently in the upper bands of the current phase across two or three different text types, more tutoring in the same phase adds very little. The useful move is either a phase conversation with the school or a pause, and a pause is a legitimate outcome. Arabic in a Dubai school continues for years, and nobody should pay for one-to-one support continuously across all of them.

The failure mode to watch for is a plan that never ends because nothing is measured. An open-ended weekly hour with warm feedback and no numbers will run for as long as a family keeps paying, and both sides will feel vaguely that it is working. Measurements make stopping possible, which is the strongest argument for insisting on them, and it is the reason a provider with nothing to measure will quietly resist the suggestion. Ask for the stopping condition in the first conversation and write down the answer.

process.title: Send the report and a photo of recent Arabic writing
process.description: A phone photograph of a page of your child's Arabic writing tells an experienced teacher more than a long conversation does. Add the latest report, with the criterion bands if the school prints them. That pair lets the first session start with tasks rather than with introductions.

process.title: Free diagnostic session, six tasks and a written note
process.description: About forty minutes of short tasks covering letter forms, vowelled and unvowelled reading, dictation, listening, speaking and free writing. You keep the written note with its numbers regardless of what you decide afterwards. No card is taken and nothing begins automatically.

process.title: Pick the block, not the subject
process.description: The note names one target, usually decoding, handwriting or written range. We agree the block length, the session pattern, and the date the measurement gets repeated. Dubai slots sit between 4pm and 7pm on weekdays, with weekend mornings available for written work.

process.title: Repeat the same measurement, then decide
process.description: At the midpoint and end of the block the opening tasks are run again, identically, and the numbers are put side by side. Buy another block, change the target, change the tutor, or stop. All four are real options and we will tell you which one we would choose.

whyPoints.title: Measurements a parent can read
whyPoints.description: Timed reading, letter-form counts and dated bands do not require you to understand Arabic. That is deliberate. A family paying for a language they cannot read deserves evidence that does not depend on trusting a description of it.

whyPoints.title: The same test twice, not a different one
whyPoints.description: Progress claims only mean something when the measurement is identical on both occasions. We repeat the opening tasks exactly rather than running an easier version later, which is how a flattering number gets produced without anything having changed.

whyPoints.title: Order before effort
whyPoints.description: Letter forms, then vowelled fluency, then unvowelled recognition, then pattern reading. Working on comprehension while a student is still decoding letter by letter wastes a term. The diagnostic exists to establish where in that order a student actually sits.

whyPoints.title: Short sessions where short sessions work
whyPoints.description: Script and oral work tire quickly, so thirty to forty-five minutes twice a week beats a long single session. That shape is awkward for anybody driving across Dubai and straightforward over video, which is a practical reason for the format rather than a philosophical one.

whyPoints.title: A stated point at which to stop
whyPoints.description: Every block has an end condition written down at the start. When it is met we say so. Open-ended Arabic support with warm feedback and no numbers can run for years, and a family should not have to be the one to call time on it.

faqs.question: Does IB Gram offer in-home Arabic lessons in Dubai?
faqs.answer: No. In-home teaching is a service offered only in India, and every UAE lesson is one-to-one over live video on Gulf Standard Time. The Dubai in-home market exists independently and charges roughly AED 180 to 500 an hour with travel inside the figure, according to Bestimate's 2026 rate table and independent listings. For Arabic specifically the online format is not a compromise on script work: stroke order faces the right way on a shared screen, and annotated writing comes back in two days rather than at the next visit.

faqs.question: How is Arabic reading progress actually measured?
faqs.answer: By timing the same passage twice, once printed with short vowels and once without, and tracking the ratio between the two times month by month. Alongside that, a twelve-letter check across initial, medial and final positions counts how many forms are still being guessed. Both numbers are readable by a parent who does not read Arabic, both take minutes to repeat, and both move in a predictable order as the underlying skills arrive. Anything vaguer than that cannot be compared with last month, which is the entire point of measuring.

faqs.question: What does the first Arabic session test?
faqs.answer: Six short tasks across about forty minutes: twelve letters read in all three positions, a sentence read vowelled and then unvowelled, five words from dictation, three questions on a short audio clip, two minutes of unprepared speaking, and four sentences written with no time limit. Nothing is meant to be passed. The point is to separate problems that look identical from outside, because a student who cannot read and a student who can only read with vowels printed need entirely different work for different lengths of time.

faqs.question: Why can my child speak Arabic but not read it?
faqs.answer: Because those are different skills built from different input, and Dubai supplies a great deal of one and very little of the other. Spoken exposure comes from daily life, usually in Gulf, Levantine or Egyptian dialect. Reading requires letter forms, short vowels and eventually the ability to decode unvowelled text in Modern Standard Arabic, which almost nobody absorbs incidentally. The gap is normal rather than a sign of inattention, and it is the single most fixable thing in the subject once it has been measured properly.

faqs.question: How long does it take to read unvowelled Arabic confidently?
faqs.answer: For a middle-phase student having two short sessions a week, letter forms usually come clean in two to four weeks, vowelled fluency in three to five, and reliable recognition of known words without harakat in six to ten. Pattern reading, which is what makes an unfamiliar word decodable rather than unknown, takes eight to fourteen. Reading unseen unvowelled text for meaning takes a term or more. Those are planning figures for an average starting point, not promises, and the order matters more than the totals.

faqs.question: Is my child's Arabic handwriting costing them marks?
faqs.answer: Quite possibly, and nobody will have mentioned it. Arabic letters change shape by position, six never join forwards, and short vowels sit off the line. A student who absorbed those rules approximately produces writing a sympathetic teacher reads and a careful marker penalises. The common faults are joining a letter that should not join, using a medial form in an initial position, inconsistent word spacing, and ambiguous harakat placement. Four short sessions of deliberate form work clears most of it, and the benefit shows in every written task afterwards.

faqs.question: Can Arabic script be taught properly over a screen?
faqs.answer: Yes, and on several specifics it works better than sitting across a table. Stroke order is the thing that makes letter forms stick, and on a shared screen the student sees the strokes in the correct orientation rather than watching an upside-down hand. Demonstrations can be replayed. Writing still happens on paper because handwriting is the skill being built; the page is photographed and annotated in a shared file, which returns a correction while the attempt is still fresh in the student's memory.

faqs.question: How do we set up Arabic typing for written tasks at home?
faqs.answer: Add an Arabic keyboard in the device settings, learn where the harakat keys sit, and practise handling a document that mixes right-to-left Arabic with left-to-right numbers or English, because that mixing is what confuses students mid-task. Fifteen minutes in an early session covers all of it. Worth doing early for a practical reason: some Dubai schools accept typed submissions for written tasks and others do not, and discovering the difference the night before a deadline wastes time that has nothing to do with language.

faqs.question: What should we keep in a folder to show the Arabic teacher?
faqs.answer: Four things, dated and in one place. The opening diagnostic note with its numbers. The sequence of timed reading checks. The banded written tasks, each with its criterion letter. And two or three oral recordings on the same prompt, where consent was given. A one-page summary drawn from that evidence changes the tone of any conversation with a school, because teachers act on evidence and have nothing to act on when presented with a parental impression however strongly it is held.

faqs.question: What do the harakat do, and why does the school stop printing them?
faqs.answer: Harakat are the short vowel marks written above and below the letters, and they tell a reader how a word is pronounced. Beginner material prints them; almost everything else does not, because fluent readers infer vowels from root and pattern. The transition is the biggest cliff in the subject and it arrives without announcement, so a student who was doing well appears to decline. Nothing got harder. The vowels were removed, and the skill that replaces them has to be taught deliberately.

faqs.question: How do we know Arabic tutoring is working before the next report?
faqs.answer: Repeat the opening measurements. The vowelled and unvowelled reading times, the twelve-letter check, and a written task banded against the same phase descriptor as before. Do it at the midpoint of a block and at the end, in exactly the same form, and put the numbers next to each other. An MYP report averages judgements across a whole period and lags real change by weeks, so it confirms or contradicts something you should already know rather than being the first news you get.

faqs.question: Who is allowed to charge for Arabic lessons in the UAE?
faqs.answer: Anyone charging for private lessons is expected to hold the MoHRE private tuition work permit, introduced under Ministerial Resolution No. 710 of 2023. The u.ae guidance states it is granted free of charge for two years and lists eligible categories including school teachers, government and private sector employees, unemployed residents, university students and school students aged 15 to 18. It also states that tutoring without a permit attracts fines and penalties under the applicable laws, with no published schedule, so treat any amount quoted at you as unverified.

faqs.question: How does Ramadan change Arabic lessons for a Dubai student?
faqs.answer: School hours shorten, afternoons quieten, and the evening reorganises around Iftar, so the late-afternoon slot that worked all year becomes the hardest hour of the day for concentration. Script drilling in particular needs energy and does not travel well into a fasting afternoon. Most families move to a morning slot or to a session well after Iftar, and shift the balance towards reading and written tasks for the month. Agree the pattern before the month starts rather than cancelling week by week.

faqs.question: When should we stop paying for Arabic support?
faqs.answer: For a decoding block, when the gap between vowelled and unvowelled reading has closed to the point where unfamiliar words are being worked out rather than recognised, and all twelve letter forms are clean in every position. For written work, when banded scripts sit in the upper bands of the current phase across two or three different text types. At that point the next useful conversation is with the school about phase, not with a tutor about more hours, and a pause is a legitimate outcome.

faqs.question: Can a tutor work from the school's own Arabic scheme?
faqs.answer: For the mandatory subjects they effectively must. KHDA guidance states that using different or additional content for Arabic, Islamic Education and Social Studies, without prior permission from the Ministry of Education, is strictly prohibited. Support therefore works from the school's own scheme and the student's own set tasks rather than from a separate course. That is also cheaper for a family, because there is no material to buy, and it is a reason to be wary of anybody marketing their own Arabic curriculum for this purpose.

After that the same tasks get repeated at the midpoint and the end of a block, so the decision to continue or stop rests on two comparable measurements rather than on anybody's impression. Lessons are one-to-one over live video on Gulf Standard Time; IB Gram does not sell in-home visits in Dubai.

intro.heading: The price of Arabic in Dubai depends on which Arabic your child is actually studying
paragraphs: Parents ringing round for Arabic help in Dubai get quoted numbers that make no sense next to each other. AED 60 an hour from one person, AED 400 from another, for what sounds like the same lesson. Both can be honest quotes. Arabic in a Dubai MYP school is not one subject, the people who teach it are drawn from two very different pools, and half the quotes you receive include marking while the other half do not.

The structural fact behind the pricing is a regulatory one. Arabic is mandatory in every Dubai private school whatever curriculum the school is licensed for, and KHDA guidance requires separate classes for Arabs and non-Arabs in Arabic as a first language, Islamic Education and Social Studies, stating that combined classes for both groups are strictly prohibited because the curriculum expectations and the language of instruction differ. Two streams, two sets of expectations, two labour markets.

A non-Arab student generally studies Arabic as an additional language, which inside the MYP sits in the Language Acquisition framework with its six phases and its four criteria. An Arab student generally studies Arabic as a first language, which is a literature-based course and reported differently. The second needs a teacher trained in Arabic literature and rhetoric. That pool is far smaller in the private tutoring market than the pool of people who can teach a beginner the alphabet, and the price follows the scarcity rather than the difficulty.

Then there is the question of what an hour contains. An hour of spoken practice and an hour that ends with a written task banded against a phase descriptor and returned before the next session are priced as though they were the same product. They are not, and the difference is the part that moves a grade. Ask any quote one question: does this include marking written work, and how quickly does it come back? The answer explains most of the gap between AED 80 and AED 300.

Everything below is attributed. The bands come from Bestimate's Dubai 2026 tutoring rate table and from prices published by EdFlik, Tutopiya, Unitors, TutorChase and BartyED, each at the figure they publish. They are market rates and not an IB Gram price list, which is quoted after a free first session. Lessons are delivered one-to-one over live video; IB Gram does not send tutors to homes in Dubai, and the in-home figures here are market context rather than an offer. One more framing point before the numbers. Nothing on this page is a judgement about which band a family should buy from. The budget band exists because there are real jobs it does well, and the specialist band exists because there are jobs nothing else does at all. The point of publishing the whole range with its sources is that a parent can see which job they are actually buying, which is the one piece of information this market almost never supplies.

The budget question in the MYP is usually how many years of support a family is committing to, because a phase takes terms rather than weeks to move and the mandatory requirement does not go away.
programmes.countryNote: Dubai families commonly discover the cost in MYP 3, when the Arabic grade stops being generous and the gap between a child's speaking and their reading becomes a number on a report. Starting in MYP 1 or 2 is cheaper over five years than starting in MYP 4, because reading is the slow part and it is far less expensive to build early than to repair late.

programmes.name: Primary Years Programme
programmes.description: Arabic in the primary years is taught without criterion bands, which makes it hard for a parent to judge whether the mandatory lessons are landing. Cost at this stage is low because the teaching is low-stakes and widely available, and families who spend anything here usually spend it on script confidence rather than on grades.
programmes.countryNote: KHDA calculates mandatory-subject instructional time from a 40-minute lesson unit, allows schools to vary lesson length provided the weekly total is met, and advises that no mandatory subject lesson runs shorter than 25 minutes. Knowing how many of those units your school timetables tells you whether a weekly paid session is topping up adequate provision or compensating for thin provision.

programmes.name: Diploma Programme
programmes.description: Arabic continues as Language B at Standard or Higher Level, as ab initio for a genuine beginner, or as Language A where the school offers it. Rates rise in the Diploma years across every subject, and specialist bands of AED 200 to 450 and above become the norm rather than the top of the market.
programmes.countryNote: The expensive scenario for a Dubai family is a student arriving in Year 12 with a weak MYP Arabic record who then needs two years of specialist support at Diploma rates. Spending at MYP rates to protect the option is usually the cheaper path, and the decision point is the end of MYP 4 rather than the start of Year 12.

dubai/ib-myp-arabic-tutor.subjectsIntro: Arabic bookings in Dubai divide by stream and by task, and each division carries a different market price. These are the pieces of Arabic work IB Gram is asked for, with a note on what drives the rate in each case.

subjects.name: Arabic as an additional language, Phases 1-2
subjects.description: Alphabet, sound-symbol mapping and short vowels. The widest pool of available tutors and the lowest market rates, from the budget band upwards. Progress here is fast and cheap, which is why starting early costs a family far less across five years.

subjects.name: Arabic as an additional language, Phases 3-4
subjects.description: Where most Dubai students stall, because unvowelled text arrives and reading slows. Rates sit in the qualified-teacher band since the work needs somebody who can band a script rather than hold a conversation. Two shorter sessions a week is the usual pattern.

subjects.name: Arabic as an additional language, Phases 5-6
subjects.levels: MYP 5 and bridging into Language B
subjects.description: Authentic text, abstract topics and controlled register. The tutor pool narrows sharply and rates move into the specialist band of AED 200 to 450 and above, as published by Bestimate and TutorChase for programme specialists generally.

subjects.name: Arabic as a first language
subjects.description: A literature-based course needing a teacher trained in Arabic literary analysis, not a fluent speaker. The smallest pool and the firmest prices. Families are often quoted the same rate as for a Diploma subject, and that is a fair reflection of scarcity.

subjects.name: Arabic reading and script intensive
subjects.description: A short block, usually six weeks twice a week, aimed only at decoding speed on unvowelled text. Priced per hour at the mid band, and the shorter sessions push the per-hour figure up while making the block work better than a long weekly hour would.

subjects.name: Arabic oral and listening
subjects.description: The cheapest Arabic hour available in Dubai because conversation partners are plentiful. It is also the criterion many students already score well on, so spending here is frequently the clearest example of paying for the wrong thing.

subjects.name: Islamic Education taught in Arabic
subjects.description: KHDA requires Standard Arabic as the main language of instruction for Islamic Education for Arabs and for Arabic as a first language. Support here works from the school's own scheme, since the guidance prohibits different or additional content without prior Ministry of Education permission.

subjects.name: UAE Social Studies in Arabic
subjects.description: KHDA requires Arabic as the primary language for Social Studies for Arab students and the school's licensed-curriculum language for non-Arabs in Moral, Social and Cultural studies. Rates track the Arabic additional-language band rather than a humanities band.

subjects.name: Handwriting and orthography repair
subjects.description: Letter forms, joining and the position of short vowels. Short, cheap and oddly high-return, because illegible script costs marks in every written criterion. Usually sold as a handful of thirty-minute sessions rather than as a term.

dubai/ib-myp-arabic-tutor.regionsIntro: Arabic demand is not spread evenly across Dubai, and neither is the local supply of people who can teach it well. These are the communities IB Gram is asked for Arabic support from most often, with the practical point that affects cost or scheduling in each.

regions.name: Jumeirah and Al Safa
regions.note: A high concentration of long-established international schools, so local in-home Arabic tutors are easy to find and priced accordingly at the upper end. Online booking is what families here use to buy the first-language stream, which is far scarcer than the additional-language one.

regions.name: Al Barsha and Al Quoz
regions.note: Short commutes mean 4pm slots are realistic, which allows the twice-weekly short-session pattern that suits script work. Families in this corridor frequently book two children in consecutive slots and ask whether that reduces the hourly figure.

regions.name: Deira, Al Mamzar and Al Qusais
regions.note: Older communities with large Arabic-speaking populations, so dialect exposure is high and reading confidence often lags behind speaking by more than elsewhere. The script intensive is the most common booking shape here.

regions.name: Mirdif and Al Khawaneej
regions.note: Long evening drives to several school clusters, which pushes in-home rates up and makes the travel component of a quote visible. Later online slots after 5.30pm are the norm and cost nothing extra.

regions.name: Dubai Festival City and Nad Al Hamar
regions.note: Mixed school destinations and unpredictable arrival times. Families here tend to buy a block of hours rather than a standing weekly slot, so that a missed week is deferred instead of lost.

regions.name: International City and Warsan
regions.note: Price sensitivity is highest in this part of the city and budget-band quotes are everywhere. The useful check is whether marking is included, because an AED 70 hour without written feedback is rarely the cheaper option over a term.

regions.name: Jumeirah Park and Al Furjan
regions.note: Newer villa communities with long school bus runs in both directions. Weekend sessions dominate, which suits reading and written tasks and makes a six-week block easier to schedule than a weekday evening slot.

schoolClusters.city: Al Barsha, Al Quoz and the Sheikh Zayed Road corridor
schoolClusters.note: The densest school corridor in the city, which keeps local in-home Arabic rates competitive at the additional-language end and does very little for first-language availability. Students we support here are mostly non-Arab, in Phases 2 to 4, with reading as the target criterion.

schoolClusters.city: Al Jaddaf, Dubai Healthcare City and Festival City
schoolClusters.note: Smaller Arabic cohorts and more mixed-phase teaching, which raises the value of one-to-one work because a mixed class rarely pitches at any one phase. Requests from this cluster include a higher share of first-language Arabic than elsewhere in Dubai.

modes.title: Weekly hour with marking included
modes.description: One sixty-minute session a week with a written task banded against the phase descriptor between sessions. The marking is inside the quoted rate rather than attached as an extra, because a rate without marking looks cheaper on a phone call and costs more per band moved. This is the default shape for a student sitting below the school's expectation.

The market offers small-group rates per student that sit well below one-to-one, and the honest trade is attention for money.

sections.heading: What an IB MYP Arabic tutor costs in Dubai, by stream and phase
paragraphs: The direct answer: a qualified Arabic teacher working online one-to-one is quoted roughly AED 150 to 300 an hour in Dubai, programme specialists AED 200 to 450 and above, budget and university-student tutors from around AED 45, and in-home visits AED 180 to 500 with travel inside the figure. Those bands come from Bestimate's Dubai 2026 rate table and from prices published by EdFlik, Tutopiya, Unitors, TutorChase and BartyED. They are the market rather than our price list.

The table splits those bands by what a Dubai family is actually buying, because stream and phase move the number more than anything else does. Arabic as an additional language in the early phases is the cheapest serious language hour available in this city. Arabic as a first language, taught as literature, sits at the top because the pool of people who can teach it is small. The monthly figures assume the session pattern most families settle on rather than a theoretical maximum.

Two honest caveats before reading it. First, every one of these is a market figure with a source, not a quote from us; we price after a free first session once the stream and the target criterion are known. Second, monthly spend is a weak comparison on its own. A cheaper monthly figure built from one unmarked ninety-minute session usually buys less movement than a dearer one built from two short marked sessions, and the invoice will not say so.

sections.heading: Two Arabic streams, and why they are not priced the same
paragraphs: KHDA guidance on mandatory subjects requires schools to organise separate classes for Arabs and non-Arabs in Arabic as a first language, Islamic Education and Social Studies, and states that combined classes for both groups are strictly prohibited because the curriculum expectations and the language of instruction differ between them. That is a teaching rule rather than a pricing rule, but it creates two separate labour markets and the prices diverge accordingly.

The additional-language stream is taught to non-Arab students and, inside the MYP, runs through the six Language Acquisition phases with four criteria marked on bands out of eight. A great many people in Dubai can teach the early phases of it competently. The first-language stream is a literature course for Arab students, assessed on textual analysis and expression, and the teachers who can do it well are the same people schools compete for. Supply decides the rate.

The practical mistake families make is buying the wrong stream's tutor. A fluent, warm, inexpensive conversation tutor cannot move a first-language literature grade, and a literature specialist charging AED 400 is poor value for a Phase 1 student learning the alphabet. Ask the school which stream your child is formally in and how the grade is reported, then buy against that answer. KHDA guidance also requires that teachers of Islamic Education and Arabic hold appropriate KHDA approval to teach those subjects in school, which is a reasonable thing to ask your school about.

sections.heading: What actually moves the hourly number in this emirate
paragraphs: Six variables explain almost every gap between two Dubai quotes, and only one of them is the tutor's skill. The others are the stream, whether marking is inside the rate, the session length, whether anybody is driving, and when in the term you are asking. Knowing which lever is being pulled turns a confusing set of numbers into a comparison you can actually make, and it usually reveals that the cheapest quote is cheap for a reason you would not have chosen.

Marking is the lever that hides best. A tutor quoting AED 120 for an hour of talking and a tutor quoting AED 250 for an hour plus a banded written task are selling different things, and in Language Acquisition the written task is where Criterion D marks come from. Ask the question flatly: does this rate include setting and marking written work, and how fast does it come back? A tutor who charges separately for marking will say so when asked, and then the two quotes are comparable.

Timing is the lever parents notice too late. Demand in Dubai spikes in the weeks before internal assessment and reporting windows, and the specialist end of the market books out first. The family that starts looking three weeks before a report is choosing from whoever is left, at whatever they are asking. Starting a block mid-term, when diaries are open, buys a better teacher at a calmer price, and that is as close to a free saving as this market offers.

sections.heading: Modern Standard Arabic and the dialect spoken at the school gate
paragraphs: This is the thing that confuses non-Arab families in Dubai more than the price does. The Arabic assessed in school is Modern Standard Arabic, and the Arabic a child hears in a Dubai playground, in a taxi or at a friend's house is Gulf dialect, with Levantine and Egyptian close behind depending on the community. They share a root and they are not the same language in practice. Vocabulary, verb endings and everyday phrasing all differ.

The consequence is a profile that looks contradictory on a report. A student who has lived in Dubai for six years may handle a shop conversation comfortably and still score in the lower bands for reading and writing, because none of the input they have absorbed is the registered form being assessed. Parents read that as a lack of effort. It is a mismatch between what the child has been exposed to and what the criteria reward, and it is entirely fixable.

For a tutor the implication is practical rather than ideological. Dialect exposure is an asset for listening and for confidence, so there is no reason to suppress it, but written and reading work has to be done in Standard Arabic because that is what the descriptors are written for. A good Arabic tutor will name which form they are teaching in any given task, and a student who understands that there are two forms stops feeling that their existing Arabic is somehow wrong.

sections.heading: The mandatory-subject timetable and what it means for your budget
paragraphs: Before buying hours, find out how many your school already provides. KHDA calculates mandatory-subject instructional time from a 40-minute lesson unit, allows schools to vary lesson length so long as the weekly total is met, and advises that no mandatory subject lesson runs shorter than 25 minutes. Schools differ in how they arrange that, and a school delivering its full weekly total well needs topping up rather than replacing, which is a cheaper problem.

The federal position behind this is that private schools are not obliged to follow a specific curriculum beyond Arabic language, social studies and Islamic studies, while adhering to the Ministry's general regulations. Dubai layers its own requirements on top through KHDA, including the separate-class rule and the language-of-instruction rules. None of this is optional for the school, which means the Arabic lessons on your child's timetable are not a school preference you can negotiate away.

A constraint worth knowing before you buy material: KHDA guidance states that for the mandatory subjects the use of any different or additional content, without prior permission from the Ministry of Education, is strictly prohibited. Tutoring on mandatory Arabic therefore works from the school's own scheme and the student's own tasks rather than from an alternative course a provider happens to sell. That is a reason to be sceptical of anybody marketing their own Arabic curriculum for this purpose. It also keeps the cost down, because there is nothing to buy beyond the hours themselves.

sections.heading: Arabic tutoring cost in context for a Dubai household
paragraphs: Tutoring spend only makes sense against the rest of the education bill. KHDA confirmed on 22 May 2026 that there would be no increase in private school fees in Dubai for the 2026-27 academic year, under the emirate's second economic incentives package valued at AED 1.5 billion. Fees are capped by regulation and tutoring is not, so the one line in the budget that can drift is the one a family controls entirely.

The table sets a monthly Arabic figure against that backdrop, using Bestimate's own monthly estimates for weekly one-hour sessions as the sanity check: roughly AED 240 to 600 at the budget end, AED 600 to 1,200 mid-market, and AED 1,000 to 2,000 and above for specialist exam-year support. A Dubai family buying one mid-band Arabic session a week is therefore looking at a figure similar to a mid-market monthly estimate for any other subject.

The sensible way to size the spend is by target rather than by habit. A six-week reading block has an end date and a measurable outcome. An open-ended weekly hour that nobody is measuring tends to run for two years because cancelling feels like giving up. Decide the criterion, decide the block length, and re-decide at the end of it. That discipline saves more money in this market than negotiating an hourly rate does. It also makes the conversation with a tutor easier, because a block with a target gives them something to be judged on and most good teachers would rather be judged than renewed out of politeness.

sections.heading: Where the marks go in MYP Arabic, and which ones are cheap to win
paragraphs: Arabic as an additional language is marked on the same four criteria as any other MYP language: listening, reading, speaking and writing, each on a band out of eight. For most non-Arab students in Dubai the profile is lopsided. Speaking and listening sit respectably because the city supplies constant input. Reading sits low because unvowelled text is a different skill from spoken comprehension, and writing sits low because the script itself slows everything down.

That profile tells you where the cheap marks are. Script and handwriting repair is short, inexpensive work with a disproportionate effect, because illegible or inconsistent letter forms cost marks in every written task regardless of the quality of the ideas. Short-vowel awareness is similar: a handful of sessions on where harakat sit and when they are omitted changes reading speed measurably, and reading speed is what the comprehension bands actually depend on.

The expensive marks are the ones families usually buy first. More conversation practice when speaking is already the strongest criterion adds very little to the grade, however enjoyable the sessions are. A term of general Arabic with no target criterion is the most common way to spend AED 4,000 and see a report that has not moved. Name the criterion, buy against it, and measure it the same way twice before deciding whether to continue. The order matters as much as the choice: fix the script, then reading speed, then comprehension, then written register. Working on register while a student is still decoding slowly is paying specialist rates for a problem that has not arrived yet.

sections.heading: Arabic, Islamic Education and the Ministry of Education equivalency count
paragraphs: Families planning a UAE university application eventually meet the equivalency process, and there is one widely misunderstood detail about Arabic in it. For the British track the Ministry requires five accredited subjects in GCSE or IGCSE certificates at a grade no lower than E or grade 3, plus one accredited subject at Advanced Level at no less than E, or two at Advanced Subsidiary Level at the same grade. Arabic and Islamic education are not included among the five required subjects.

That detail is worth knowing because at least one competing page in this market publishes a different subject count, and a parent who plans around the wrong number can find themselves a subject short in Year 13. The American-track requirements are separate again: English proficiency through a score of 5 in IELTS academic, 61 in TOEFL iBT, or 450 in the reading and writing section of the SAT, with at least 450 in SAT Math.

Two cautions follow. The IB equivalency position is not covered by the source above, so no points threshold for the Diploma should be relied on without reading it on the Ministry's own pages or the emirate attestation authority's site. And equivalency is a process families complete with the authorities directly; it is not something a tutoring service performs, guarantees or shortens. Verify everything here against moe.gov.ae before making a decision that depends on it. None of this means a student needs paid Arabic tutoring to clear equivalency; the requirement is a subject count and a grade floor, and plenty of students meet both without buying an hour.

sections.heading: Telling a cheap Arabic tutor from a false economy
paragraphs: A low rate is not automatically poor value and a high one is not automatically good. The budget band exists for real reasons: a university student who speaks Arabic well can teach the alphabet and basic exchanges perfectly adequately, and paying specialist rates for that is waste. The question is always whether the person in front of you matches the job, and the job is defined by the stream, the phase and the target criterion rather than by the subject name.

Three questions separate a bargain from a false economy. Does the rate include setting and marking written work, and how fast is it returned? Can you band this piece of my child's writing and tell me what the next band asks for? Which phase do you think my child is in and what in the work tells you that? A tutor at AED 90 who answers all three well is a genuine find. One at AED 300 who cannot answer the second is not.

The false economy has a recognisable shape. Ninety-minute sessions because the price is per session rather than per hour, no written work between lessons, warm reports of good progress, and a report card in March that has not moved. By then a family has spent a term's budget and lost a term's time, and the second is worse. Buy the smallest block that can be measured, measure it, and only then commit to more. A tutor who objects to being measured that way has told you something useful about the next six months.

process.title: Tell us the stream, the phase and the target
process.description: Which Arabic stream the school has your child in, the phase if the report shows one, and what you want to change. Those three facts decide the tutor and the rate. Guessing the stream is the single most expensive mistake in this subject, so ask the school if the report does not say.

process.title: Free first session, with a band at the end of it
process.description: Sixty minutes that samples all four criteria and finishes by banding a real piece of work against the phase descriptor. You keep the written phase estimate and the target criterion whichever way you decide. No card is taken and nothing starts automatically afterwards.

process.title: Agree the price and the shape together
process.description: We quote after that session, with marking inside the figure rather than attached to it, and we say which shape fits: a weekly hour, an agreed pair, or a six-week block. The rate holds for the term and is not re-quoted because a reporting window is approaching.

process.title: Re-decide at the end of the block
process.description: A block ends and gets reviewed rather than rolling on by default. A fresh task banded against the same descriptor set says whether the money moved anything. If it did not, we change the method or the tutor and we tell you which we think it was.

whyPoints.title: Every figure carries its source
whyPoints.description: The AED bands on this page are attributed to Bestimate's 2026 Dubai table or to the provider that published them. A rate quoted with no source and no date is a number somebody made up, and in this market there are a great many of them.

whyPoints.title: Marking is priced in, not bolted on
whyPoints.description: A quote that excludes marking looks cheaper and costs more per band moved, because written feedback is where Criterion D progress comes from. Our rate includes setting and banding a written task between sessions, with the turnaround stated.

whyPoints.title: We ask which Arabic you need
whyPoints.description: First language and additional language are different courses taught by different people at different prices. Matching a literature specialist to a beginner, or the reverse, wastes money in both directions, so the stream question comes before the rate question.

whyPoints.title: Blocks with end dates
whyPoints.description: Open-ended weekly hours drift for years because stopping feels like failing. A six-week block with one target and a measurement at the end is cheaper, clearer, and easier to stop. It is also easier to justify extending when it has visibly worked.

whyPoints.title: Honest about scarcity
whyPoints.description: First-language Arabic and the upper phases are thin everywhere, including with us. Where no suitable specialist is free for your slot we say so and name the nearest real alternative rather than sending a fluent speaker to fill the hour at the same price.

faqs.question: How much does an MYP Arabic tutor cost per hour in Dubai?
faqs.answer: Market rates for a qualified subject teacher working online run roughly AED 150 to 300 an hour, with programme specialists quoted between AED 200 and 450 and above, budget and university-student tutors from around AED 45, and in-home visits between AED 180 and 500 with travel inside the figure. Those bands come from Bestimate's Dubai 2026 rate table and from figures published by EdFlik, Tutopiya, Unitors, TutorChase and BartyED. They are the market rather than our price list; we quote after a free first session once the stream and target criterion are clear.

faqs.question: Why is Arabic more expensive to tutor than French or Spanish in Dubai?
faqs.answer: At the beginner end it usually is not; Phase 1 and 2 Arabic is among the cheapest serious language hours in the city because so many people can teach it. The gap appears higher up. Arabic as a first language is a literature course, and the teachers who can mark literary analysis in Arabic are the same people schools compete to employ, so the pool is small and the rates are firm. Upper-phase additional-language Arabic is scarce for the same reason. Scarcity rather than difficulty sets the price.

faqs.question: Is Arabic as a first language dearer to support than Arabic as an additional language?
faqs.answer: Generally yes, and markedly so at the top. The additional-language stream is taught to non-Arab students through the Language Acquisition phases and has a wide supply of competent teachers, especially in the early phases. First-language Arabic is literature-based, assessed on textual analysis and expression, and needs a specialist. Expect first-language quotes to sit alongside Diploma subject rates rather than beginner language rates. The practical advice is to confirm with the school which stream your child is formally in before comparing any quotes at all.

faqs.question: Does putting two children in one session halve the cost?
faqs.answer: It reduces the per-student rate but not by half, and it only works where both students are within a phase of each other. A shared hour works well for reading, listening and written feedback, because those can be set at a common level and marked separately. It works badly for speaking, since a shared hour halves each child's talking time and Criterion C depends on exactly that. Where phases are two or more apart we will not run it, because one of the two children ends up being taught at the wrong level.

faqs.question: Should we pay per session or buy a block of Arabic hours?
faqs.answer: A block is usually better value and always better discipline. Per-session billing drifts: the hour renews every week, nobody measures anything, and two years pass. A six-week block has a named target, a fixed price agreed in advance, a rescheduling rule for missed weeks, and a measurement at the end that tells you whether to buy another one. The rate per hour inside a block is often slightly higher, because the sessions are shorter and more frequent, and that is the pattern that actually moves reading.

faqs.question: Do Arabic tutoring rates in Dubai rise before the reporting window?
faqs.answer: Effective prices rise, even where headline rates do not, because the specialist end of the market books out first and what remains available is whatever is left. A family that starts looking three weeks before a report is choosing from a thinner pool at whatever that pool is asking. Starting mid-term, when diaries are open, is the closest thing to a free saving available here. Our rate is fixed for the term it is agreed in and is not re-quoted because an assessment window is approaching.

faqs.question: Does the quoted Arabic rate include marking and written feedback?
faqs.answer: With us, yes, and you should ask every provider the same question because it is the largest hidden variable in any quote. An hour of conversation and an hour that ends with a written task banded against the phase descriptor and returned before the next session are different products at similar advertised prices. Ask flatly whether the rate includes setting and marking written work and how fast it comes back. Once both quotes are answering that question, they become comparable, and the cheaper one is often no longer cheaper.

faqs.question: How many hours of MYP Arabic should a Dubai family budget for a term?
faqs.answer: For a middle-phase student with reading as the target, twelve to sixteen hours across a term is the pattern that produces visible movement, usually as two shorter sessions a week for part of the term rather than one hour every week for all of it. At mid-band market rates that is AED 1,800 to 4,800 for the term. For script and handwriting repair alone, four to six short sessions is often enough. Decide by target rather than by calendar, and review at the end of the block rather than rolling on.

faqs.question: Will a Standard Arabic tutor help if my child only hears dialect at home?
faqs.answer: Yes, and the two are complementary rather than in conflict. School assessment is in Modern Standard Arabic, while a Dubai childhood supplies Gulf, Levantine or Egyptian dialect. Dialect exposure builds listening confidence and is a genuine asset for Criterion A and C. Reading and writing have to be done in the standard form because the descriptors are written for it. A good tutor names which form a task is in, which stops a child from feeling that the Arabic they already have is somehow wrong.

faqs.question: Does my child's Arabic grade count towards Ministry of Education equivalency?
faqs.answer: For the British track it does not count towards the five required subjects. The Ministry requires five accredited subjects in GCSE or IGCSE certificates at no less than E or grade 3, plus one Advanced Level at no less than E or two Advanced Subsidiary Levels at the same grade, and Arabic and Islamic education are not included among the five. The IB position is not covered by that source, so do not rely on any published IB points threshold without reading it on moe.gov.ae. Equivalency is completed with the authorities directly, not through a tutoring service.

faqs.question: Why does my child sit in a separate Arabic class from their Arab classmates?
faqs.answer: Because KHDA requires it. Its mandatory-subjects guidance states that for Arabic as a first language, Islamic Education and Social Studies, schools must organise separate classes for Arabs and non-Arabs, and that combined classes for both groups are strictly prohibited because the curriculum expectations and the language of instruction differ. It is not a judgement about your child's ability. It does mean the two groups are working towards different things, so comparing your child's Arabic grade with a classmate's across that line is not a useful comparison.

faqs.question: How much Arabic time does the KHDA requirement take in the timetable?
faqs.answer: KHDA calculates mandatory-subject instructional time from a 40-minute lesson unit and allows schools to vary lesson length provided the required weekly total is met, with advice that no mandatory subject lesson should run shorter than 25 minutes. The weekly total differs by year group and subject, so the only reliable answer is the one your own school gives you. Ask for it in writing before buying hours: a school delivering its full allocation well needs topping up, which is a cheaper and shorter job than compensating for thin provision.

faqs.question: Is a cheaper Arabic tutor at AED 80 an hour worth trying?
faqs.answer: Possibly, and the test is the job rather than the rate. For alphabet work, basic exchanges and script practice at Phase 1 or 2, a tutor at AED 80 who can show you a plan is good value and specialist rates would be waste. For a Phase 4 student losing marks on unvowelled reading, or for first-language literature, the same rate almost never buys somebody who can band a script. Ask them to band a piece of your child's writing and name what the next band needs. The answer settles it in five minutes.

faqs.question: Can one Arabic tutor cover reading, writing and the oral at the same rate?
faqs.answer: Usually yes, since all four criteria belong to one subject and a competent MYP Arabic teacher works across them. What changes is the session shape rather than the rate. Reading and writing suit a weekly hour with marked work in between. Oral practice suits two short slots a week. Where a family wants both patterns simultaneously the hours go up even though the hourly figure does not, and that is the honest way to describe the extra cost rather than quoting a higher rate.

faqs.question: What happens to the price if no MYP Arabic specialist is free for our slot?
faqs.answer: The price does not change and the answer might be no. First-language Arabic and the upper additional-language phases are thin across the whole market, ourselves included. Where nobody suitable is free for your time we will offer a different weekday, a shorter twice-weekly pattern, or a tutor strong in the specific criterion you need rather than across the whole subject, at the rate that matches what they actually do. What we will not do is put a fluent speaker in a specialist slot and charge the specialist rate.

dubai/ib-myp-arabic-tutor.closingHeading: Name the stream, then talk about money
dubai/ib-myp-arabic-tutor.closingBody: Find out from the school which Arabic stream your child is formally in and which phase, if the report shows one. With those two facts a rate conversation takes a minute instead of a week, because the stream is what decides who should be teaching and therefore what it costs. The first session is free and ends with a band on a real piece of work plus a written phase estimate, which you keep either way. We quote after that, with marking inside the figure and the rate fixed for the term. Lessons are one-to-one over live video on Gulf Standard Time; IB Gram does not send tutors to homes in Dubai.

intro.heading: What this actually costs in Dubai, and why nobody will tell you
paragraphs: Price is the first question every parent asks and the one this corner of the market refuses to answer. Of the competitor pages examined for this project, three published no figure at all, one published an hourly rate that contradicted its own structured data, and two quoted in US dollars, which is not a currency a Dubai family transacts in. One page's own frequently asked questions asked how much tutoring costs and then declined to say. So here are the numbers, attributed, with the date they were read.

Across Dubai providers in October 2026: budget online tutoring, often delivered by university students, runs roughly AED 45 to 150 an hour, with EdFlik listing from AED 45 to 65 and Tutopiya from AED 33 to 52. A qualified subject tutor working online runs AED 150 to 300, with Unitors listing IGCSE from AED 150 and IB from AED 200. An in-home one-to-one visit runs AED 180 to 500 with travel inside the rate. An IB or IGCSE specialist runs AED 200 to 450 or more, with TutorChase publishing AED 270. At the top, BartyED publishes AED 650 for examiner-led work. Monthly packages advertised in this market include AED 799 for eight online sessions and AED 1,599 to 1,799 for four two-hour in-home sessions.

None of those are IB Gram's prices and this page does not publish one, for a reason worth stating. An MYP 2 student rotating through three arts disciplines for a term each, an MYP 4 student who needs two sessions on writing a real artistic intention, and an MYP 5 student with an exhibition in three weeks and an empty process journal are three different jobs. A single number for all three would be either dishonest or useless. Our first lesson is free, and the rate is quoted after it, when the scope is known.

What is worth your attention is the second half of this page: the eight factors that actually move a Dubai rate. Discipline scarcity matters, because arts specialists are a thinner pool than maths tutors. Community matters, because the travel component of an in-home rate is distance. Timing matters, because demand spikes before school exhibitions and productions. Session length, package commitment, group size, tutor status and whether marking between sessions is included all move the figure, often by more than the headline band suggests.

One structural saving is worth naming at the start. IB Gram does not offer home visits in Dubai or anywhere else in the UAE; home visits are a service we run only in India. Lessons here are one-to-one over live video on Gulf Standard Time. That removes the forty to fifty minutes of term-time driving each way that sits inside every Dubai in-home rate, and it removes the geographic filter that selects an arts tutor by postcode before expertise. For a subject assessed largely through a journal and recordings, neither is a loss.

dubai/ib-myp-arts-home-tutor.programmesIntro: Cost behaves differently across the three IB programmes, mostly because the amount of documented work a student has to sustain rises sharply at each stage.

programmes.name: Primary Years Programme
programmes.description: Arts tutoring at this stage is rarely about grades and usually about instrument lessons or enjoyment, so the market is the general music and art teaching market rather than the IB specialist one. Rates sit lower, and the cheapest effective spend is usually materials and gallery visits rather than tuition hours.
programmes.countryNote: Dubai school arts enrichment is often included in fees or offered as a paid after-school club at modest cost, which is better value than private tuition for a nine-year-old. Ask the school what is already available before paying anyone an hourly rate for something the timetable supplies.

programmes.name: Middle Years Programme
programmes.ageRange: Ages 11-16 · Years 7-11, labelled MYP 1 to MYP 5
programmes.description: Where specialist rates start to apply, because the work becomes criterion-referenced and a general art or music teacher cannot mark it. The rate reflects scarcity: a tutor who knows the four MYP Arts criteria and reads a process journal as an assessor would is a narrower pool than a tutor who can teach drawing.
programmes.countryNote: Dubai schools often run arts on rotation through MYP 1 to 3, which means short bursts of need rather than sustained tutoring. Families who understand that buy four sessions around an assessment point rather than a year of weekly lessons, and spend considerably less for a better result.

programmes.name: Diploma Programme
programmes.description: Group 6 subjects carry substantial documented components over eighteen months, so demand is sustained rather than bursty and the specialist premium is at its highest. This is also where examiner-led providers quote their top rates, and where the question of what that premium actually buys deserves a direct answer.
programmes.countryNote: Dubai DP arts cohorts are small, which cuts both ways: specialist supply is thin, and school teachers are usually accessible. Before paying a specialist premium, check what the school's own Group 6 teacher offers in terms of feedback, because it is frequently more than families assume.

dubai/ib-myp-arts-home-tutor.subjectsIntro: What families in Dubai pay for inside MYP Arts, and roughly where each sits in the market. Arts disciplines differ in supply, which is the main reason two quotes for apparently the same service differ by a hundred dirhams.

subjects.name: MYP Visual Arts, criteria and journal work
subjects.description: The best-supplied arts discipline in Dubai and therefore the most competitively priced. Plenty of practising artists teach; the narrower pool is those who mark against the four criteria. Expect the qualified-subject band rather than the budget band if criterion marking is included.

subjects.name: MYP Music performance
subjects.description: Priced as instrumental teaching, which is a separate and well-established Dubai market with its own rates. Worth separating from MYP criterion support: an instrumental teacher raising technique and a tutor evidencing Criterion C are different purchases, and paying one rate for both usually gets one of them.

subjects.name: MYP Music composition
subjects.description: Thinner supply than performance teaching and priced accordingly. The work is mostly intention and structure rather than notation software, and two or three sessions on turning a vague brief into a testable musical intention typically achieves more than a term of general lessons.

subjects.name: MYP Drama and theatre
subjects.description: Ensemble assessment means the valuable work is individual journal evidence, which is desk work and does not need a studio. Supply in Dubai is moderate. Sessions cluster around production periods, so booking early matters more for availability than for price.

subjects.name: MYP Film and media arts
subjects.description: Technical vocabulary is teachable and reliably worth marks, and the whole discipline sits naturally on a screen, so online delivery carries no penalty at all. Supply is thin in Dubai, which pushes it towards the specialist band.

subjects.name: MYP Dance
subjects.description: The thinnest arts supply in this market, because fewer Dubai schools offer it within MYP Arts. Criterion and journal work transfers from other disciplines, which is often the practical answer when no dance specialist is available at a sensible rate.

subjects.name: Process journal and intention sessions
subjects.description: Discipline-agnostic, because the four criteria are identical across art forms. This is the cheapest high-value purchase in the subject: a handful of sessions on stating and exploring an artistic intention, applicable whether the student paints, composes or performs.

subjects.name: Criterion D critique coaching
subjects.description: Structured critique writing, usually two to four sessions. Pairs well with a Dubai gallery or venue visit the family arranges themselves, which costs little or nothing and supplies better material than any textbook. The strand most often left unevidenced and among the cheapest to fix.

subjects.name: Exhibition and showcase preparation
subjects.description: A fixed block before a school event, covering realisation of the stated intention, curatorial or programme-note writing and the response strand. Demand spikes here, which is the one point in the Dubai year when availability rather than price is the binding constraint.

subjects.name: Group 6 transition planning
subjects.description: One or two sessions, often the best-value purchase of all: a frank read of the journal against what Visual Arts, Music, Theatre or Film will demand over eighteen months, before the options form is signed. Cheaper than a term of DP1 catch-up tutoring by an order of magnitude.

dubai/ib-myp-arts-home-tutor.regionsTitle: Dubai communities and what the travel component looks like from each
dubai/ib-myp-arts-home-tutor.regionsIntro: The in-home portion of a Dubai tutoring rate is distance and traffic. These are the communities we hear from most, with what an in-home arrangement would actually involve from each, and what an online slot removes.

regions.name: Jumeirah Village Triangle
regions.note: Villa and townhouse community with a long run to the Al Barsha and Al Quoz school belt. An in-home arts tutor here is typically quoted at the middle of the AED 180 to 500 band, with most of the premium accounted for by the Al Khail Road crawl at five in the afternoon.

regions.name: Al Furjan and Discovery Gardens
regions.note: Dense, Metro-served and growing fast, with several schools in or near the community. In-home supply is better than in outlying areas and the travel premium correspondingly lower, though arts specialists remain a thinner pool than core-subject tutors wherever you live.

regions.name: Remraam and Dubailand South
regions.note: Among the longest tutor journeys in the city. Several Dubai providers quote the top of their in-home band for communities this far out, which means a sixty-minute session can carry more travel cost than teaching cost. The clearest case for online delivery anywhere in the emirate.

regions.name: Dubai Sports City
regions.note: Compact and well served by schools within the development, so in-home travel is short and the premium small. Here the argument for online is not cost but supply: a local general art tutor is easy to find and a tutor who reads a process journal as an assessor would is not.

regions.name: Al Qusais and Al Nahda
regions.note: Established, densely populated and close to the older school cluster. Tutoring is priced competitively across this corridor because supply is high, and families here are more likely than most to be comparing a tuition centre group rate against private one-to-one.

regions.name: Bur Dubai and Oud Metha
regions.note: Long-standing schools, short distances and the lowest in-home travel component in the city. Also the easiest place to buy art materials cheaply, which matters more to a visual arts budget than most families expect once they add up a term of consumables.

regions.name: Mirdif and Uptown Mirdif
regions.note: Family housing with late school-bus arrivals, pushing weekday sessions to half past six and shrinking the window an in-home tutor can realistically serve. Weekend slots are the usual answer, and they are the slots that cost the most to secure in person.

schoolClusters.city: Al Furjan, JVT and Dubai Sports City
schoolClusters.note: Western and southern communities where several schools added IB programmes relatively recently. Students we support here are often in early MYP cohorts, so families are buying short bursts of criterion support around assessment points rather than sustained weekly tuition.

schoolClusters.city: Dubailand, Remraam and The Sustainable City
schoolClusters.note: The outer southern belt, where travel distances make the in-home arithmetic worst and the online case strongest. Students we support in this cluster commonly book exhibition-preparation blocks, where availability rather than hourly rate is what families end up competing for.

sections.heading: The Dubai market, tier by tier, with sources and dates
paragraphs: Below is the rate table this market has been avoiding. Each band is attributed to the provider or survey that published it, and the whole table was read in October 2026. Rates move, so treat the date as part of the figure. None of these are IB Gram's prices, and we have not put ours in the table because a single number across MYP 1 to MYP 5 and five arts disciplines would be meaningless.

Two observations about the shape of it. The spread is enormous — a factor of roughly fourteen between the bottom of the budget band and the top of the premium one — and the middle is where almost all honest MYP arts work happens. A tutor at AED 45 an hour is not marking against four criteria and reading a process journal as an assessor would; a tutor at AED 650 is usually selling examiner status, which for MYP arts is close to meaningless because MYP portfolio work is moderated rather than examined in the way Diploma components are.

The second observation is that the in-home band overlaps the specialist band without delivering specialist expertise. AED 180 to 500 buys a person in the room, selected substantially by who will make the drive. AED 200 to 450 buys a subject specialist selected from a national or international pool. Those are different products at a similar price, and the comparison is the single most useful thing a Dubai parent can hold in their head while making calls.

One compliance note on every figure here. We are not stating how UAE VAT applies to tuition fees, because we have no Federal Tax Authority citation for it and publishing a tax position without one would be irresponsible across thousands of pages. What you should do is ask any provider two direct questions: is the quoted figure inclusive of VAT, and do you hold a Tax Registration Number. A provider who cannot answer both quickly is telling you something about their invoicing.

sections.heading: The eight things that move the number in Dubai
paragraphs: A band of AED 150 to 450 is wide enough to be unhelpful unless you know what pushes a quote up or down inside it. These eight factors explain almost every difference between two apparently identical quotes, and knowing them turns a negotiation into a specification: you can ask for the version of the service you actually need rather than accepting whichever one a provider defaults to.

Scarcity of the discipline is the largest single factor in arts. Visual arts teaching is well supplied in Dubai; dance and composition are not. A provider quoting for a dance specialist in this market is quoting against thin supply, and the honest answer is sometimes that criterion work from another arts discipline delivers more per dirham than paying a scarcity premium for the exact art form.

Travel is the second and it is purely geographic. The forty to fifty minutes each way between the Al Barsha school belt and the outer southern communities in term-time traffic is real cost. A sixty-minute in-home session in Remraam can carry more travel than teaching, which is why providers quote the top of their band for distance rather than for difficulty.

The other six are timing, session length, commitment, group size, tutor status and inclusions. Demand spikes before exhibitions and productions, which tightens availability more than it raises published rates. Ninety-minute sessions usually carry a lower per-hour figure than sixty. Blocks and packages discount against single sessions. Group work is cheaper per student and weaker on individual diagnosis. Claimed examiner status commands a premium that means little at MYP level. And whether marking between sessions is included is the inclusion that differs most often between two quotes at the same headline rate.
