sections.heading: Tutoring cost in context: the whole Dubai arts line in a household budget
paragraphs: An hourly rate in isolation tells you nothing about affordability. Set against school fees, materials, instrument costs and the occasional exhibition expense, tutoring is usually a smaller line than families fear and a more variable one than they expect. Putting the whole picture on one page also tends to change the decision, because it reveals where the cheap wins are.

The anchor for the Dubai context is a real and dated fact: KHDA confirmed in May 2026 that there would be no increase in private school fees in the emirate for the 2026-27 academic year, under Dubai's second economic incentives package, valued at AED 1.5 billion within a AED 2.5 billion total. School costs are flat this year. For context on the sector's scale, Dubai had 387,441 students across 227 private schools offering 17 different curricula in 2024-25, and the 2026-27 intake adds seven new private schools creating 16,846 places.

Against that, the arts line is modest and front-loadable. A term of visual arts consumables is tens of dirhams rather than hundreds if bought sensibly. Gallery access in Dubai is often free, which makes the single most valuable Criterion D activity available at no cost. Instrument hire or purchase is the one genuinely large item, and school schemes frequently undercut retail. The tutoring itself, at fortnightly cadence through one unit, is a smaller annual figure than most families assume once they stop pricing it as weekly for a year.

The table puts the items side by side with periods attached, so they can be compared honestly. Figures marked as indicative are budgeting aids rather than quotations: they move, and your own receipts are the only numbers that belong in a project costing or a household spreadsheet. Note also what is not in the table, because we do not have a sourced figure for it: how VAT applies to tuition in the UAE, which you should establish directly with any provider.

sections.heading: Why the in-home premium exists, and the one thing it genuinely buys
paragraphs: It would be easy to present the in-home premium as pure waste, and that would be unfair. There is one thing a person in the room buys that a screen does not, and it is worth naming honestly before explaining why we still do not sell it in the UAE: supervision of attention. A twelve-year-old who drifts is harder to drift past when an adult is sitting at the same table. For some students at some ages, that is a real service and it is what parents are actually buying.

Everything else in the premium is logistics. Forty to fifty minutes of term-time driving each way between the school belt and the outer communities. Building access, visitor parking, lift queues in the tower communities, security gates in the villa compounds. A tutor who can serve three households a day instead of five has to price accordingly, and that arithmetic is why Dubai in-home rates sit at AED 180 to 500 rather than at the online band.

The hidden cost is larger than the visible one for a minority subject. An in-home arts tutor is drawn from whoever will make that drive on a Tuesday at five. For visual arts in a central community that pool is adequate. For composition, film or dance it is close to empty, and what gets substituted is a general art or music teacher who cannot mark against four criteria or read a process journal the way a moderator will. The family pays a premium and receives a less specialist service, which is the worst available combination.

IB Gram does not offer home visits in Dubai or anywhere in the UAE; home visits are a service we run only in India. Our answer to the attention problem is structural rather than geographic: shorter sessions where appropriate, work set between them, a parent-readable record of what was marked, and a free trial lesson so a family can see how their own child behaves on a video session before paying for anything. For most MYP-age students, with a journal and a stated intention to work from, that is sufficient.

sections.heading: Group classes, school provision and the free options nobody mentions
paragraphs: A page about cost that only compares private tutoring options is not being straight with you. For a good number of Dubai MYP arts students, the right answer is not a tutor at all, and saying so costs us a booking and keeps the page honest. Three alternatives deserve checking before anybody pays an hourly rate.

The first is the school's own arts department. MYP arts teachers in Dubai are generally accessible, and the single most useful thing a student can do is ask their teacher which criterion is weakest and what evidence is missing from the journal. That conversation is free, authoritative and specific to the school's own marking. Many families pay for a tutor to deliver a less accurate version of it because nobody thought to ask.

The second is school enrichment. Arts clubs, ensembles, productions and studio access are often included in fees or offered at modest cost, and they generate exactly the sustained practice and documented development that Criterion B and C reward. An hour of supervised studio time a week for a term usually does more for a visual arts grade than four paid sessions.

The third is the city itself. Gallery access in Dubai is frequently free, including the commercial spaces at Alserkal Avenue in Al Quoz and institutional programming elsewhere. A student who visits, photographs, annotates and writes four structured sentences about one work has produced Criterion D evidence at no cost. Group classes at Dubai tuition centres, at roughly AED 90 to 180 per student, sit between these free options and one-to-one: fine for shared technique and vocabulary, weak for individual criterion diagnosis. Where a tutor is genuinely the right purchase, it is usually for intention, critique and journal structure, which are the things a club cannot supply.

sections.heading: Eight questions to ask before you pay any Dubai tutor
paragraphs: Hourly rate is the least informative question in this market, because two providers at AED 250 can be selling substantially different things. These eight questions separate them, they can all be asked in a single phone call, and the speed and specificity of the answers is itself diagnostic. A provider who answers all eight directly is a different proposition from one who redirects to a sales call.

Ask whether the tutor holds a current MoHRE private tuition work permit. Private tuition in the UAE runs under Ministerial Resolution No. 710 of 2023, the permit is granted free of charge for two years, and u.ae states that individuals tutoring without one are subject to fines and penalties under the applicable laws. No fine schedule is published, so any amount quoted at you is unverifiable. Ask who employs the tutor, and ask whether any student they teach attends their own school, because in Abu Dhabi ADEK's professional-ethics rules bar school staff from paid tutoring of their own enrolled students and the permit's code of conduct points the same way.

Ask whether the quoted figure includes VAT and whether the provider holds a Tax Registration Number. Ask whether marking between sessions is inside the rate. Ask what happens if the match is wrong, and whether a replacement costs anything. Ask whether unused sessions in a package lapse or carry over. Ask what the cancellation notice is on a single session. And ask for one sentence describing what your child will have in writing after four weeks.

Two things nobody should be able to offer you. A promise of a particular grade, which no tutor can deliver in any subject and which is a reliable signal to walk away. And any form of standing in for the student: a provider offering to supply a finished Personal Project report, or to make arts work a student then submits as their own, is proposing something that puts the student at risk of an IB academic-honesty finding, not the tutor. One competitor in this market sells completed Internal Assessments. That is the standard the honest end of the market is being compared against.

Is the quoted figure VAT-inclusive, and do you hold a TRN?
Is marking between sessions inside the rate or billed separately?
What happens if the match is wrong, and does a replacement cost anything?
Do unused package sessions lapse, carry over or get returned?
What notice is needed to cancel a single session?
What will we have in writing after four weeks?
Who employs the tutor, and does any student attend their own school?

sections.heading: What IB Gram actually charges, and why the first lesson is free
paragraphs: We do not publish a single rate for this page, and the reason is not coyness. MYP Arts spans five disciplines and five year groups, and the work ranges from two sessions writing an artistic intention to a six-session exhibition block with journal marking between each one. A headline number across all of that would have to be either the highest figure, which would be dishonest, or an average, which would be useless to everyone.

What we do instead: the first lesson is free, it produces something you keep, and the rate is quoted after it when the scope is known. The free lesson is sixty minutes with an arts specialist who reads the journal as an assessor would and ends the session with your child having written a real artistic intention for their current piece. There is no card required to book it and no obligation afterwards. If the tutor is not right for your child, you have spent an hour and gained an intention and a journal diagnosis.

Where we sit in the bands above: the qualified-subject and IB-specialist tiers, not the budget tier, because criterion marking and journal reading take time outside the lesson and a rate that does not cover that produces a tutor who does not do it. We are not in the premium examiner-led tier, because examiner positioning has little meaning for MYP portfolio work and we do not describe tutors as examiners without current evidence of that status.

Three things we will not do, stated plainly because the alternative is implied by silence. We hold no KHDA, ADEK, SPEA, MoE, MoHRE, IB or Cambridge approval, accreditation, licensing or partnership, and we will not imply one; we are an independent tutor-matching platform. We make no promise about a grade or a level of improvement, in arts or anything else. And a tutor will not make work or write journal entries a student submits as their own, because the consequence of that falls on your child.

sections.heading: Timing the spend across a Dubai school year
paragraphs: Most families overspend on arts tutoring by buying it evenly across the year when the need is lumpy. Dubai MYP arts assessment clusters: unit assessment points through the term, an exhibition or showcase before the winter break, a whole-school production often in the spring, and for MYP 5 a portfolio deadline that the school sets well ahead of anything external. Spending matched to those points costs less and achieves more than a flat weekly commitment.

The highest-value purchase in the year is early and small: one or two sessions at the start of a unit to write a real artistic intention and set up the journal. Everything downstream in Criteria C and D depends on that, and it costs a fraction of trying to reconstruct it at the end. The second highest-value purchase is a short block before the school's own assessment point, focused on realisation and critique rather than on new making.

Ramadan and the holiday periods change availability as well as timing. School days shorten, rehearsal and studio access changes, and the weeks either side of long breaks are poor bets for anything needing a full cast or a technician. Sessions shift to early afternoon or after iftar, and for arts the early-afternoon slot often works well because journal and critique work tolerates a quieter kind of attention than performance practice does. Book the shift a fortnight ahead; the good slots go first.

One last piece of arithmetic worth doing before committing to anything. Count the sessions you would buy across a year on a weekly basis, multiply by the band you have been quoted, and compare that figure with a fortnightly cadence through two units plus one six-session block before an exhibition. The second plan is usually a little over half the cost of the first, and for journal-led criteria it is the better pedagogy as well as the cheaper one. That is a genuinely unusual position for a tutoring page to take, and it is the one the evidence supports.

process.title: Tell us the discipline, the year and the deadline
process.description: Which art form, which MYP year, which school, and the next date anything is actually assessed. The deadline matters more than the subject for pricing, because a six-session exhibition block and two sessions on an artistic intention are different purchases with different totals.

process.title: Take the free trial lesson first
process.description: Sixty minutes with an arts specialist, no payment and no card. The tutor reads the journal as an assessor would, and the session ends with your child having written a real artistic intention for their current piece. You keep that and the written journal diagnosis whatever you decide afterwards.

process.title: Get the quote in writing, with inclusions listed
process.description: After the trial we quote for the scope that the trial established, stating session length, whether marking between sessions is included, what happens to unused sessions and what a rematch costs. Ask the same of anyone else you are considering; the comparison is only meaningful at that level of detail.

process.title: Choose the cadence that fits the criteria
process.description: Fortnightly for journal, intention and critique work, because development happens between sessions. Weekly only for discipline technique. A fixed block before a school event. We will say which we think fits and why, including when the answer is fewer sessions than you asked for.

process.title: Review at the school's assessment point, then stop or continue
process.description: Arrangements end on a date rather than rolling on. At the school's assessment point the journal is read again against all four criteria and the gaps listed, and that is the natural moment to continue, change focus, change tutor or finish. Finishing is a normal outcome.

whyPoints.title: The numbers are on the page, attributed
whyPoints.description: Every AED band here names the provider or survey that published it and the month it was read. Three of the six competitor pages examined for this project publish no price at all and two quote in dollars. A sourced figure you can check beats a rate quoted on a sales call.

whyPoints.title: No travel in the rate, because there is no travel
whyPoints.description: Dubai in-home rates of AED 180 to 500 an hour carry forty to fifty minutes of term-time driving each way. Online delivery removes that and the geographic filter behind it, which for thin-supply arts disciplines is the difference between a specialist and whoever was nearby.

whyPoints.title: We will tell you when not to buy
whyPoints.description: The school's own arts teacher, school enrichment and free gallery access solve a fair share of MYP arts problems at no cost, and that is on this page in full. Where a tutor is the right purchase, it is usually for intention, critique and journal structure rather than for hours.

whyPoints.title: Fortnightly recommended over weekly where it fits
whyPoints.description: For journal-led criteria, development happens between sessions, so a fortnightly cadence through two units plus one pre-exhibition block costs little over half a weekly year and usually achieves more. We say so even though it halves the invoice.

whyPoints.title: The first lesson is free and leaves something behind
whyPoints.description: No card, no obligation, sixty minutes with a specialist. You keep a written journal diagnosis against the four criteria and a real artistic intention for the current piece. Any condition attached to a free offer should be stated on the same screen, and those are the only two: one lesson, one student.

whyPoints.title: Nothing claimed that cannot be shown
whyPoints.description: No regulator or board approval, because we hold none. No promises about what grade a student will reach. No examiner status without current evidence. No producing work a student submits as their own. And no fine amounts quoted for permit breaches, because no schedule is published.

faqs.question: How much does an MYP Arts tutor cost per hour in Dubai?
faqs.answer: Published Dubai rates read in October 2026 span roughly AED 45 to 150 for budget online tutoring, AED 150 to 300 for a qualified subject tutor online, AED 180 to 500 for an in-home visit with travel inside the rate, AED 200 to 450 or more for an IB specialist, and AED 650 at the premium end from one provider. Those are other providers' published figures, not ours. Honest MYP arts work, with criterion marking and journal reading, sits in the middle two bands. IB Gram quotes after a free trial lesson.

faqs.question: Why is an in-home arts tutor in Dubai so much more expensive?
faqs.answer: Mostly driving. Forty to fifty minutes each way in term-time traffic between the school belt and the outer communities sits inside the rate whether or not it is itemised, along with parking, building access and the fact that a tutor can serve fewer households a day. The second cost is invisible and larger for a minority subject: the tutor is drawn from whoever will make that drive, so in arts you often pay a premium and receive a generalist rather than a criterion specialist.

faqs.question: Does the rate differ between visual arts, music and drama?
faqs.answer: Yes, and the driver is supply rather than difficulty. Visual arts teaching is well supplied in Dubai and prices competitively. Music performance is priced as instrumental teaching, a separate and established market. Composition, film and dance are thinner, which pushes quotes towards the specialist band. Because the four MYP Arts criteria are identical across disciplines, intention and critique work transfers, so paying a scarcity premium for an exact art form is sometimes avoidable without losing anything.

faqs.question: Do tutoring rates in Dubai rise before exhibitions and productions?
faqs.answer: Published rates mostly hold; availability is what changes. Demand clusters in the weeks before a school exhibition, showcase or production, and the usable weekday slots between half past five and half past seven fill first. The practical consequence is that booking a pre-event block three or four weeks ahead costs the same as booking it one week ahead and is far more likely to get the slot you want. For MYP 5 portfolio deadlines the same applies, earlier.

faqs.question: Is the figure quoted per hour or per lesson, and is marking included?
faqs.answer: Ask both, because providers differ and the second question is where two equal-looking quotes separate. A ninety-minute session usually carries a lower per-hour figure than a sixty-minute one, since set-up cost spreads over more teaching. Marking between sessions takes real time outside the lesson: reading a process journal properly against four criteria is not a five-minute job, so a rate that does not account for it tends to produce a tutor who does not do it.

faqs.question: Is VAT included in a Dubai tutoring rate?
faqs.answer: Ask the provider directly, and ask whether they hold a Tax Registration Number. We deliberately do not state how UAE VAT applies to tuition fees on these pages, because we have no Federal Tax Authority citation for it and publishing a tax position without one across thousands of pages would be irresponsible. What matters to you is narrower and answerable: is the number you have been quoted the number you will pay, and can the provider invoice you properly.

faqs.question: What does a realistic monthly arts tutoring budget look like in Dubai?
faqs.answer: Lower than most families assume, because the need is lumpy rather than constant. A fortnightly cadence through a ten-week unit is five sessions, not twenty. Add a four-to-six session block before an exhibition or portfolio deadline and that is a year's sensible spend for most MYP arts students. Advertised packages in this market include AED 799 for eight online sessions, which gives a sense of the scale. Count sessions against assessment points rather than against weeks and the figure drops sharply.

faqs.question: How much should we budget for arts materials and instruments?
faqs.answer: Visual arts consumables for a term run roughly AED 60 to 250 bought at Dubai stationers and Al Quoz suppliers, and those are indicative ranges rather than quotations. Gallery access in this city is frequently free, which makes the highest-value Criterion D activity cost nothing. Instrument hire or purchase is the one genuinely large item, and school music departments often run schemes that undercut retail, so ask there before buying. Keep receipts; they are also project evidence.

faqs.question: Is a package cheaper than paying session by session?
faqs.answer: Usually, because providers trade a discount for certainty. Advertised examples in the Dubai market include AED 799 a month for eight online sessions and AED 1,599 to 1,799 for four two-hour in-home sessions. Before paying for one, ask three questions: do unused sessions lapse, carry over or come back to you; what notice cancels a single session; and is marking between sessions included. A package with unfavourable answers to those is more expensive than it looks.

faqs.question: Are group arts classes better value than one-to-one?
faqs.answer: Cheaper per student and weaker on the thing MYP Arts grades turn on. Dubai tuition centres commonly advertise group rates around AED 90 to 180 per student, and a group is a reasonable way to buy shared technique and vocabulary. What a group cannot easily deliver is individual criterion diagnosis: whether this student's artistic intention is a theme word, whether their journal shows exploration, whether their critique analyses or merely approves. That work is individual by nature.

faqs.question: What are the free or low-cost options in Dubai before we pay anyone?
faqs.answer: Three, all worth exhausting first. The school's own arts teacher, who can say which criterion is weakest and what the journal is missing, free and specific to that school's marking. School enrichment: arts clubs, ensembles, productions and studio access, often included in fees, which generate exactly the documented development Criteria B and C reward. And the city: gallery access here is frequently free, including the Al Quoz spaces, so structured critique of real work costs nothing but a Saturday.

faqs.question: What happens if we stop after the first paid session?
faqs.answer: You stop. Our first lesson is free in any case, and paid arrangements are quoted as single sessions or as blocks with a stated end date rather than as rolling commitments. Ask any Dubai provider what notice cancels a session and what happens to a part-used package before you pay, because that answer varies far more across this market than the hourly rate does. No tutor can promise a particular outcome, so an arrangement you can leave cleanly is the protection that actually matters.

faqs.question: Does a higher rate mean a better tutor for MYP Arts?
faqs.answer: Up to a point, then no. Below roughly the qualified-subject band, a rate cannot cover the time it takes to read a process journal against four criteria, so marking tends not to happen. Above the specialist band, the premium is usually examiner positioning, which means little for MYP portfolio work because it is moderated rather than examined as Diploma components are. The useful question is not the number but what the number includes: criterion marking, journal reading, and a specialist in the right discipline.

faqs.question: Do you charge more for a tutor to visit our home in Dubai?
faqs.answer: We do not offer it at any price. IB Gram does not provide home visits in Dubai or anywhere in the UAE; home visits are a service we run only in India. UAE lessons are one-to-one over live video on Gulf Standard Time. For MYP Arts that removes the travel component from the rate and widens the tutor pool from a drive radius to a specialist market, which matters most in exactly the disciplines where Dubai supply is thinnest: composition, film and dance.

faqs.question: Is a private tuition permit something we end up paying for?
faqs.answer: No, and nobody should be passing a cost for it to you. The MoHRE private tutor work permit, introduced under Ministerial Resolution No. 710 of 2023, is granted free of charge for two years, and MoHRE's own service page lists no fee and a two-working-day completion time. Eligible applicants include registered school teachers, government and private-sector employees, unemployed residents, university students and school students aged 15 to 18. Individuals tutoring without a permit face fines and penalties under the applicable laws, though no schedule of amounts is published.

dubai/ib-myp-arts-home-tutor.closingHeading: Price the scope, not the hour
dubai/ib-myp-arts-home-tutor.closingBody: The useful question is not what an hour costs in Dubai but how many hours this actually needs, and that is answerable in one free lesson. An arts specialist reads the process journal against the four criteria, your child writes a real artistic intention for their current piece, and you get both in writing along with a list of the strands that have nothing pointing at them. Then the quote covers that scope: two sessions, a fortnightly unit, or a block before an exhibition. No card to book, no obligation afterwards, and no travel in the rate because nobody is driving. Tell us the discipline, the MYP year and the next date anything is assessed.

dubai/ib-myp-arts-tutor.tutorsIntro: The tutors below teach within the MYP arts framework rather than offering general art, music or drama lessons. That means reading a process journal before looking at a finished piece, and marking against criteria rather than against taste.

intro.heading: Why strong work and a middling grade go together so often in MYP Arts
paragraphs: Arts is the MYP subject where the gap between quality and grade is widest, and the reason is structural. Four criteria, eight marks each. Criterion A is knowing and understanding: the concepts, processes and vocabulary of the art form, its role in context, and the use of that knowledge to inform the student's own work. Criterion B is developing skills: the acquisition of technique and its application to create, perform or present. Criterion C is thinking creatively: a feasible, clear, imaginative and coherent artistic intention, a range of creative-thinking behaviours, and the exploration of ideas through to realisation. Criterion D is responding: constructing meaning, transferring learning to new settings, creating a response that reflects on or affects the world, and critiquing the work of self and others.

Read that list and the pattern becomes obvious. Criterion B is the one most parents assume is the subject, and it is a quarter of the marks. A student who paints well, plays well or performs well has secured eight marks and is competing for twenty-four others on grounds that have nothing to do with how good the output is. The talented student who makes beautiful work and documents nothing finishes level with a less fluent student who stated an intention, explored it visibly, and critiqued the result honestly.

Criterion C is where most Dubai MYP arts students lose the grade. A clear artistic intention is a sentence, written before the work begins, stating what the piece is trying to do and for whom. Students write titles instead: 'Identity', 'Belonging', 'Water'. A theme is not an intention. 'I want to make a viewer notice how much water a household wastes by turning the sound of a running tap into something uncomfortable' is an intention, because it can be explored, revised and judged against. Without one, the exploration strand has nothing to explore and the realisation strand has nothing to arrive at.

Criterion D is the second leak and the easier fix. Responding asks for critique, of the student's own work and of other artists', and for a response that connects outwards. 'I like this painting because the colours are nice' scores nothing. A critique names what a work does, how it does it technically, what it is for, and what the student takes from it into their own practice. Dubai is unusually good terrain for this, because the city has real galleries and venues a student can actually visit, which beats writing about a reproduction in a textbook.

Lessons are delivered online, one-to-one, over live video. IB Gram does not offer home visits in Dubai or anywhere else in the UAE; home visits are a service we run only in India. For arts this works better than families expect. Journal pages, photographs of work in progress, recordings of a performance and score files are all screen artefacts, and reviewing them on a shared screen is how an assessor will see them too. For music and drama, a recording can be stopped, replayed and discussed, which a live room rarely allows.
bullets: Four criteria of eight marks each; technique is only one of them
An artistic intention is a sentence with a purpose, not a theme word
Criterion D wants critique and connection, not preference
The process journal is the evidence base for all four criteria
Dubai's galleries and venues make Criterion D work easier than most cities
Lessons are online one-to-one with journal and portfolio on screen

dubai/ib-myp-arts-tutor.programmesIntro: Arts runs through all three IB programmes in different shapes, and the documentation habits built in the middle years are what make the Diploma versions manageable.

programmes.name: Primary Years Programme
programmes.description: Arts appears as a subject and inside units of inquiry, assessed descriptively rather than against criteria. The habit that pays off later is talking about intention before making: asking a nine-year-old what they want a viewer to feel, and writing the answer down, is the same skill Criterion C will assess at fifteen.
programmes.countryNote: Dubai PYP arts provision varies from specialist teachers and dedicated studios to a classroom corner. If arts matters to your family, ask at a Year 5 open evening who teaches it, how many timetabled sessions there are, and whether students keep a journal, because the answer predicts the MYP experience.

programmes.name: Middle Years Programme
programmes.ageRange: Ages 11-16 · Years 7-11, labelled MYP 1 to MYP 5
programmes.description: Arts is one of the eight subject groups, covering visual arts, music, drama or theatre, dance and film or media depending on what the school offers. The four criteria are the same across every discipline, which is why a music student and a visual arts student have identical problems with Criterion C despite working in different media.
programmes.countryNote: Many Dubai schools run arts on a rotation in MYP 1 to 3, with students taking two or three disciplines for a term each before specialising in MYP 4 and 5. That makes early grades hard to compare and makes the MYP 4 choice more consequential than it looks on the options form.

programmes.name: Diploma Programme
programmes.description: Group 6 holds Visual Arts, Music, Theatre, Film and Dance. Each has a substantial documented component — a process portfolio, an exhibition, a research presentation or a project — and each rewards precisely the journal habits MYP Arts is trying to build. Students who documented properly in MYP 5 find DP1 recognisable; students who did not find it brutal.
programmes.countryNote: Not every Dubai IB school offers every Group 6 subject, and some require students to take a second science or humanity instead. Ask in MYP 4 which Group 6 options are timetabled and which ran last year, because a subject offered on paper and a subject that filled are different things.

dubai/ib-myp-arts-tutor.subjectsIntro: MYP Arts covers several disciplines under one set of criteria. These are the ones Dubai families ask us about, with what the work actually involves in each.

subjects.name: MYP Visual Arts
subjects.description: Drawing, painting, print, sculpture, digital and mixed media. Criterion B is technique and its application; the marks usually missing are in the journal, where exploration of a stated intention should be visible across pages rather than appearing fully formed in a final piece.

subjects.name: MYP Music
subjects.description: Performance, composition and listening. Criterion A rewards real vocabulary about structure, harmony and context rather than general enthusiasm. Composition work is where intention matters most, because a piece written without a stated purpose cannot be revised towards anything.

subjects.name: MYP Drama and Theatre
subjects.description: Devising, performing and responding, often with ensemble work that complicates individual assessment. The journal carries the individual evidence: rehearsal notes, decisions taken, what changed after feedback. Students who rely on the performance alone lose Criterion C and D entirely.

subjects.name: MYP Dance
subjects.description: Choreography and performance against the same four criteria. Recorded rehearsals are the most useful evidence, because they show development over time rather than an outcome. Dubai schools offering dance within MYP Arts are fewer than those offering music or visual arts.

subjects.name: MYP Film and Media Arts
subjects.description: Moving image, editing and media language. Criterion A vocabulary here is technical and teachable, which makes it a reliable source of marks. Criterion D works well in this discipline because critique of a film is a familiar activity that just needs structuring.

subjects.name: The MYP Arts process journal
subjects.description: The evidence base for all four criteria across every discipline. Not a sketchbook of good drawings and not a diary: a record of intention, experiments, failures, research into other practitioners, and critique. Strands not evidenced here are difficult to award however strong the final piece.

subjects.name: DP Visual Arts
subjects.description: A comparative study, a process portfolio and an exhibition with curatorial rationale. The process portfolio is a direct continuation of a well-kept MYP journal, which is the single strongest argument for taking the journal seriously three years earlier.

subjects.name: DP Music
subjects.description: Exploring music in context, experimenting with music, and presenting music, with a contemporary music-maker project at HL. Requires written reflection on practice, so students arriving from MYP with reflective habits have a real head start over more technically fluent peers without them.

subjects.name: DP Theatre
subjects.description: Director's notebook, research presentation, collaborative project and, at HL, a solo theatre piece. Documentation-heavy in a way that surprises students who chose it for the performing, and smooth for anyone who kept real rehearsal notes in MYP.

subjects.name: DP Film
subjects.description: Textual analysis, comparative study and a film portfolio. Transfers well from MYP film or media arts, and also from visual arts for students comfortable with sustained written analysis of an image.

subjects.name: MYP Personal Project
subjects.description: Arts students often choose a creative Personal Project, which is a good fit and a common trap, because the Personal Project criteria are not the Arts criteria. A tutor questions the goal, discusses sources and gives feedback. The student writes every word of the report and the process journal themselves.

dubai/ib-myp-arts-tutor.regionsTitle: Dubai communities and the arts resources near them
dubai/ib-myp-arts-tutor.regionsIntro: Criterion D rewards engagement with real work by real practitioners, and Dubai supplies more of that than most cities its size. The notes below pair each community with what is genuinely reachable from it.

regions.name: Al Quoz and Alserkal Avenue
regions.note: Dubai's gallery district, built into converted warehouses, with commercial galleries and project spaces within walking distance of each other. A single afternoon here produces enough primary material for a term of Criterion D critique, which beats writing about reproductions.

regions.name: Dubai Design District and Business Bay
regions.note: Design-led studios, exhibitions and events through the year, and the venues that host design week programming. Useful for students whose intention sits between art and design, and for film and media students looking at commercial practice.

regions.name: Jaddaf Waterfront and Dubai Healthcare City
regions.note: Home to a major contemporary art institution with a permanent collection, library and public programme. Free or low-cost access and a genuine research library make it the most useful single destination for a Dubai MYP arts student building Criterion A context.

regions.name: Umm Suqeim and Al Manara
regions.note: Villa communities within a short drive of both Al Quoz and the beach-side cultural venues. Schools here often have strong arts departments and well-attended productions, which makes ensemble drama assessment common and individual journal evidence correspondingly important.

regions.name: Downtown Dubai and Opera District
regions.note: A full-scale opera house with a year-round programme of music and theatre. For MYP music and drama students, a live professional performance with a programme to annotate is better Criterion D material than any recording, and the venue is reachable by Metro.

regions.name: Mirdif and Al Warqa
regions.note: Family communities with long bus routes and later evenings, so sessions start at six or half past. Arts requests from here skew towards music performance and composition, often alongside external instrumental grades that the MYP criteria do not directly recognise.

regions.name: The Springs, The Meadows and Jumeirah Park
regions.note: Villa belt with good home space for making, which helps visual arts students more than it helps musicians in attached housing. Practice-noise constraints are a real scheduling factor for percussion and brass students here, and shape when sessions can run.

schoolClusters.city: Al Quoz, Al Manara and Umm Suqeim
schoolClusters.note: Schools in Dubai's central belt, close to the gallery district. Students we support in this cluster often have strong technical teaching and well-resourced studios, so the work in sessions is usually intention, journal development and critique rather than skills.

schoolClusters.city: Mirdif, Al Warqa and Dubai Festival City
schoolClusters.note: The eastern residential belt, where arts requests lean towards music and performance. Students we support here frequently hold external instrumental grades, and part of the work is translating that technical ability into evidence the MYP criteria actually reward.

dubai/ib-myp-arts-tutor.modesIntro: Three formats cover most MYP Arts requests. All are delivered online one-to-one, with the student's journal, portfolio or recordings shared on screen.

modes.title: Journal and intention sessions, fortnightly
modes.description: The format that moves Criterion C and D. Every fortnight the student brings the journal as it stands and the tutor reads it the way an assessor would: is there a stated intention, is exploration visible, is there critique of self and others. Work is set between sessions and reviewed in the next.

Fortnightly cadence, because development needs time to happen

Criterion B is a quarter of the marks and it is the most teachable quarter.

sections.heading: The four Arts criteria and the strands behind each of them
paragraphs: MYP Arts is scored on four criteria of eight marks each, the same four across visual arts, music, drama, dance and film. That uniformity is the most useful fact about the subject, because it means a student's problem is rarely medium-specific. A painter who cannot state an intention and a composer who cannot state an intention are losing marks in exactly the same strand, and the fix is the same conversation.

Criterion A, knowing and understanding, asks for knowledge of the art form including concepts, processes and vocabulary, knowledge of its role in context, and the use of that knowledge to inform the student's own work. The third of those is the one students miss: knowing about an artist is not the same as showing that the knowledge changed what they made. Criterion B, developing skills, asks for the acquisition and development of technique and its application to create, perform or present. It is the most teachable criterion and the one that improves with practice rather than with insight.

Criterion C, thinking creatively, asks for a feasible, clear, imaginative and coherent artistic intention, a range and depth of creative-thinking behaviours, and the exploration of ideas to shape that intention through to a point of realisation. Criterion D, responding, asks the student to construct meaning and transfer learning to new settings, to create an artistic response that reflects on or affects the world around them, and to critique the artwork of self and others.

Read the table against the student's journal rather than against the finished pieces, because the journal is where three of the four criteria are actually evidenced. A folder with excellent final work and no stated intention, no recorded exploration and no critique is a predictable five, and that is as true at an outstanding Dubai school with a well-equipped studio as it is anywhere else.

sections.heading: Artistic intention: one sentence that carries eight marks and shapes the rest
paragraphs: The single highest-value exercise in MYP Arts takes twenty minutes and most students have never been made to do it. Write, in one or two sentences, what this piece is trying to do, to whom, and by what means. Not what it is about. What it is trying to do. The difference is the difference between a theme and an intention, and Criterion C assesses the second one.

Compare two versions. 'My piece is about identity' is a theme; it cannot be explored, because there is no claim to test and no audience to affect. 'I want a viewer who has moved countries as a child to recognise the feeling of having two accents, by layering two self-portraits so neither is fully visible' is an intention. It is feasible, it is clear, it names a means, and it can be revised: the layering can be tried three ways and the best one chosen for a stated reason. That is the exploration strand, evidenced automatically by work that was already going to happen.

The same logic holds in every discipline. A composition brief of 'something sad' gives a student nothing to revise towards; 'a thirty-second cue that makes a listener expect something that never arrives, using an unresolved suspension' can be drafted, tested on a listener and improved. A devised drama piece about 'bullying' is a theme; 'a two-minute scene where the audience realises they have been laughing with the aggressor' is an intention that can be rehearsed towards.

In Dubai this exercise has an additional benefit worth naming. MYP arts cohorts here are highly international and most students have genuine material in their own experience — moving countries, holding two languages, living between a passport country and a home city. That specificity makes intentions easier to write and far more interesting to realise than the generic themes students default to. The tutor's job is mostly to refuse the theme and wait for the sentence.

sections.heading: The process journal: what an assessor is looking for on each page
paragraphs: Two misconceptions about the arts journal are near-universal. The first is that it is a sketchbook of good work, so students put their best drawings in it and keep the experiments elsewhere. The second is that it is a diary, so they write about how they felt and what they did at the weekend. It is neither. It is the evidence base from which three of the four criteria are assessed, and it should look like a working document rather than a presentation piece.

What belongs in it: the stated intention, dated. Experiments, including the ones that failed, with a line about what the failure showed. Research into practitioners, with a note about what was taken from them into the student's own work, which is the third strand of Criterion A. Feedback received and what changed because of it. Critique of the student's own work in progress. Technical notes about media, instruments or staging. Photographs or recordings of stages, dated so development is visible.

What does not belong: pages of copied biography about a famous artist with no connection to the student's own work, final pieces presented without the stages that led to them, and reflections written in one sitting the night before submission. That last one is visible, because a journal written retrospectively has uniform handwriting, consistent ink and no mess, which is a different document from one kept over ten weeks.

For Dubai students working digitally, a digital journal is fine and often better, provided the dating is genuine and the development visible. Layer histories, version files and dated screenshots are strong evidence. What does not work is a tidy slide deck assembled at the end, for the same reason the retrospective sketchbook does not: the criteria reward the process, and a document with no process in it cannot evidence process however attractive it looks.

sections.heading: Criterion D: turning 'I like it' into a critique that scores
paragraphs: Criterion D is the second big leak in MYP Arts and the one that improves fastest with a structure. It asks three things: construct meaning and transfer learning to new settings, create an artistic response that reflects on or affects the world around the student, and critique the artwork of self and others. The strand that trips everybody is the critique, because students have been taught to be polite about art rather than analytical about it.

A critique that scores does four things. It describes what the work actually does, in the vocabulary of the art form. It explains how, technically. It says what the work appears to be for, and on what evidence. And it states what the student takes from it into their own practice, which is the bridge to Criterion A's third strand. Four sentences, in that order, about one work, is worth more than a page of appreciation about five works.

Dubai makes the raw material easy. The city has a contemporary art institution with a permanent collection and research library at Jaddaf Waterfront, a gallery district in converted warehouses at Alserkal Avenue in Al Quoz, a full-scale opera house in Downtown, design-led exhibition programming in Dubai Design District, and major institutions a short drive away in Sharjah and Abu Dhabi. A student who writes about work they have stood in front of produces better critique than one working from a textbook plate, and the difference is visible in the marking.

The response strand is the one to take seriously rather than literally. 'Reflects or impacts on the world around them' does not require a political statement; it requires a connection outwards from the student's own practice to something real. A piece about water use in a villa community, a composition responding to the sound of a particular neighbourhood, a scene about arriving at a new school mid-year: all of these connect outward, and all are more honest than a grand gesture a fifteen-year-old does not mean.

sections.heading: Five disciplines, one set of criteria: what changes and what does not
paragraphs: Dubai schools offer different combinations of arts disciplines, and many run a rotation in MYP 1 to 3 before students specialise in MYP 4 and 5. Parents reasonably assume that a music grade and a visual arts grade mean different things. They do not: the criteria are identical, the strands are identical, and the weighting is identical. What changes is what Criterion B evidence looks like and what the journal physically contains.

That has a practical consequence for tutoring. A student struggling with Criterion C in music does not need a composition specialist to fix the intention problem; they need someone who will refuse to accept 'something sad' as a brief. Skills work is discipline-specific and needs the right specialist. Intention, exploration and critique work transfers across disciplines, which is useful in a city where some arts specialisms are thinly staffed.

It also matters for the MYP 4 choice. A student who has rotated through three disciplines has three partial grades that are not really comparable, because an eight-week rotation cannot evidence development the way a year can. Choosing a specialism on the basis of those grades is a mistake; choosing on the basis of which journal the student actually enjoyed keeping is a better predictor of a good MYP 5 and of whether Group 6 at Diploma is a sensible plan.

The table sets out what each discipline's evidence looks like in practice, plus the Dubai-specific constraint we encounter most often in each. The constraints are mundane — practice noise in attached housing, rehearsal time competing with a school production, recording equipment — and they are the kind of thing that decides whether a session is productive or a polite hour.

sections.heading: Performances, exhibitions and the Dubai school calendar
paragraphs: Arts assessment in Dubai schools tends to cluster around two kinds of event: an end-of-unit exhibition or showcase, and a whole-school production or concert. Both compress several criteria into a short window, and both tend to eat the journal. Students rehearse or install for three weeks and write nothing, then submit a folder with a gap exactly where the most interesting development happened.

The fix is cheap and has to be insisted on. A phone photograph, a thirty-second voice note or three sentences a day during an intense period preserves the evidence that the period generated. Rehearsal notes written on the day are worth more than a polished reflection written afterwards, because they record decisions rather than reconstructing them. For an ensemble production, this is often the only individual evidence a student will have, and without it the marks default to the group's outcome.

The Dubai calendar adds its own shape. Productions and showcases cluster before the winter break and in the spring term. Ramadan shortens school days, changes rehearsal availability and moves evening events, and the weeks either side of long holidays are poor bets for anything requiring a full cast or a technician. A student with a spring exhibition should be building the journal through the winter term rather than planning to catch up.

One scheduling note specific to how we work: sessions sit mostly between half past five and half past seven Gulf Standard Time, because Dubai school buses from the outer communities do not deliver students home much before five. During a production run, families often switch to a single longer session at the weekend instead of a weekday slot, which is straightforward when nobody has to drive anywhere, and genuinely difficult in an in-home arrangement where the tutor's travel window is fixed.

sections.heading: Subject matter, context and making work in the UAE
paragraphs: This comes up in almost every honest conversation with a Dubai arts family and almost never in anything published about the subject. Students here make work in a country with its own cultural norms and content expectations, and part of becoming a thoughtful artist is understanding the context you are working in rather than ignoring it or being quietly steered away from ideas without explanation.

The practical guidance we give is simple. Discuss the intention with the arts teacher before committing weeks of work to it, because a teacher knows the school's own position and will say so directly if asked early. Where an idea needs reshaping, treat that as a constraint to design within rather than a veto: constraints are normal in commissioned art and the ability to realise an intention within them is a genuinely higher-order skill than ignoring them. And separate the subject of a piece from its intention, because the same intention can usually be realised through different material.

There is a parallel in the formal curriculum worth knowing. Arabic, Islamic Education and Social and Moral Studies are required in every Dubai private school whatever international curriculum it is licensed for, with KHDA's requirements to be implemented from the start of the 2025-26 academic year, and KHDA specifies separate classes for Arabs and non-Arabs in Arabic as a first language, Islamic Education and Social Studies. For the mandatory subjects, using different or additional content without prior Ministry of Education permission is not permitted. Arts is not one of those subjects and has far more latitude, but the same instinct applies: ask first, design within the answer.

The upside is real and underused. Students who engage seriously with where they are making work produce more specific, more interesting pieces than those who import a generic international-school theme. Dubai's own cultural infrastructure, from the Al Quoz gallery district to institutions in Sharjah and Abu Dhabi, is a resource for exactly that, and a student whose practitioner research includes artists working in this region has a Criterion A advantage over one whose research stops at the usual textbook names.

sections.heading: MYP Arts into Group 6, and what to settle in MYP 4
paragraphs: Group 6 at Diploma holds Visual Arts, Music, Theatre, Film and Dance, and every one of them is more documentation-heavy than students expect. The comparative study and process portfolio in Visual Arts, the director's notebook and research presentation in Theatre, the written reflection in Music, the textual analysis in Film: all of them reward the journal habits MYP Arts is trying to install. A student who kept a real journal in MYP 5 arrives prepared. A student who did not finds the first term of DP1 unpleasant in a way that has nothing to do with talent.

The decision does not have to be made in MYP 4, but two things do. First, whether the school timetables the Group 6 subject in question, and whether last year's group actually ran: a subject offered in a prospectus and a subject that filled are different, and the alternative is usually a second science or humanity. Second, whether the student wants arts as a Diploma subject at all, because some universities and some course choices make a sixth-subject arts option costly in a way that is worth discussing honestly rather than romantically.

The honest framing we use with families is this. Take Group 6 arts if the student enjoys the documented, iterative part of making and not only the making. The students who thrive at DP level in these subjects are not always the most naturally gifted; they are the ones who can sustain a developing body of work over eighteen months and write about it clearly. That is a predictable trait and it is visible in MYP 4 to anyone who looks at the journal rather than at the final pieces.

For students not continuing with arts, the transferable gain is still substantial and worth stating. Writing a clear intention and then testing it against evidence is the same intellectual move as a science internal assessment hypothesis or an extended essay research question. A student who learns it in MYP Arts carries it into subjects where it is marked even more heavily, which is a reasonable answer to the parent who asks what the point of the journal was.

process.title: Tell us the discipline and send the journal
process.description: Which art form, which MYP year, which school, and the four criterion marks from the last report if the school publishes them. Then photographs or a scan of the journal as it stands, even if it is eight pages. The journal tells a specialist more in ten minutes than a conversation about how the subject is going.

process.title: A free trial lesson that produces an intention
process.description: Sixty minutes, no payment. The tutor reads the journal as an assessor would and the session ends with the student having written a real artistic intention for their current piece, in their own words. That sentence is usually the most valuable thing the first hour produces.

process.title: Decide which criterion is the focus
process.description: One criterion is named for the first month. For most Dubai arts students it is C or D rather than B, which occasionally disappoints a family hoping for technique lessons. The journal evidence decides it, and the decision is explained rather than asserted.

process.title: Work set between sessions, reviewed in the next
process.description: Arts development happens between lessons, not during them, which is why fortnightly often beats weekly for journal work. Each session ends with specific tasks: three variations to try, one practitioner to research with a taken-from note, one critique to write in four sentences.

process.title: Review before the school's assessment point
process.description: Before an exhibition, showcase or internal deadline, the journal gets read again against all four criteria and the gaps are listed. That review is the natural point to continue, change focus, change tutor or stop, and stopping is a legitimate outcome rather than a failure of the arrangement.

whyPoints.title: The journal read as an assessor reads it
whyPoints.description: Three of the four Arts criteria are evidenced in the journal rather than in the finished work, so that is where sessions start. Feedback names which strands a page evidences and which are empty, in the same framework the school marks against.

whyPoints.title: Intention before technique
whyPoints.description: The highest-value twenty minutes in this subject is writing a real artistic intention instead of a theme word. It is also the step almost nobody is made to take. Everything in Criterion C depends on it, and Criterion D gets easier once it exists.

whyPoints.title: Criterion work transfers across disciplines
whyPoints.description: The four criteria are identical in visual arts, music, drama, dance and film, so intention and critique work does not need a discipline specialist. That matters in a city where some arts specialisms are thinly staffed, because it widens who can usefully help.

whyPoints.title: Dubai's own cultural resources put to work
whyPoints.description: Criterion D rewards critique of real work, and this city supplies it: the Al Quoz gallery district, a contemporary art institution with a research library at Jaddaf Waterfront, an opera house in Downtown, and major institutions in Sharjah and Abu Dhabi. Standing in front of the work beats a textbook plate.

whyPoints.title: Honest about where the grade is going
whyPoints.description: If the technique is already strong, we say the marks are elsewhere rather than selling technique lessons. No tutor can promise a grade in this subject or any other, and the useful promise is a journal an assessor can award marks from.

whyPoints.title: A clear line on authorship
whyPoints.description: A tutor teaches technique, challenges an intention, suggests practitioners to look at and critiques work the student has made. The student makes the work and writes the journal. For the MYP Personal Project in particular that boundary is set out in writing, because an IB academic-honesty finding follows the student.

faqs.question: What are the four MYP Arts criteria and how much is each worth?
faqs.answer: Four criteria of eight marks each, identical across visual arts, music, drama, dance and film. Criterion A is knowing and understanding, covering the art form's concepts, processes and vocabulary, its role in context, and using that knowledge to inform the student's own work. Criterion B is developing skills. Criterion C is thinking creatively, including the artistic intention. Criterion D is responding, including critique of the student's own and others' work. Technique is therefore a quarter of the available marks, which surprises most families and explains a lot of grades.

faqs.question: My child's artwork is genuinely good but the Arts grade is a five. What is missing?
faqs.answer: Almost always Criterion C and Criterion D. Strong final pieces secure Criterion B and little else by themselves. If there is no artistic intention stated before the work started, the exploration strand has nothing to explore and the realisation strand has nothing to arrive at. If the journal contains no critique of other practitioners or of the student's own work in progress, Criterion D is largely unevidenced. That is up to sixteen marks sitting unclaimed next to excellent making, and it is fixable in a term.

faqs.question: What is an artistic intention, and why does it matter so much?
faqs.answer: A sentence or two, written before making, stating what the piece is trying to do, to whom, and by what means. 'My piece is about identity' is a theme and cannot be explored. 'I want a viewer who moved countries as a child to recognise the feeling of having two accents, by layering two self-portraits so neither is fully visible' is an intention: feasible, clear, with a named means, and revisable. Criterion C assesses the intention, the creative thinking around it, and its realisation, so one weak sentence costs marks three times over.

faqs.question: What should an MYP Arts process journal actually contain?
faqs.answer: The dated intention. Experiments, including failures, each with a line on what the failure showed. Practitioner research with a note on what was taken into the student's own work. Feedback received and what changed because of it. Self-critique while work is in progress. Technical notes. Dated photographs or recordings of stages so development is visible. What does not belong: copied artist biographies with no link to the work, final pieces with no stages behind them, and a folder written in one sitting the night before, which is visible to anyone reading it.

faqs.question: How do you tutor visual arts over video without being in the room?
faqs.answer: The camera points at the work rather than at the student, which is how studio critique functions anyway. Journal pages, studies and stages are reviewed on a shared screen, which is also how an assessor will see them. Media handling can be demonstrated and watched. What a video session cannot do is fix a piece physically, and it should not: the work has to be the student's. For digital and film work, screen sharing is simply better than looking over a shoulder at a laptop.

faqs.question: Can a tutor help with MYP Music composition without writing it?
faqs.answer: Yes, and the boundary is the same as in every discipline. A tutor can challenge a vague brief until a real intention exists, teach harmonic and structural vocabulary, listen to drafts and say precisely where the piece does not do what the student said it should, and show how to notate or produce it properly. A tutor does not compose bars the student submits as their own. That line is set out in writing before the first session, because an academic-honesty finding under IB rules attaches to the student.

faqs.question: How is MYP Drama assessed when the performance is an ensemble piece?
faqs.answer: Against the same four criteria as every other arts discipline, which creates a specific problem: the performance is shared and the marks are individual. The journal is the solution and often the only individual evidence available. Rehearsal notes written on the day, decisions the student personally took, what changed after feedback, and self-critique of their own contribution. A student who performs well in a strong ensemble and writes nothing is relying on the group's outcome to carry three criteria.

faqs.question: What does Criterion D 'responding' want in practice?
faqs.answer: Three things: constructing meaning and transferring learning to new settings, making work that reflects on or affects the world around the student, and critiquing their own and others' work. The critique is where marks are won. Describe what a work does in the vocabulary of the art form, explain how technically, say what it appears to be for and on what evidence, then state what you take from it into your own practice. Four sentences about one work beats a page of appreciation about five.

faqs.question: Is MYP Arts examined, or assessed by portfolio?
faqs.answer: Where a Dubai school registers MYP 5 students for IB MYP eAssessment, Arts is a portfolio subject, externally moderated against the same four criteria used throughout the programme. The two-hour on-screen examinations sit in Language and Literature, Individuals and Societies, Mathematics, Sciences and interdisciplinary learning. Plenty of Dubai IB continuum schools do not register at all and move students straight into the Diploma. Ask your MYP coordinator which route your school takes, and confirm all deadlines with the school and the IB's own guidance.

faqs.question: My child did three arts disciplines on rotation. How do we choose a specialism for MYP 4?
faqs.answer: Not from the rotation grades, which are not really comparable: an eight-week block cannot evidence development the way a year can, so the marks reflect the block more than the student. A better question is which journal the student actually enjoyed keeping, because Group 6 at Diploma and MYP 5 both reward sustained documented development rather than a single strong outcome. Ask the student which discipline they went back to voluntarily. That is a more reliable predictor than any of the three grades.

faqs.question: Are there limits on what subject matter my child can use in a Dubai school?
faqs.answer: Schools here work within UAE cultural norms and each has its own position, so the practical answer is to discuss the intention with the arts teacher before committing weeks of work to it. Where an idea needs reshaping, treat it as a design constraint rather than a veto; realising an intention within a constraint is a higher-order skill than ignoring one. It also helps to separate the subject of a piece from its intention, because the same intention can usually be realised through different material.

faqs.question: Where in Dubai can my child see work to support Criterion D?
faqs.answer: The Al Quoz gallery district at Alserkal Avenue holds commercial galleries and project spaces within walking distance of each other. There is a contemporary art institution with a permanent collection and a research library at Jaddaf Waterfront. Downtown has a full-scale opera house with a year-round music and theatre programme. Dubai Design District runs design-led exhibitions. Major institutions in Sharjah and Abu Dhabi are a drive away. Critique of work a student has stood in front of marks better than critique of a textbook plate.

faqs.question: How many sessions does MYP Arts support usually need?
faqs.answer: Fortnightly tends to beat weekly for journal, intention and critique work, because development happens between sessions rather than during them. A typical arrangement is fortnightly through a unit, with a block of four to six sessions before an exhibition, showcase or internal deadline. Technique work in a specific discipline suits weekly. Most Dubai families we work with run a term of fortnightly sessions, then stop once the student is keeping the journal properly without being chased.

faqs.question: What does arts tutoring cost in Dubai per hour?
faqs.answer: Market rates read across Dubai providers in October 2026 run roughly AED 45 to 150 for budget online tutoring, AED 150 to 300 for a qualified subject tutor online, AED 180 to 500 for an in-home visit with travel inside the rate, and AED 200 to 450 or more for an IB specialist. One premium provider publishes AED 650. Those are other providers' figures, not ours. Arts is a smaller pool than the sciences, so specialist bands apply more often. IB Gram quotes after the free trial lesson.

faqs.question: Should my child take an arts subject in the Diploma at all?
faqs.answer: Take Group 6 if the student enjoys the documented, iterative side of making and not only the making itself. Every Group 6 subject is documentation-heavy: a comparative study and process portfolio in Visual Arts, a director's notebook in Theatre, written reflection in Music, textual analysis in Film. The students who do well are not always the most naturally gifted but the ones who sustain a developing body of work over eighteen months. Check too that the school timetables the subject and that last year's group actually filled.

dubai/ib-myp-arts-tutor.closingHeading: Send the journal, not the best piece
dubai/ib-myp-arts-tutor.closingBody: If an arts grade is lower than the work deserves, the diagnosis is almost always in the journal rather than in the portfolio. Three of the four criteria are evidenced there: the stated intention, the visible exploration, the practitioner research that changed something, and the critique. A specialist can read it as an assessor would in about ten minutes and tell you which strands have nothing pointing at them. That is what the free trial lesson produces, along with a real artistic intention for the current piece written in your child's own words. Tell us the discipline, the MYP year and the school, and we will match an arts specialist.

intro.heading: What a Dubai MYP Biology hour really costs
paragraphs: Pricing is the question almost every Dubai tutoring page avoids. Of the UAE providers reviewed for this site in October 2026, three published no figure at all, and two quoted in US dollars, a currency no family here transacts in. One agency's own frequently-asked-questions block asks what tutoring costs and then declines to answer. So the first useful thing a page about an IB MYP Biology home tutor in Dubai can do is publish the bands, say where they came from, and be clear about which of them is a market figure rather than an IB Gram figure.

The ranges are wide for a reason. An hour of MYP Biology support is not one product. At the bottom of the market sits a university student working online from outside the Gulf, with published entry rates from around AED 33 to 65 an hour. In the middle sits a qualified subject teacher online, generally AED 150 to 300. Above that sit IB and IGCSE specialists at roughly AED 200 to 450, and a small premium tier quoting AED 500 to 650 for named or examiner-experienced tutors. In-home visits cut across those tiers and add travel: a rate survey of the Dubai market puts in-home one-to-one at AED 180 to 350, while independent home tutors advertise AED 200 to 500.

The gap between the online and in-home band is not a quality gap. It is a logistics gap. A tutor who drives to a villa in Arabian Ranches for a 17:00 session has committed perhaps two and a half hours to deliver sixty minutes of teaching, and the rate has to carry the other ninety. That is defensible economics, and it is also why in-home tutoring tends to be bought in two-hour blocks: the travel only makes sense if the sitting is long. For a twelve-year-old working on one criterion strand of an MYP Sciences investigation, a two-hour sitting is not better teaching. It is just more of it.

There is a second cost nobody itemises, which is the narrowing of the pool. Inside a 20-minute drive of any Dubai community there may be a handful of tutors who can teach science to a secondary student. There are far fewer who have taught the MYP Sciences criteria, can read a criterion sheet, and know the difference between what criterion B wants and what criterion C wants. Buying by postcode means buying from whoever is near, and for a criterion-marked programme that is the wrong selection filter at any price.

IB Gram does not send a tutor to a Dubai address. Home visits are a service we run only in India, and there are no home visits anywhere in the UAE. Every UAE lesson is one-to-one over live video, scheduled in Gulf Standard Time, with the student's own marked work shared on screen. That removes the travel component from the price and replaces a geographic shortlist with a subject shortlist, which for MYP Biology is the part that actually changes the grade.

The rest of this page is the arithmetic. What the market charges by tier and format, what a term and a year come to at one and two sessions a week, how tutoring sits beside Dubai school fees now that KHDA has confirmed no fee increase for 2026-27, what the MoHRE permit does and does not add to your bill, and how to read a quote so that two Dubai providers can actually be compared.
