sections.heading: Can an extended tutor be shared between two children?
paragraphs: Families in villa communities ask this constantly, and the honest answer is mostly no, with two useful exceptions. Two students in different programme years are working on different content and usually different criteria, so a shared live session shortchanges both: the younger one watches work they cannot access, the older one waits. Where the children are in the same extended set at the same school, a paired session can work for content teaching, though not for criterion coaching, because the assessed work has to stay individual.

What can genuinely be shared is the diagnostic and the file. A single household review that reads both children's marked work costs less than two separate intakes and produces a plan the family reads once. Staggered slots on the same evening are the other practical economy: two consecutive sessions are far easier for a Dubai household to protect than two commitments on different nights, and protecting the slot is worth more than any discount.

Group classes at tuition centres are the other version of this question. They are cheaper per hour and are a different product: the centre's sequence at a shared pace, with no engagement with your child's task sheet or clarification. For broad revision in an examination year that can be reasonable value. For extended algebra, where the whole difficulty is sequencing against one student's specific gap, it is not.

One thing to avoid: paying specialist rates for a group. If a provider offers extended-route coaching in a group of four at a near-specialist rate, ask how the hour divides and what happens when the four students need different topics, which they will by the second week. Extended content is unforgiving about sequencing, and a shared pace reintroduces exactly the problem the tutoring was bought to solve.

sections.heading: Ministry of Education equivalency: what you do not need to buy
paragraphs: Extended-route families planning UAE university applications often ask whether tutoring is needed for the Ministry of Education equivalency process. It is not. Equivalency is an administrative recognition of a certificate against stated requirements, handled through the official channel, and no tutoring provider performs it, guarantees it or speeds it up. Anyone implying otherwise is selling urgency about a regulatory process, which is a thing to walk away from.

The published requirements are worth knowing because they are specific and one ranking competitor states them wrongly. For the British track, students must show one accredited subject at Advanced Level with a grade no lower than E, or two accredited subjects at Advanced Subsidiary Level at the same grade, and must pass five accredited subjects at GCSE or International GCSE with a grade no lower than E or grade 3. Arabic and Islamic education are not included among the five required subjects. A competitor page stating that UAE candidates must take six International GCSE subjects is simply incorrect on the published rule.

For the American track, English proficiency is evidenced by a score of 5 in the IELTS academic test, 61 in the TOEFL iBT, or 450 in the reading and writing section of the SAT, and mathematics requires at least 450 in the SAT Math test before applying. For the International Baccalaureate there is no points figure we are prepared to publish, because the source we read does not state one. Verify any IB equivalency threshold on the Ministry's own site or with the attestation authority rather than taking it from a tutoring page, including this one.

The table summarises what each track must show and where to verify it. The point of including it on a page about tutoring cost is subtraction: this is a part of the process you do not need to spend money on, and knowing that is worth as much as any rate comparison.

sections.heading: What a premium does not buy, and how lessons are delivered
paragraphs: Some things cost more and are worth it: recognition of the problem in the first session, correct sequencing of extended topics, and an estimate of hours you can hold a provider to. Some things cost more and are not. A tutor described as an examiner, where the status cannot be evidenced, is a marketing claim rather than a teaching advantage, and examiner status does not grant access to marking, boundaries or paper content. Any implication otherwise should be treated with scepticism.

Nor does a premium buy an outcome. No honest tutor promises a grade, a points total or a specific improvement, and any provider offering money back against a grade has either published terms that make the promise conditional on things outside your control, or has not thought about it. We publish no grade promise, no star rating of our own invention, and no statistic about our students without the sample size, date and method on the same page.

Delivery is online, one-to-one, over live video on Gulf Standard Time, with a shared whiteboard the student writes on and a recording the family keeps. IB Gram does not arrange home visits in Dubai; home tutoring is a service we offer only in India. The in-home figures quoted throughout this page are market context for a service we do not sell, published because the question is reasonable and deserves an answer rather than a deflection.

Private tutoring in the UAE is regulated, and that is in your favour when assessing a quote. Individuals providing private lessons need a private tuition work permit from the Ministry of Human Resources and Emiratisation, introduced under Ministerial Resolution No. 710 of 2023 and granted free of charge for two years to eligible applicants, who include registered school teachers, government and private sector employees, unemployed residents, university students and school students aged 15 to 18. Working without one attracts fines and penalties under the applicable laws; the ministry has published no fine schedule, so any specific amount you are quoted is unverified. Since the permit is free, a tutor who lacks one has told you something useful.

process.title: Name the extended topic
process.description: Algebraic fractions, function transformations, non-right-angled trigonometry, criterion B justification, or catch-up after an absence. Extended work is block-shaped, so naming the topic produces an estimate rather than a subscription, and lets us tell you whether groundwork is needed first.

process.title: Ask the school what the set covered
process.description: Especially after travel. One email to the department asking which topics and assessments the set covered in your child's absence scopes the catch-up precisely. Without it, the first two sessions are reconnaissance you are paying specialist rates for.

process.title: Free 45-minute trial, one per family
process.description: A specialist reads marked work with your child present, tests whether the underlying algebra supports the extended topic, and gives a session estimate with a stated measure of success. No card details are taken. If the honest answer is that the set placement should be discussed with the school, you will hear that.

process.title: Book the block, not the year
process.description: Four to six sessions against the named topic, scheduled three weeks ahead of any related deadline, at a slot the household can protect. Weekly commitments are for students who are behind the set broadly rather than missing one topic, and the diagnosis says which.

process.title: Re-test cold, then decide on the next block
process.description: Each block ends with a cold attempt at the topic set or a comparison against a school-marked task. Then you decide again, with the four-year picture in view: the Year 10 route question, the bridging summer, and whether the Diploma course you are aiming at actually needs this route.

whyPoints.title: Quantities, not just rates
whyPoints.description: Every extended topic on this page carries a session estimate and a test of whether it landed. A rate without a quantity is an open-ended commitment, and extended content is naturally block-shaped, so there is no good reason to sell it as a subscription.

whyPoints.title: The premium explained rather than asserted
whyPoints.description: The specialist band exists because the pool able to teach algebraic fractions, function work and formal justification is small, not because the hour is harder to deliver. That is testable in two minutes with one question about getting from a second difference to a justified rule.

whyPoints.title: Absence treated as a trigger
whyPoints.description: Extended schemes of work meet a topic once and move on, so two weeks away is three to five sessions if booked promptly and two or three times that if left to the next report. We prioritise pace recovery for precisely that reason.

whyPoints.title: Coverage and fallback published
whyPoints.description: The coverage table says what we can staff, how long matching takes and what we do when no specialist is free. No competitor in the researched set discloses a coverage limit, and a published limit is more useful to you than a pretence.

whyPoints.title: The four-year picture before the Year 10 decision
whyPoints.description: Extended Middle Years blocks, a bridging summer, a Diploma year and an exploration block are the units this budget is made of. One diagnostic session at the end of Year 10 often removes most of them, if the intended Diploma course does not require the route.

whyPoints.title: Sourced figures and restrained claims
whyPoints.description: Every AED band here belongs to the provider or survey named beside it, read October 2026. We claim no regulator or board approval, describe no tutor as an examiner without evidence, promise no grade, and run no home visits in the UAE.

faqs.question: Why am I quoted more for extended maths than for standard?
faqs.answer: Because fewer tutors can teach it well, not because the hour is harder to deliver. Published bands in this market put qualified online subject tutors at AED 150 to AED 300 and specialists at AED 200 to AED 450 and above, with one provider at AED 650, all read in October 2026. Extended content such as algebraic fractions, function transformations and formal justification narrows the pool sharply. You can test whether a quote is justified in two minutes: ask how the tutor would move a student from a correct second-difference calculation to a justified quadratic rule.

faqs.question: How many sessions does algebraic fractions actually take?
faqs.answer: Four to six for most extended-route students, plus groundwork if factorisation is not secure, which it frequently is not. The dependency is the thing families are not told: algebraic fraction work rests on confident factorisation, and attempting the fractions first wastes two sessions and some confidence. A tutor should say so at the trial lesson rather than discover it in session four. The block should end with a cold set of mixed questions attempted without prompts, which is a clearer test than any amount of in-session agreement that it makes sense now.

faqs.question: My son missed two weeks of his extended set. What does catching up cost?
faqs.answer: Three to five sessions if you book promptly, and roughly double that if you wait for the next report. Extended schemes of work teach a topic in a unit, assess it and do not return, so two weeks away is one specific load-bearing topic missing rather than a general lag. Email the department and ask which topics and assessments the set covered while he was away: that single answer scopes the work precisely. Without it, a specialist spends the first two sessions working out what was missed, at specialist rates.

faqs.question: Is the extended route worth paying for if he will take Applications and Interpretation?
faqs.answer: Probably not as a requirement, though it can be a reasonable stretch if the student wants it. The extended route exists to prepare students for higher-level Analysis and Approaches, and a student heading to Applications and Interpretation has paid for two years of additional algebra and trigonometry the Diploma course does not assume. That is why the single best-value purchase on this page is one diagnostic session at the end of Year 10, with the intended Diploma course named. The answer frequently removes a large part of the planned spend.

faqs.question: What does the bridging summer into higher level cost in sessions?
faqs.answer: Fifteen to twenty sessions for a student coming from the extended route with the usual gaps, covering harder factorisation, algebraic fractions, function notation and transformations, trigonometric identities and formal generalisation. Book it by May, because July and August fill early in the specialist pool. The same work bought in the first term of Year 12 competes with five other Diploma subjects and the extended essay, which makes it slower, less effective and no cheaper. A standard-route student aiming at the same destination needs a longer bridge.

faqs.question: Do extended-route rates rise before the spring examination window?
faqs.answer: Availability tightens rather than headline rates moving, and on a narrow specialism that amounts to the same thing. Demand surges twice: from January towards the spring window and internal deadlines, and more briefly in the autumn around the November board series and first reports. The 5pm to 7pm Gulf Standard Time slots go first and the narrowest specialisms go earliest. Booking a criterion B block three weeks ahead of a submission costs less and achieves more than the same block four days out, which buys tidying rather than teaching.

faqs.question: Can my two children share one extended maths tutor?
faqs.answer: Not a live session, unless they are in the same extended set at the same school, and even then only for content teaching rather than criterion coaching, because assessed work has to stay individual. What can be shared is the diagnostic review and one household file, which costs less than two separate intakes. The other practical economy is staggered consecutive slots on the same evening: far easier for a Dubai household to protect than two commitments on different nights, and protecting the slot is worth more than a discount.

faqs.question: Is a group class a cheaper way to cover extended algebra?
faqs.answer: Cheaper per hour and poorly matched to the problem. Extended content is unforgiving about sequencing, and the whole value of one-to-one here is working the specific gap in the right order for one student. A group of four needs different topics by the second week, at which point the shared pace reintroduces exactly what you were paying to fix. For broad revision in an examination year a class can be reasonable value. If a provider offers extended coaching in a small group at a near-specialist rate, ask how the hour divides.

faqs.question: Should I pay extra for a tutor described as an examiner?
faqs.answer: Only if the status can be evidenced, and even then judge the teaching rather than the title. Examiner status does not grant access to marking, grade boundaries or paper content, and it does not predict whether someone can sequence algebraic fractions after factorisation for a Year 10 student. Our position is that we do not describe tutors as examiners for individuals whose current status we cannot evidence. A better question than any credential is the two-minute method question: how would you get this student from a second difference to a justified rule?

faqs.question: Does tutoring help with UAE Ministry of Education equivalency?
faqs.answer: No, and no provider performs or accelerates it. Equivalency is an administrative recognition handled through the official government channel. The published British-track requirement is five accredited GCSE or International GCSE subjects at no lower than E or grade 3, excluding Arabic and Islamic education, plus one A Level at E or two AS Levels at the same grade. The American track specifies SAT Math 450 and English via IELTS 5, TOEFL iBT 61 or SAT reading and writing 450. We publish no International Baccalaureate points figure, because the source we read states none.

faqs.question: What should be in writing before I pay for an extended block?
faqs.answer: Five things. The named topic and the session estimate. The rate and whether it is per hour or per session. What happens to unused sessions and the notice period for pausing, which matters in a city where families relocate mid-year. Who specifically will teach and what happens if they become unavailable. And the measure of success: what a cold re-test or the next school-marked task should show. A provider who answers all five in writing is keeping records; one who answers in reassurance is not.

faqs.question: How quickly can you find an extended specialist for a weekday evening?
faqs.answer: Two to four working days for extended algebra and function work, three to five for non-right-angled trigonometry, and three to seven for criterion B justification at extended depth, which is the narrowest pool we staff. Pace recovery after an absence is prioritised because delay compounds the cost. Where nothing suitable is free in your preferred slot, we say so and offer a later slot with the right specialist, a sequenced start on the groundwork, or a weekend session, rather than filling the slot with a generalist and letting the mismatch surface later.

faqs.question: Did the Dubai fee freeze make tutoring more expensive this year?
faqs.answer: There is no evidence for that and the mechanism runs the other way. The Knowledge and Human Development Authority confirmed in May 2026 that private school fees in the emirate would not rise for 2026-27, under Dubai's second economic incentives package valued at AED 1.5 billion within a AED 2.5 billion total, and the emirate added seven schools and 16,846 places. A frozen fee line and new capacity free up discretionary budget, which increases demand for tutoring rather than its cost base. Treat a provider citing rising costs as justification for a higher rate with ordinary scepticism.

faqs.question: What is the total if we support extended maths properly across MYP 4 and MYP 5?
faqs.answer: Roughly twenty to thirty sessions for a student with no inherited gaps, bought as blocks rather than weekly: four to six on algebraic fractions, three to five on functions, three to four on non-right-angled trigonometry, four to six on criterion B justification, two to four on modelling, plus pace recovery as needed. Multiply by whichever published band applies to your chosen provider to get a figure. A student with weak underlying algebra needs groundwork on top, and a student who is broadly behind the set is a different plan altogether.

faqs.question: When would you tell us not to buy extended tutoring at all?
faqs.answer: Three situations come up regularly. The student is coping with the set and the apparent problem is one unit the class also found hard, in which case waiting a fortnight costs nothing. The student is in the wrong set, in which case the conversation is with the school rather than a purchase. Or the student is tired rather than behind, because an extended set plus the mandatory Arabic, Islamic Education and Social Studies stream plus activities has filled every evening. We say all three in the trial lesson when the evidence supports them.

dubai/ib-myp-french-home-tutor.tutorsIntro: The tutors here teach MYP French by phase and quote one figure that includes setting and marking written work. Tell us the phase on the last report and the pattern you want, weekly or twice-weekly, and the price conversation takes one exchange rather than three.

intro.heading: Two French quotes for the same child can differ by AED 300 an hour, and both can be honest
paragraphs: Ring four providers in Dubai about MYP French and you will be given four numbers with no shared basis. One quotes per session and one per hour. One includes marking and one treats it as goodwill. One assumes ninety minutes because they are driving to Mudon and one assumes thirty because they are not. The numbers are not comparable, and almost nobody in this market makes the basis explicit, which is how a family ends up choosing on instinct.

This page separates the parts. The honest components of a French tutoring price in Dubai are the phase being taught, whether written work is set and marked, how long the minimum session is, how often it happens, and whether somebody is travelling. Five variables. Once each one is written down, two quotes that looked incomparable turn out to differ in two specific places, and you can decide whether those two differences are worth what they cost.

The travel component deserves its own line because it is the largest invisible charge in the market. Bestimate's Dubai 2026 rate table puts in-home one-to-one at AED 180 to 350 an hour and independent listings reach AED 500, against roughly AED 150 to 300 for a qualified subject teacher working online. The gap is not the teaching. It is a drive across the city at the worst hour of the day, bought at a teacher's hourly rate.

The second invisible charge is minimum session length. Nobody drives to Remraam for thirty minutes, so in-home bookings come as ninety minutes or two hours. That raises the monthly bill even when the hourly rate is identical, and for French specifically it buys the wrong shape: oral fluency improves on frequency, so two short slots a week beat one long session, and the long session is the only one an in-home model can sell profitably.

IB Gram does not offer home visits anywhere in the UAE; that service exists only in India. Dubai lessons are one-to-one over live video on Gulf Standard Time. Everything priced below is market data with its source attached, published so that a parent can see which band a quote belongs in. Our own figure is given after a free first session, once the phase and the target are known, with marking inside it rather than bolted on afterwards.

A word on why a tutoring page is publishing other providers' prices at all. Three of the six pages ranking for searches like this one publish no price whatsoever, and the two that do quote in US dollars, which is not a currency a Dubai household transacts in. A parent trying to work out whether AED 250 an hour is reasonable currently has nowhere to check. Putting the whole range on one page, with each band attributed to the provider or table that published it and dated, is more useful than another paragraph about quality, and it lets a family argue with us on the numbers.

dubai/ib-myp-french-home-tutor.programmesIntro: French costs different amounts at different stages, and the increases are not gradual. Two moments raise the price sharply: the move into the upper phases, and the move into the Diploma. Planning around those two is worth more than negotiating an hourly rate.

programmes.name: Middle Years Programme
programmes.description: French runs across six phases with four criteria, each on a band out of eight. Pricing tracks the phase rather than the year group, because the pool of tutors who can teach Phase 5 register work is far smaller than the pool who can teach a beginner. The cost curve is therefore flat through the early phases and steepens noticeably from Phase 4 upwards.
programmes.countryNote: For a Dubai family the cheap years are MYP 1 to MYP 3, and that is also when work is most effective, because habits are still forming. Buying support in MYP 2 at the lower band is consistently cheaper across five years than buying it in MYP 5 at the specialist band, and the second option also arrives too late to change the Diploma route.

programmes.name: Primary Years Programme
programmes.description: Primary French is cheap to support and rarely needs paying for, because the assessment stakes are nil and the content is widely taught. Where families do spend, it is usually on confidence before a school change rather than on grades, and a handful of short sessions is the sensible shape.
programmes.countryNote: Dubai schools timetable wildly different amounts of primary French, from thirty minutes a week to several lessons. That variation is the real cost driver later, because a child with minimal primary French starts MYP 1 in an early phase and may need two years of support to reach the phase their classmates began in.

programmes.name: Diploma Programme
programmes.description: French B at Standard or Higher Level, ab initio for a genuine beginner, or French A as literature. Diploma rates are higher across every subject, with specialist bands of AED 200 to 450 and above becoming standard rather than premium, and two years of support at those rates is a substantial commitment.
programmes.countryNote: The expensive path for a Dubai household is a weak MYP 5 French record followed by two years of Diploma support at specialist rates. The cheaper path is a targeted block in MYP 4 that protects the Higher Level option. The decision point is a year earlier than most families realise, because Year 12 option blocks are built well in advance.

dubai/ib-myp-french-home-tutor.subjectsIntro: French requests divide into tasks with genuinely different price points, because each needs a different kind of tutor and a different session length. These are the ones Dubai families ask for, with the band each one sits in.

subjects.name: Phases 1-2 beginner support
subjects.description: The widest supply and the lowest rates, from the budget band upwards. Vocabulary, present tense, greetings and gender habits. Genuinely good value at AED 100 to 150 an hour if the person can show you a plan, and specialist rates here are simply waste.

subjects.name: Phases 3-4 writing and tense accuracy
subjects.description: The mid band, and where most Dubai spending goes. Perfect against imperfect, agreement, text types. Needs somebody who can band a script rather than correct it, which is the skill that separates AED 150 from AED 300 an hour in practice.

subjects.name: Phases 5-6 register and analysis
subjects.description: The specialist band, AED 200 to 450 and above on published market figures. Subjunctive, controlled register, analytical vocabulary, unadapted text. The supply of tutors who can do this in Dubai is thin, and the price reflects scarcity rather than effort.

subjects.name: Oral-only short slots
subjects.description: Fifteen to thirty minutes, twice a week, on unprepared turns. Priced per hour at the mid band, so the monthly figure is similar to a weekly hour while the frequency is doubled. Not viable at all as an in-home booking, since nobody drives for twenty minutes.

subjects.name: Listening log block
subjects.description: Four to six short sessions tagging failed question types: numbers, negatives, speaker attitude. Cheap, narrow and unusually effective, because it replaces hours of general listening practice with targeted work on the two or three types that actually fail.

subjects.name: MYP 5 ePortfolio text-type block
subjects.description: Four to six sessions on the conventions of the text types a portfolio needs, plus a range audit of what has already been collected. Priced as a block. Teaching and feedback on the student's own work only; nothing in a portfolio may be produced by a tutor.

subjects.name: Phase placement evidence, one-off
subjects.description: A single session plus a written page banding three tasks against two phases, for a family disputing a placement. One of the few genuinely one-off purchases in this market, and the cheapest thing on this list relative to what it can change.

subjects.name: Holiday intensive before DP1
subjects.description: Daily sessions across one or two weeks of a Dubai school holiday, aimed at a specific gap before French B starts. Costs AED 2,000 to 4,500 at specialist rates, and the gains fade without some follow-up in term time, which is worth budgeting for at the same moment.

subjects.name: Paired sessions at the same phase
subjects.description: Two students within a phase of each other sharing a session at a reduced rate each. Works for reading, listening and written feedback, works badly for speaking since the talking time halves. Declined where the phases are two or more apart.

dubai/ib-myp-french-home-tutor.regionsIntro: Where a family lives changes the in-home figure considerably and the online figure not at all, which is the single clearest argument in the comparison. These are the Dubai communities French bookings come from, with the cost or scheduling point that applies in each.

regions.name: Za'abeel and World Trade Centre
regions.note: Central, so in-home travel premiums are at their lowest here and local quotes are competitive. The constraint is a quiet room in an apartment rather than a drive, and short sessions work better than long ones.

regions.name: Al Wasl and Jumeirah 2
regions.note: A high concentration of francophone households and established schools, which keeps local French supply reasonable at the lower phases and does nothing for Phase 5. That gap is what online booking is used for here.

regions.name: Mudon and Arabian Ranches 3
regions.note: Towards the southern edge of the city, where the travel component inside an in-home rate is at its largest and sessions stretch to two hours to justify the journey. The monthly difference against an online pattern is substantial.

regions.name: Remraam and Dubai Production City
regions.note: Long drives in both directions, so in-home quotes here sit at the top of the published range. Families tend to buy blocks rather than standing weekly slots, so a missed week is deferred rather than lost.

regions.name: Dubai Science Park and Al Thanyah
regions.note: Close to several schools with shorter commutes, which makes a 4.30pm slot realistic and the twice-weekly short pattern genuinely workable without anybody rushing dinner.

regions.name: Majan and Dubai Residence Complex
regions.note: Price sensitivity is high here and budget-band quotes are common. The useful test is whether marking is included, because an unmarked hour at AED 90 is rarely the cheaper option across a term.

regions.name: Jumeirah Islands and Jumeirah Heights
regions.note: Villa communities with heavy weekend activity schedules. The pattern that survives is a fixed weekday evening slot plus a weekend written task, which also happens to be the cheapest useful shape for Criterion D work.

schoolClusters.city: The western school corridor

sections.heading: What an IB MYP French home tutor costs in Dubai, by phase and task
paragraphs: The direct answer first. A qualified subject teacher working online one-to-one is quoted roughly AED 150 to 300 an hour in Dubai, programme specialists AED 200 to 450 and above, budget and university-student tutors from around AED 45, and in-home visits AED 180 to 500 with travel inside the figure. Those bands come from Bestimate's Dubai 2026 rate table and from prices published by EdFlik, Tutopiya, Unitors, TutorChase and BartyED.

The table below splits those bands by what a family is actually buying, because the phase and the task move the number more than the format does. Beginner French is the cheapest serious language hour available in the city. Phase 5 and 6 work sits at the specialist end because the supply of people who can teach controlled register and analytical vocabulary in French is small. The monthly column assumes the session pattern most families settle into rather than a maximum.

Two things to hold in mind while reading it. These are market figures with sources attached, not our price list; ours is quoted after a free first session once the phase and the target are known. And a monthly total is a weak comparison on its own, because a cheaper month built from one unmarked ninety-minute session usually buys less movement than a dearer month built from two short marked ones.

One row is worth pointing at. Oral-only short slots are not viable as an in-home purchase at any price, because the economics of driving across Dubai require a long session. That is not a criticism of in-home teaching; it is a structural limit. For a student whose problem is Criterion C speaking, the format decides what can be bought before the rate is even discussed.

sections.heading: What a home visit adds to the bill, component by component
paragraphs: The useful way to compare an in-home quote with an online one is to take the in-home figure apart rather than argue about formats. Four components explain almost all of the difference, and three of them are logistics rather than teaching. None of this makes in-home teaching poor value in general; it makes it expensive for a subject whose marks respond to frequency and to fast marking, which is exactly what a language subject does.

Travel is the biggest single line. Against an online qualified-teacher band of roughly AED 150 to 300, the published in-home range of AED 180 to 500 implies somewhere between AED 50 and 150 an hour of journey, varying with distance and the time of day. A family in Mudon or Remraam pays near the top of that; a family near the Trade Centre pays near the bottom. It is a real cost, honestly incurred, and it buys no teaching.

Minimum session length is the component parents miss. A ninety-minute minimum raises the monthly bill by half against a sixty-minute one even when the hourly rate is identical, and the extra thirty minutes is frequently spent on something other than the fault that needed fixing. For French, concentration on grammar correction and oral work is not linear; the back half of a two-hour session is rarely worth what the front half is.

The last two components, marking turnaround and cancellations, cost nothing to improve online and are almost impossible to improve in-home. A correction returned in two days teaches a rule; the same correction at the next visit a fortnight later reads as a verdict on work the student has forgotten. And a session lost to Dubai evening traffic is money gone, whereas a video session can usually be moved inside the same week.

sections.heading: Native-speaker status is not the price driver parents expect
paragraphs: Families assume a native speaker costs more and is worth more, and in the MYP neither half of that is reliably true. Dubai has a large francophone population, so native speakers are plentiful and the budget end of the market is full of them. What is scarce is somebody who can read a piece of writing, name the Criterion D band it sits in against phase descriptors, and say what the next band requires. Those are different skills and the market prices them separately.

Where native fluency genuinely matters is Criterion C and Criterion A. A confident model of spoken French, with natural pace, liaison and idiom, is what a student needs to practise against, and recorded playback is more useful when the model is authentic. For oral-only short slots a native speaker at a mid rate is excellent value. For a student losing marks on written register, the same person may be no help at all.

The practical test costs nothing and settles it in five minutes. Send a piece of your child's writing and ask the tutor to band it and name the next move. A trained non-native teacher will often do this better than a fluent speaker with no assessment training, and the difference is visible immediately in how specific the answer is. Vague praise about the writing being good is an answer to a different question.

The most expensive mistake available here is paying a specialist rate for native fluency alone. The second most expensive is paying a budget rate for assessment expertise you then do not get. Both come from treating the subject as French rather than as MYP French, and the fix is to decide which criterion you are buying for before looking at anybody's rate card.

sections.heading: Session length and frequency: what you are actually paying for
paragraphs: Hold the monthly spend constant and the shape of the sessions becomes the only variable, which is the right way to compare options. Four hours a month can be one weekly hour, two short slots a week, or a long session every fortnight, and those three buy very different results in a language subject. The table prices all of them at the same mid-band figure so the comparison is about what works rather than about what costs.

The pattern that loses most often is the long fortnightly session, and it is also the one families default to when weeks are unpredictable. Two weeks is long enough for the previous session to fade, so each lesson spends its first twenty minutes re-establishing ground. For grammar that needs to become automatic, and for oral fluency, the gaps undo much of the work, which is why the cheapest monthly figure on the table is rarely the best value on it.

The pattern that wins for writing is the weekly hour with a marked task, because the task is where the learning happens and the session is where it is corrected. The pattern that wins for speaking and listening is two short slots, which fit between a Dubai school bus and dinner and double the contact at the same monthly cost. Most students need one of those two rather than something in between.

Holiday intensives are a special case worth pricing separately. Daily sessions across one or two weeks of a Dubai school break can close a specific gap quickly, particularly before French B starts, and the published specialist bands put a two-week intensive at AED 2,000 to 4,500. Gains fade without some term-time follow-up, so budget for a few sessions afterwards at the same moment rather than discovering the need in October.

sections.heading: Paired and group French: where sharing works and where it does not
paragraphs: Sharing a session is the most common way Dubai families try to reduce the bill, and it works for some of the subject and not for other parts of it. The economics are straightforward: two students at a reduced rate each costs less per family than two separate hours. The teaching question is what gets halved, and in a language subject one of the four criteria gets halved much more severely than the others.

Reading, listening and written feedback share well. A reading passage can be set at a level both students can access, listening tasks are answered individually and discussed together, and written work is marked separately so neither student loses anything at all on Criterion D. For those three criteria a shared session is close to a free saving, provided the two students are genuinely within a phase of each other.

Speaking does not share. Criterion C improves on time spent talking, and a shared hour halves it. Worse, in a pair one student usually dominates and the quieter one practises less than half, so the arithmetic is more punishing than it looks. For a student whose target is speaking, two short individual slots a week at the same monthly cost is a better purchase than a shared hour at a lower rate.

There is one hard limit worth stating. Where two students are two or more phases apart, we decline the pair rather than run it, because the session is then pitched wrongly for at least one of them and both families are paying for something that only half works. A sibling discount is not worth a term of teaching the younger child above their level and the older one below theirs.

sections.heading: The francophone demand curve in Dubai, and what it does to prices
paragraphs: French pricing in Dubai behaves differently from most subjects because supply and demand are unevenly matched across the phases. The city holds a substantial francophone professional population and two French-system schools, which means a large supply of fluent speakers available at the budget and mid bands. That keeps beginner and middle-phase French cheaper here than it would be in a city without that population.

At the top of the subject the picture reverses. The teachers who can work on Phase 5 and 6 register, analytical vocabulary and unadapted text are mostly employed by schools, and the private pool is small. So the cost curve across the phases is unusually flat at the bottom and unusually steep at the top, which is the opposite of what parents expect when they assume prices rise smoothly with age.

Demand is seasonal on top of that, and the seasons are set by school calendars rather than by public exams. Requests concentrate in the weeks before internal assessment and reporting windows, and in the run-up to Diploma option choices at the end of MYP 4 and MYP 5. The specialist end books out first in each of those periods, so families arriving late choose from whatever remains rather than from the whole market.

The practical consequence is a timing decision worth more than a negotiation. Starting a block mid-term, when diaries are open, buys a better teacher at a calmer price than starting three weeks before a report. KHDA's confirmation in May 2026 that private school fees in Dubai would not rise for 2026-27 is a useful reminder that the tutoring line is the part of the education budget nobody caps, which makes the timing discipline yours to impose.

sections.heading: Budgeting French across MYP 4 and MYP 5
paragraphs: These are the two years where French spending actually changes an outcome, because the MYP 5 record determines the Diploma route and the route determines two further years of cost. Treating them as a single two-year budget rather than as a term-by-term decision tends to produce both a lower total and a better result, since the work can be placed where it has leverage instead of where the panic happens to be.

A sensible shape for a student aiming to protect French B Higher Level looks like this. A targeted block in MYP 4 on whichever of reading or writing is weaker, since those are the criteria a school examines when allocating Higher Level. A lighter term afterwards, or none at all, with school provision carrying the load. Then a short text-type block in the first half of MYP 5, timed to the school's internal portfolio deadlines rather than to any public window.

At mid-band market rates that comes to roughly a term of weekly sessions plus two short blocks, rather than two continuous years of weekly hours. The saving against an open-ended arrangement across the same period is considerable, and the result is usually better because each block has a target and an end. The money goes where the criterion is rather than where the calendar is.

One final note on the ePortfolio year. MYP 5 Language Acquisition is assessed through a moderated portfolio of the student's own work rather than an on-screen examination, so there is no single date to buy revision for. What is worth paying for is text-type range and the student's own command of the descriptors, since a portfolio that repeats one register caps itself. A tutor may teach and give feedback on the student's work and must not produce any part of it.

sections.heading: Hidden extras: marking, materials, cancellations and tax
paragraphs: Four things routinely appear after a rate has been agreed, and all four are avoidable by asking in advance. Marking is the largest. An hour of teaching and an hour that includes setting, banding and returning a written task are different products, and when marking is charged separately the headline rate stops being comparable. Ask whether it is inside the figure and what the turnaround is, then compare quotes on that basis rather than on the hourly number alone.

Materials are the second. For MYP French the honest position is that most of what is needed is the student's own school tasks plus authentic text, so there should be little to buy. Treat a required course pack with some suspicion, and note that official syllabus documents, past papers and mark schemes belong to the awarding bodies and should be referenced and linked rather than copied or supplied as downloads by anybody.

Cancellation terms are the third and the most commonly disputed. Dubai evenings produce genuine clashes, so the question is how much notice avoids a charge and whether a missed session can be deferred inside a block. Get the answer before booking rather than during the first argument about it, and prefer a block with a deferral rule over a standing slot that is simply lost when a fixture is rescheduled.

Tax is the fourth, and the only honest thing to say is narrow. We will tell you whether a figure we quote is inclusive of any applicable tax; we will not characterise the UAE VAT treatment of tuition generally, because that requires a Federal Tax Authority source and is not something to take from a tutoring page. Ask any provider to state plainly whether their quoted AED figure is what will leave your account.

sections.heading: Three ways Dubai families overpay for French
paragraphs: The first is paying for discovery. A tutor who spends four sessions working out what is wrong is being paid at a teaching rate to do a diagnosis, and the diagnosis is a forty-minute job if somebody asks the right questions. Send a page of written French and the last report before the first session, insist that the first session ends with a phase estimate and a named target, and the four weeks that would have gone on orientation go on teaching instead.

The second is paying for the wrong criterion. Most Dubai French students have an uneven profile, and more conversation practice for a student whose speaking is already their strongest criterion adds very little to a grade however enjoyable the sessions are. Half the marks in the subject sit in reading and writing. Buying against the criterion that is actually losing marks is the single largest saving available, and it costs nothing to work out first.

The third is the arrangement that never ends. An open-ended weekly hour with warm feedback and no measurement will run for as long as a family keeps paying, because stopping feels like giving up on the child rather than on the arrangement. Blocks with named targets and end dates cost more per hour and far less in total. A provider who resists being measured that way has told you something useful about the next two years.

None of the three is about hourly rates, which is why negotiating one is usually the least productive conversation available. Decide the criterion, decide the pattern, agree what marking is included, fix an end date, and the total falls by more than any discount would have delivered. Then judge the spending on a banded script rather than on how the sessions felt.

process.title: Review at the end of the block, not by default
process.description: A block ends and gets a decision rather than rolling over. A fresh task banded against the same descriptor set shows whether the money moved anything. Buy another block, change the target, change the tutor, or stop; all four are real answers and we will say which we would pick.

whyPoints.description: The quote covers teaching, setting and banding written work, with the turnaround stated. Rates that exclude marking look cheaper and cost more per band moved, which is the most common way a French tutoring bill grows after the price has been agreed.

whyPoints.description: A weekly hour, two short slots and a fortnightly long session cost similar amounts and produce very different results in a language subject. We recommend by criterion rather than by convenience, including when that means selling fewer hours this term.

whyPoints.description: Every block carries a named target and a stated end date agreed before it starts. Open-ended weekly arrangements are the most expensive thing in this market, not because the rate is high but because nothing ever triggers the decision to stop.

faqs.question: How much does an MYP French home tutor cost in Dubai?
faqs.answer: In-home one-to-one across Dubai is published at AED 180 to 350 an hour in Bestimate's 2026 rate table, with independent listings reaching AED 500 and monthly packages of AED 1,599 to 1,799 advertised for four two-hour visits. Travel sits inside those figures. Online one-to-one with a qualified subject teacher runs roughly AED 150 to 300, and programme specialists AED 200 to 450 and above. IB Gram does not sell home visits in the UAE, so those in-home figures are market context rather than an offer from us.

faqs.question: What does the travel part of an in-home French rate actually cost?
faqs.answer: Comparing the published ranges gives a usable estimate. Against an online qualified-teacher band of about AED 150 to 300 an hour, in-home rates of AED 180 to 500 imply somewhere between AED 50 and 150 an hour of journey, varying with distance and the time of day. A family in Mudon or Remraam sits near the top of that; one near the Trade Centre sits near the bottom. It is an honest cost honestly charged, and it buys no teaching whatsoever.

faqs.question: Is paying extra for a native French speaker worth it in the MYP?
faqs.answer: For speaking and listening, often yes; for written work, frequently not. Dubai has a large francophone population, so native speakers are plentiful at the budget and mid bands and are good value for oral-only slots where an authentic model matters. What is scarce is somebody who can band a piece of writing against phase descriptors and name the next move. Test it directly: send a script and ask for a band and a next step. Specificity in the answer is worth more than fluency in the speaker.

faqs.question: Is a ninety-minute French session better value than an hour?
faqs.answer: Usually not, and in-home economics rather than teaching is what produces the longer session. Concentration on grammar correction and oral practice is not linear, so the back half of a long session tends to deliver less than the front half. A ninety-minute minimum also raises the monthly bill by half at an identical hourly rate. For most MYP students a weekly hour with a marked task, or two shorter slots, buys more movement at the same or lower monthly spend.

faqs.question: How much should we budget for French across MYP 4 and MYP 5?
faqs.answer: Think in blocks rather than in continuous terms. A sensible shape is a targeted block in MYP 4 on whichever of reading or writing is weaker, a lighter term or none afterwards with school provision carrying the load, then a short text-type block in the first half of MYP 5 timed to the school's internal portfolio deadlines. At mid-band market rates that is roughly a term of weekly sessions plus two short blocks, which costs materially less than two years of weekly hours and usually works better.

faqs.question: Does sharing a French session with a classmate cut the cost?
faqs.answer: It reduces the per-family figure and only works for part of the subject. Reading, listening and written feedback share well, because the material can be pitched for both and writing is still marked individually. Speaking does not share: Criterion C depends on time spent talking, a shared hour halves it, and in practice one student dominates so the quieter one gets less than half. Where the two students are two or more phases apart we decline the pair, since the session is then pitched wrongly for at least one of them.

faqs.question: Why does Phase 5 French cost more than Phase 2 in Dubai?
faqs.answer: Supply. Dubai has a large francophone population and two French-system schools, so fluent speakers who can teach beginner and middle-phase French are plentiful and the lower bands stay competitive. Teachers who can work on Phase 5 and 6 register, analytical vocabulary and unadapted text are mostly employed by schools, and the private pool is small. The cost curve across the phases is therefore flat at the bottom and steep at the top, which is not how parents expect pricing to behave.

faqs.question: Is marking included in a French tutoring rate?
faqs.answer: With us it is, and it is the question worth asking every provider first. An hour of teaching and an hour that includes setting a written task, banding it against the phase descriptor and returning it before the next session are different products often advertised at similar prices. Ask whether marking is inside the figure and what the turnaround is. Once both quotes answer that, they become comparable, and the apparently cheaper one frequently is not cheaper at all.

faqs.question: Do French rates in Dubai go up before report cards?
faqs.answer: Headline rates often stay still while effective prices rise, because the specialist end books out first and what remains is whatever is left. A family looking three weeks before an internal assessment or a reporting window is choosing from a thinner pool at whatever that pool asks. Starting a block mid-term, when diaries are open, is the nearest thing to a free saving in this market. Our rate is fixed for the term in which it is agreed and is not re-quoted as a deadline approaches.

faqs.question: Are the AED figures on this page inclusive of tax?
faqs.answer: The figures on this page are other providers' published market rates, so what they include is a question for each of them. For our own quotes we state plainly whether the figure is inclusive of any applicable tax before anything is agreed. We deliberately do not characterise the UAE tax treatment of tuition in general, because that requires a Federal Tax Authority source and is not something any family should take from a tutoring page. Ask every provider to confirm what will actually leave your account.

faqs.question: What are the hidden extras in a French tutoring package?
faqs.answer: Four recur. Marking charged separately after an hourly rate has been agreed. Required materials, which for MYP French should be minimal because the work is the student's own school tasks plus authentic text. Cancellation terms, where the question is how much notice avoids a charge and whether a missed session can be deferred inside a block. And tax treatment of the quoted figure. All four are avoidable by asking before booking rather than during the first disagreement about an invoice.

faqs.question: Is a holiday intensive cheaper than a term of weekly French?
faqs.answer: Cheaper in total and more expensive per hour, and it suits a narrow purpose. Daily sessions across one or two weeks of a Dubai school break can close a named gap quickly, which makes it a good purchase before French B starts in Year 12. Published specialist bands put a two-week intensive at roughly AED 2,000 to 4,500. The gains fade without some term-time follow-up, so budget a few sessions after it at the same moment rather than finding out in October.

faqs.question: How do we avoid paying a tutor to work out what the problem is?
faqs.answer: Send the evidence before the first session: a page of your child's own written French, the latest report with its criterion bands if the school prints them, and where they were schooled before Dubai. Then insist the first session ends with a written phase estimate, a named target criterion and a band on marked work. That turns a diagnosis into a forty-minute job rather than four paid sessions of orientation, and the note stays useful for a year even if you book nothing else.

faqs.question: Is it cheaper to start French support in MYP 3 or wait until MYP 5?
faqs.answer: MYP 3 is cheaper per hour, cheaper in total and more effective, which is an unusual combination. Early and middle-phase work sits in the lower market bands, habits are still forming, and the same gap takes fewer hours to close. By MYP 5 the work is in the specialist band, the record that decides the Diploma route is already largely written, and the family is buying under time pressure. Waiting almost always costs more and buys a narrower set of options at the end of it.

faqs.question: If we are offered a cheaper French tutor instead, what are we losing?
faqs.answer: Ask what specifically changes, because sometimes the answer is nothing that matters. A budget-band tutor for Phase 1 or 2 vocabulary work is good value and specialist rates there are waste. What a lower rate usually removes is marking, assessment experience against phase descriptors, and the ability to say what the next band requires. For a student losing marks on written register, those three are the entire product. Have them band a script before deciding; the answer makes the trade-off obvious in five minutes.

dubai/ib-myp-french-home-tutor.closingHeading: Decide the criterion, then the price makes sense
dubai/ib-myp-french-home-tutor.closingBody: Almost every confusing French quote in Dubai becomes clear once five things are written down: the phase, whether marking is included, the minimum session length, the frequency, and whether anybody is travelling. Work those out and two numbers that looked incomparable differ in two specific places you can then judge. Send the last report and a page of your child's written French; the first session is free and ends with a phase estimate, a target criterion and a band on marked work, which you keep whatever you decide. Our quote follows, with marking inside it. Lessons are one-to-one over live video on Gulf Standard Time; IB Gram does not sell home visits in Dubai.

Send the last report with its criterion bands if the school prints them, plus one piece of your child's own written French.

intro.heading: A 5 in MYP French can mean two opposite problems
paragraphs: Dubai produces an unusual mix of French students, and it is the reason generic French tutoring so often fails here. Two French-system schools feed the city, a large francophone professional population lives in it, and a great many international schools timetable French as a standard Language Acquisition option. The result is that one MYP French classroom can hold a student who has been educated in French since the age of three sitting next to one who learned the numbers last year.

The MYP handles that with phases. French runs across six of them, and a phase describes what a student can do with the language rather than how long they have studied it. Each phase has its own descriptors, and the four criteria, listening, reading, speaking and writing, are each marked on a band out of eight against those descriptors. A grade therefore means nothing on its own. A 5 in Phase 2 and a 5 in Phase 5 describe entirely different students with entirely different problems.

The two problems are almost mirror images. The French-system arrival has fluency, instinct and idiom, and loses marks on text type, register and the accuracy that decays once a child stops writing in French daily. The English-medium learner has explicit rules, neat conjugation tables and exam habits, and loses marks on listening speed and on speaking when nothing has been rehearsed. Teaching either of them as though they were the other wastes a term and frustrates everybody involved.

Separating them takes marked evidence rather than conversation. A fluent student's writing shows agreement errors appearing exactly where attention lapses. A rule-learner's writing is accurate and thin, with one tense doing all the work. Both of those are visible on a single page of written French to somebody who knows what to look for, which is why the first session on this page is a diagnosis and the first thing produced is a band with a reason attached.

What follows is the detail: how phase placement usually falls for each kind of Dubai arrival, which grammar points start costing marks at which phase, why listening defeats children who speak French at home, and how counting one error type across four dated scripts tells you whether a rule has genuinely landed. Lessons are one-to-one over live video on Gulf Standard Time; IB Gram does not send tutors to homes in Dubai.

One thing is deliberately absent from the pages that rank for this search, and it is the reason this one is long. Nobody publishes the order in which French grammar starts costing marks, nobody sets out how placement actually falls for a child leaving the French system, and nobody explains why a francophone household can be handed a middling grade. Those three questions account for most of what a Dubai parent is really asking when they type the name of this subject into a search box, so they are answered here with tables rather than reassurance.
bullets: Six phases, each with its own descriptors; the phase comes before the grade
Two mirror-image profiles: fluent and inaccurate, or accurate and inflexible
Grammar tackled in the order it starts costing marks, not in textbook order
One error type counted across four dated scripts to prove a rule has landed
Arabic remains mandatory in Dubai alongside whichever French option is taken

dubai/ib-myp-french-tutor.programmesIntro: French appears at every stage of an IB school career in Dubai, and the decision points are not evenly spaced. Two of them matter more than the rest: the phase a student is placed in on arrival, and the Group 2 route chosen at the end of MYP 5.

programmes.name: Middle Years Programme
programmes.description: French sits in Language Acquisition with six phases and four criteria. Assessment is continuous, so a weak term is carried rather than resat, and the grade is a judgement against descriptors rather than an average of test scores. The phase assigned on arrival often persists for years, which makes it the most consequential decision in the subject and the one parents are least often consulted about.
programmes.countryNote: Dubai's mobility makes phase mismatches frequent. Families arrive mid-year from Lyon, Casablanca, Abidjan or Montreal, sit a forty-minute placement test in their first week, and get a phase. A student who should be in Phase 5 and lands in Phase 3 will coast for two years and then find Higher Level French closed to them at exactly the moment it matters.

programmes.name: Primary Years Programme
programmes.description: French in the primary years is reported narratively with no bands, and the amount timetabled varies enormously between schools. Thirty minutes a week and three lessons a week both appear on a report as French, which is why two children can arrive in MYP 1 looking identical on paper and be two phases apart in a classroom.
programmes.countryNote: Dubai families moving a child between schools at Year 6 should ask the receiving school which phase its MYP 1 French cohort starts from, and whether a child with limited primary French will be placed below it. The answer determines whether MYP 1 is a continuation or a standing start, and schools differ considerably on this.

programmes.name: Diploma Programme
programmes.description: French becomes Group 2: French B at Standard or Higher Level, French ab initio for a genuine beginner, or French A where a school offers the literature route. Schools check prior study before allowing ab initio, so a student who took French throughout the MYP will not be permitted onto the beginner course however weak their marks were.
programmes.countryNote: The MYP 5 record is what Dubai schools use to allocate these routes, and option blocks are built a year ahead. A Phase 4 student with consistent upper-band marks is a credible Higher Level candidate; the same student with mid-band reading usually gets Standard Level. Raise the question during MYP 4, because by the spring of MYP 5 the timetable has already decided.

dubai/ib-myp-french-tutor.subjectsIntro: French bookings here are made against a specific fault rather than against the subject as a whole, because the two common Dubai profiles need almost opposite work. Each item below is something that shows up in marked writing or a recorded oral, and can be counted.

subjects.name: Noun gender and article agreement
subjects.description: The most countable error in early French writing and the one that compounds, because gender drives adjective and participle agreement later. The fix is habit rather than theory: nouns learned with the article attached, never alone, and a proofreading pass that looks only at articles.

subjects.name: Perfect against imperfect
subjects.description: Where narrative writing is won and lost. The classic error is a whole story told in one past tense. Measured by counting tense choices in a short narrative, then having the student write the same story twice, once in each tense, before mixing them deliberately.

subjects.name: Adjective and past-participle agreement
subjects.description: Fluent students fail this precisely where they stop paying attention, which makes the error distribution across a page diagnostic in itself. A dedicated proofreading pass that ignores everything except agreement usually removes most of it within a month.

subjects.name: Pronoun order and placement
subjects.description: Students avoid the problem rather than make errors, dropping pronouns in speech so the sentence stays safe. That avoidance shows as repetitive, flat speaking in Criterion C. Substitution drills on three fixed frames restore it faster than explanation does.

subjects.name: The subjunctive after fixed triggers
subjects.description: Not a grammar curiosity but a band ceiling, because avoiding it flattens register in exactly the pieces where register carries marks. Five trigger phrases learned properly and used deliberately in every written task is the whole of the early work.

subjects.name: Listening: numbers, liaison and elision
subjects.description: The specific reason children who speak French at home lose Criterion A marks. Measured by logging which question types fail rather than by playing more audio, because numbers, negatives and speaker attitude fail for entirely different reasons.

subjects.name: Text types for Criterion D
subjects.description: Letters, blog entries, reports, interviews, each with its own conventions and register. The most common wasted marks in the subject belong here: an excellent piece of writing answering a different task than the one set.

subjects.name: Oral: unprepared turns and visual stimulus
subjects.description: Rehearsed answers sound excellent for ninety seconds and then run out, which is the standard Criterion C failure. Three-minute unprepared turns, recorded with consent and played back, builds recovery after an error rather than polish before one.

subjects.name: Phase placement evidence for French-system arrivals
subjects.description: Three tasks across the four criteria banded against both the assigned phase and the one above, written up for a coordinator. Used most often by families whose child was placed from a short entry test on a jet-lagged week.

dubai/ib-myp-french-tutor.regionsIntro: French demand in Dubai clusters around the francophone professional communities and around the schools that receive students leaving the French system. These are the areas bookings come from most, with the timing or placement pattern that recurs in each.

regions.name: Al Sufouh and Knowledge Village
regions.note: Close to several international schools and to a francophone working population, so arrival times are early and 4pm slots hold. A high share of requests here concern students placed below where their spoken French sits.

regions.name: Umm Suqeim and Al Manara
regions.note: Established villa communities with children spread across IB and British schools. Bookings here are typically middle-phase, with writing accuracy rather than fluency as the target criterion.

regions.name: The Springs and The Lakes
regions.note: Family communities with long activity calendars. The pattern that survives a term is two short slots on fixed weekdays, because a single long session is the first thing traded away when a fixture appears.

regions.name: Al Garhoud and Dubai Festival City
regions.note: Near the eastern school cluster, with shorter commutes than most of the city. Requests from here skew towards students who moved out of the French system two or three years ago and whose written accuracy has quietly decayed.

regions.name: Jumeirah Beach Residence
regions.note: Apartment living where the constraint is a quiet room rather than a drive. Thirty-minute oral slots work better here than long evening sessions, and headphones solve most of what parents worry about.

regions.name: Dubai Land and Liwan
regions.note: Long bus runs in both directions push realistic start times past 5.30pm. Written tasks tend to be done at the weekend, which suits the error-tally approach because the scripts arrive in a predictable rhythm.

regions.name: Arjan and Al Barsha South
regions.note: Newer communities feeding several IB schools nearby. Mixed-phase French classes are common in this cluster, which raises the value of one-to-one work because a mixed class cannot pitch at any single phase.

schoolClusters.city: The French-system schools and the IB schools receiving their students
schoolClusters.note: Students we support from this group are usually strong in listening and speaking and placed in the upper phases, with written register and text type as the real gap. The common request is help settling into MYP assessment conventions rather than help with French itself.

schoolClusters.city: IB continuum schools running French across the middle phases
schoolClusters.note: Here the typical student learned French as a timetabled subject and sits in Phase 2 to 4 with accurate but inflexible language. Requests concentrate on speaking and listening, which are the two criteria explicit rule-learning does least for.

dubai/ib-myp-french-tutor.schoolDisclaimer: Schools are named purely to describe the local context. IB Gram has no affiliation with any school or school group and claims no endorsement from one.
dubai/ib-myp-french-tutor.modesIntro: Each shape below produces a particular kind of evidence, because the two Dubai French profiles need different proof that something is working. Pick by the fault, not by the timetable.

modes.title: Weekly hour with a counted error type
modes.description: One sixty-minute session a week, one written task between sessions, and one target error type counted on every script. Agreement, tense choice or pronoun use, whichever the baseline showed. The count is reported each week alongside the Criterion D band, so a family can see whether the rule is landing separately from whether the band has moved.
bullets: One target error type at a time, counted the same way
Criterion D band reported alongside the count
Student rewrites once and finds the errors themselves
Target changes only when the count has stayed down

modes.title: Twice-weekly oral slots for fluent students
modes.description: Two short sessions a week built on unprepared three-minute turns, recorded with written consent. Designed for the French-system arrival whose speaking is already strong but whose range has narrowed through avoidance, and for the rule-learner who freezes once nothing is rehearsed. Both need frequency rather than length, and neither improves from a monthly conversation.
bullets: Unprepared turns, no rehearsed openings accepted
Recorded with consent, compared fortnightly
Pronoun and tense avoidance named out loud
Fifteen to thirty minutes, twice a week

modes.title: Placement evidence block for a new arrival
modes.description: A short block for a family who believes the entry test under-placed their child. Three tasks across the four criteria, banded against the assigned phase and the one above, written up on a single page a coordinator can read in two minutes. It ends whether or not the school agrees, because its job is to make the request documented rather than to win it.
bullets: Three tasks covering all four criteria
Banded against two phases side by side
One page written for a coordinator, not for a parent
Fixed length, with a clear end point

sections.heading: What an IB MYP French tutor in Dubai fixes first
paragraphs: The first session produces a diagnosis, and the diagnosis is almost always one of two things. Either the student has fluency without accuracy, which shows as writing that reads well and loses marks in predictable places, or they have accuracy without flexibility, which shows as neat short sentences and a recorded oral that stops after ninety seconds. Those two need different work, different session shapes and different lengths of time, and confusing them is the standard failure in Dubai French tutoring.

Telling them apart takes one page of the student's own written French and three minutes of unprepared speech. The fluent profile shows agreement errors clustered where attention lapsed, idiom used confidently, and register that drifts from formal to conversational mid-piece. The rule-learner's page is accurate, short, and built on one tense doing all the work, with no idiom at all. Both produce a middling band. Only one of them is a grammar problem.

What happens next follows from that. A fluent student gets text types, register and a dedicated proofreading pass, because their language is already there and the marks are being lost to assessment conventions. A rule-learner gets frequency: short oral slots, listening logs, and permission to be inaccurate while being flexible. The common mistake is to give both of them more grammar worksheets, which helps one of them slightly and the other not at all.

The output of the first session is written down: the phase estimate, the profile, one target error type, and the band on the piece of work that was marked. That note is worth keeping even if no further lessons are booked, because it is a sentence a parent can take to a subject teacher and get a real answer to, rather than a general worry that produces a general reassurance.

sections.heading: Phase placement for children arriving from the French system
paragraphs: Dubai schools place students into French phases from an entry assessment, usually in the first week, usually short, and often sat by a child who arrived in the country ten days earlier. For most students that works out roughly right. For children leaving the French system it frequently does not, because an entry test that samples reading and writing catches a student whose strengths are oral and whose written French has not been exercised since they changed schools.

The table sets out how placement usually falls for the main Dubai arrival routes, along with the gap each profile carries and a planning estimate for closing it. Treat the week ranges as planning figures rather than promises: they assume a weekly session with written work in between, and a student doing twice-weekly short slots on a narrow target moves faster. The point of the table is the pattern, which is that the gap is predictable once you know where a child came from.

The most commonly disputed row is the francophone home with no French schooling. These students speak and understand far above their phase and read and write far below it, so any single placement number is wrong in two directions at once. Schools tend to place on the written evidence, which feels unfair to the family and is defensible from the school's side, because the written criteria are half the marks and the student genuinely cannot access the upper phase in two of four criteria.

If you want a placement reconsidered, the route is documentary rather than argumentative. Collect three recent marked tasks across the four criteria, have them banded against both the assigned phase and the one above, and send one page to the coordinator. A written request gets a written answer and survives a change of teacher in August, which a conversation at a parents' evening does not.

sections.heading: French grammar in the order it starts costing marks
paragraphs: Textbooks teach grammar in the order a linguist would arrange it. Marks are lost in a different order entirely, and tutoring that follows the textbook spends weeks on things that are not currently costing anything. The sequence below is ordered by the phase at which each point begins to affect a band, which means it is also roughly the order in which a Dubai MYP student should be made to care about it.

Gender comes first and is the most under-rated, because it compounds. A student who defaults to masculine on unfamiliar nouns will go on to make every adjective and participle agreement error downstream of that choice, and the errors will look like agreement problems when the cause sits one step earlier. Learning nouns with the article attached is dull, unfashionable advice and it removes a whole class of later error.

At the other end, the subjunctive is not a refinement. From Phase 5 it becomes a band ceiling, because the pieces where it belongs are the pieces where register carries marks, and a student who avoids it writes in a flattened register that cannot reach the upper bands. Five trigger phrases, learned properly and used deliberately in every written task for a month, is the whole of the early work and it is far less daunting than the grammar books make it look.

One warning about the middle of the table. Agreement and tense choice are the two points where fluent students and rule-learners look most different. The fluent student makes errors where attention lapses, so the mistakes cluster in the second half of a page. The rule-learner makes no mistakes and also takes no risks, so the page is accurate and thin. The same table entry therefore implies opposite work depending on which profile is in front of you.
