sections.heading: What a Middle Years mathematics report is actually telling you
paragraphs: A Middle Years mathematics grade is built from four criterion marks, each awarded on a 0 to 8 scale against published descriptors, and then converted into a single grade from 1 to 7. The four criteria are knowing and understanding, investigating patterns, communicating, and applying mathematics in real-life contexts. A school may report all four, or report the converted grade alone, and the difference matters enormously to a parent trying to decide what to buy. Four criterion marks are a diagnosis. One grade is a headline.

Read the four marks as a shape rather than a score. A profile of 7, 3, 6, 5 is a student who knows the mathematics and cannot run an investigation, and the fix is a process, not more content. A profile of 4, 4, 4, 4 is usually a pace problem: the student is behind on the branch content, so every criterion suffers proportionally. A profile of 6, 6, 4, 4 is a communication and interpretation problem, which is the cheapest of all to move because notation habits and evaluation sentences can be rebuilt in a handful of sessions.

The conversion from a 32-mark total to a grade uses boundaries that your child's programme coordinator can show you, and they are not a simple percentage. This is why a student can gain two criterion marks and no grade, or one criterion mark and a whole grade. Before paying for anything, ask the coordinator which boundary your child is sitting under and how far the total has to move. That single question reframes the purchase from 'better at maths' to 'four marks on criterion B', which is something a tutor can actually be held to.

The table below is the working diagnostic we use in a first session. It maps each criterion to what the descriptor rewards, what counts as evidence that the mark has genuinely moved, and the stall point we see most often in Dubai classrooms. Confirm the exact descriptor wording against the task-specific clarification your school issues, because schools adapt the published wording for individual tasks.

sections.heading: The evidence file: what we keep, and what it proves
paragraphs: Tutoring is unusually easy to buy on feeling and unusually hard to audit. The honest answer to that is a file. From the first session, each student has a running document that holds every marked task, the criterion it was assessed against, the date, the correction made in the session, and the one thing the next task has to show. It is dull and it is the most valuable thing we produce, because at any point you can read it and decide whether to continue.

The file is deliberately built from your child's own work rather than from worksheets we generate. A worksheet proves a tutor was busy. A marked school task proves the student did something different in front of a teacher who did not know a tutor was involved. That distinction also keeps the arrangement honest: the student's work stays the student's work, which is a requirement rather than a courtesy in a programme where tasks carry assessment weight.

At six weeks the file should contain enough to answer three questions. Has the criterion we targeted produced a higher mark on a comparable task? Has the notation correction rate fallen? Is the student now attempting the final part of each task rather than leaving it? If the answers are no, no and no, something is wrong with the plan and we would rather say so at six weeks than at six months. Occasionally the right recommendation is fewer sessions in maths and a conversation with the school about set placement.

Families often ask whether a tutor should talk to the school. Our position is that the parent owns that relationship and the file exists to make it easy: a printed sequence of marked tasks with dates is a far better basis for a parent-teacher conversation than a general worry. We write the file so it can be handed over without translation. Nothing in it claims a grade outcome, because nobody can honestly promise one, and a document full of predictions would be worth less than one full of marked work.
bullets: Every marked task dated, with the criterion assessed written on it
One sentence per session on what the next task must show

sections.heading: The four content branches, and what the extended route actually adds
paragraphs: Middle Years mathematics content is organised into four branches: number, algebra, geometry and trigonometry, and statistics and probability. Every criterion is assessed through that content, which is why a vague request for maths help is hard to act on and a request naming a branch is easy. A student stuck on criterion B in algebra needs sequence generalisation practice. A student stuck on criterion B in geometry needs to learn to test a conjecture with a construction. Those are different sessions.

Somewhere around MYP 4, most Dubai schools split the cohort into a standard and an extended route through the same framework. Extended is not a different subject and it does not carry a separate grade scale; it adds content for students heading towards higher-level Diploma mathematics and it moves faster. The practical consequence is a consolidation gap. Extended sets meet a topic once, assess it, and move on, so a student who misses two weeks in MYP 4 for travel arrives in MYP 5 with a hole nobody has time to fill.

Set placement in Dubai schools is usually made on criterion A, because knowing and understanding is the easiest criterion to measure in a class test. That produces a predictable failure mode: students placed in extended on strong procedural fluency who are then exposed on criterion B, where harder content generates harder patterns to justify. If your child has just been moved up and the report shows a 7 on A with a 4 on B, the right purchase is investigation work, not more content.

The table maps the four branches against the two routes and names where the marks tend to go. Use it to write a specific request: 'MYP 4 extended, geometry and trigonometry, criterion B' is a brief a specialist can prepare for in advance, and it is the difference between a first session that diagnoses and a first session that interviews.

sections.heading: Investigating patterns: the criterion that moves a Dubai maths grade
paragraphs: Criterion B is where most Middle Years mathematics grades in Dubai are decided, and it is the criterion least rehearsed by ordinary homework. The descriptor asks the student to select a mathematical technique, apply it to find a pattern, describe the pattern as a general rule, verify the rule with further cases, and then justify why the rule holds. Five distinct moves. Most students perform two of them well and stop, and a mark in the middle band is the arithmetic consequence.

The description-to-generalisation step is the common wall. A student will write that the differences go up by three each time, which is a correct description, and then be unable to convert it into an expression in n. That is an algebra problem wearing an investigation costume, and it is why criterion B work and algebra work belong in the same session. The verification step is skipped for a different reason: students treat a rule as proved once it works for the cases in the table, and the descriptor expects cases beyond them.

Justification is the step that separates the top band, and it is the one that can be taught fastest. Justification does not require formal proof at Middle Years level; it requires a reason connected to the structure of the problem. If the pattern counts the edges of a growing shape, the justification explains why each new layer adds that many edges. Students who have been shown three worked justifications in different branches usually produce a fourth unaided, which is the clearest grade movement available in this subject.

Our investigation blocks therefore run as process coaching against the student's own task. The tutor does not supply a pattern, a rule, or a sentence of the write-up. The tutor asks the questions a marker would ask, in order, until the student answers them in writing. That boundary is not a marketing position: a Middle Years mathematics task carries assessment weight, and work that is not the student's own exposes the student, not the tutor.

sections.heading: Communicating mathematically: notation is marks, not neatness
paragraphs: Criterion C rewards correct mathematical notation and terminology, coherent lines of reasoning, appropriate forms of representation, and a conclusion that answers the question asked. Students and parents routinely read it as a presentation mark, which is the single most expensive misreading in the subject. A student who writes the right answer with undefined variables, inconsistent units and an unlabelled graph will be marked down by a teacher who agrees the mathematics is correct.

The corrections are small and finite. Define every variable before using it. Keep units through the working rather than bolting them onto the answer. Use an equals sign to mean equality rather than to mean 'next step'. Label both axes with quantity and unit. Choose a representation that serves the argument, not whichever one the software produced first. State a conclusion in a sentence that answers the original question. There are perhaps a dozen such habits, and a tutor correcting every single one of them in three successive sessions produces visible change in the fourth.

This is also the criterion where online delivery has a concrete advantage. Working on a shared whiteboard means the student writes, the tutor annotates in a second colour, and the student can see the corrected version next to their own. The annotated page is saved and goes into the evidence file. Over a term those annotations thin out, and the thinning is the proof. Families who want a number can count the corrections per task and watch the count fall.

One warning that applies specifically to Dubai classrooms: several schools here mark criterion C strictly in typed submissions because tasks are produced in shared documents. Mathematical typesetting in a word processor is a skill of its own, and a student who writes beautifully by hand can lose marks to a mangled fraction. If your child's school submits maths tasks digitally, ask which equation tool is expected and practise in it.

sections.heading: The first fortnight: diagnosis from marked work, not from a placement test
paragraphs: Most tutoring arrangements begin with a placement test, which tells you what a student can do under exam conditions on a Tuesday evening after a full school day. We would rather read what a teacher has already marked. The first session asks for three things: the last three marked mathematics tasks with the teacher's comments, the task-specific clarification sheets, and the current unit sheet with its statement of inquiry. Those documents contain a term of diagnostic information and they cost nothing to produce.

What they reveal is usually more specific than the parent expects. Teacher comments repeat themselves: 'show your reasoning' appears four times across three tasks, or every modelling task ends without an evaluation. The pattern in the comments is the plan. Where the comments are thin, the clarification sheet does the work instead, because it states what the marker was looking for and the gap between that and the submission is visible in minutes.

The free trial lesson is forty-five minutes, one per family, and no card details are taken. It is spent reading those documents with the student present and producing a one-page summary: which criterion to target first, what the next task has to show, and whether tutoring is the right purchase at all. Sometimes it is not. A student whose comments show a content gap from two years ago may need a short intensive on that gap rather than a weekly slot, and we would rather say so in the first forty-five minutes.

The second session starts the work, and from there the loop is the same every week: bring the task, mark it against the criterion, rewrite the weakest part inside the session, record what the next task must show. Dubai families travel often and term dates vary across schools here, so the loop is designed to survive a missed week. The file carries the continuity, which means a tutor covering a session can pick up without a handover meeting.

sections.heading: A Dubai school year in Middle Years maths, counted term by term
paragraphs: A Dubai academic year runs from late August or early September to early July, with assessment weeks clustered before each reporting point and a long winter break in December. Mapping tutoring onto that calendar matters more in a criterion-marked subject than in an examined one, because the marks that make up the grade are collected throughout the year rather than in one sitting. A session in the week a criterion B task is set is worth several in the week after it is returned.

Ramadan reshapes the spring term every year. School days shorten, timetables compress, and evening energy shifts after Iftar. Families here routinely move sessions to a post-Iftar slot for the month, and the practical effect on a maths plan is that content teaching should be front-loaded into the weeks before, leaving consolidation and notation work for the shorter days. Planning that in advance is the difference between losing a month and using it.

The other fixed point is the Year 9 set decision and, in schools that switch, the Year 10 fork between continuing the programme and moving to International GCSE. Both are decided on evidence gathered the term before, which means the useful tutoring happens earlier than most families book it. A parent asking in March what the September set will look like has time to act; a parent asking in August does not.

Specific internal deadlines vary by school and must come from your child's programme coordinator; Cambridge and Pearson dates for families on the International GCSE route are published on the boards' own sites and should be read there rather than taken from any tutoring page.

sections.heading: End-of-programme on-screen mathematics: what changes in MYP 5
paragraphs: Some Dubai schools enter MYP 5 students for the end-of-programme on-screen mathematics examination; others close the programme with internal assessment alone. Whether your child sits one is a school decision, and the first step is to ask the programme coordinator directly rather than assume. The distinction matters because it changes the final year of preparation from criterion coaching into something much closer to examination technique.

For students who are entered, the shift is a timing shift. Five years of untimed, redraftable, criterion-marked tasks do not prepare a student to produce mathematical reasoning on screen against a fixed clock. The mathematics is familiar. The conditions are not. Students lose marks by over-planning the first task, by typing reasoning they would have written fluently by hand, and by failing to leave time for the interpretation that criterion D style questions still demand.

Preparation therefore rehearses conditions rather than content. Sessions run to a real clock, with the stimulus read on screen and planning done on paper, and the first thing most students need is permission to plan less. The second is typing practice for mathematical notation, which is slower than handwriting for everyone and much slower for a student meeting the equation tool for the first time in the examination room.

A note on dates: this project does not publish specific IB session or results dates, because they could not be confirmed from the IB's own site during research. Treat the May session as the one Dubai schools sit, and get the actual windows from your school's coordinator or the IB's published assessment pages. Any tutoring page that states an IB examination date without naming its source should be read with scepticism, including on the question of whether the date has since been revised.

sections.heading: Academic honesty in a marked mathematics task
paragraphs: Middle Years tasks carry assessment weight, and the line a tutor must not cross is specific rather than vague. A tutor may teach content, explain a descriptor, ask the questions a marker would ask, correct notation on completed work, and coach the process of investigating or modelling. A tutor may not supply the conjecture, provide the general rule, dictate the justification, or hand over sentences that end up in a submission. The student writes every word that is assessed. We say that in the first session, to the student, with the parent present.

This is not an abstract rule in this market. The competitor set for these searches includes operators who sell completed internal assessments outright, at published prices. That trade exposes the student to a malpractice finding, which is a far worse outcome than a middling grade, and it is why our investigation blocks are described as process coaching with a boundary rather than as help with a task. If a tutor ever offers to produce assessed work, that is the moment to end the arrangement.

The practical mechanics are easy to get right. The student's task document stays in the student's account and is not edited by the tutor. Feedback is given as questions and annotations on a copy, or verbally while the student types. Where a school requires a declaration of assistance, we encourage families to declare the tutoring plainly, because declared teaching support is ordinary and undeclared authorship is not.

We also do not supply board materials. Syllabus documents, past papers, mark schemes and subject guides belong to the IB, Cambridge and Pearson, and we link to the official sources rather than redistributing them. Practice material used in sessions is written for the session or taken from the student's own school resources, which has the side benefit of matching the task-specific wording the student will actually be marked against.

sections.heading: How these lessons run, and what we will not claim
paragraphs: Delivery is online, one-to-one, over live video, with a shared whiteboard and a recording the family keeps. IB Gram does not arrange home visits in Dubai; home tutoring is a service we offer only in India, and every country page on this site says the same thing. If a provider promises a specialist in Middle Years investigation work at a Dubai address next Tuesday at 5pm, ask who exactly is driving and what they have marked.

The reason we are comfortable with that limitation is the one in this subject's favour: criterion-marked mathematics rewards a tutor who has seen hundreds of these tasks, and that person is not necessarily in your community. Online delivery makes the relevant pool the whole pool. Where no suitable specialist is free at the slot a family needs, we say so and offer the nearest honest alternative, which is sometimes a different slot and sometimes a different tutor profile. We would rather lose the booking than fill it badly.

Private tutoring in the UAE is regulated. Individuals providing private lessons need a private tuition work permit from the Ministry of Human Resources and Emiratisation, introduced under Ministerial Resolution No. 710 of 2023, and the permit is granted free of charge for two years to eligible applicants including registered teachers, public and private sector employees, unemployed residents, university students and school students aged 15 to 18. Those working without one are subject to fines and penalties under the applicable laws. No fine schedule is published, so no amount should be quoted to you.

What we will not claim: any regulator or examination board approval, because IB Gram holds none; any grade outcome, because nobody can honestly promise one; any statistic about our own students without the sample size, date and method on the same page. Market rates quoted anywhere on this site are attributed to the provider or source that published them. What we offer instead is a free 45-minute trial, a named tutor, and a file of marked work you can audit at six weeks.

faqs.question: What does an IB MYP mathematics tutor in Dubai actually work on first?
faqs.answer: The marked work. A first session reads three recent mathematics tasks with the teacher's comments, the task-specific clarification sheets and the current unit sheet, then names one criterion to target and one requirement for the next task. That is faster and more accurate than a placement test, because it shows what your child produced for a teacher over a full term rather than on one evening. Where the comments repeat the same instruction across three tasks, the plan is already written. The output of the first session is a one-page summary you keep, including an honest view on whether weekly tutoring is the right purchase at all.

faqs.question: Which criterion letters does Middle Years mathematics use, and what is each worth?
faqs.answer: Four: knowing and understanding, investigating patterns, communicating, and applying mathematics in real-life contexts. Each is marked from 0 to 8 against published descriptors, giving a 32-mark total that the school converts into a subject grade from 1 to 7. The conversion uses boundaries rather than a percentage, which is why two extra criterion marks sometimes move a grade and sometimes do not. Ask your child's programme coordinator which boundary the current total sits under and how far it has to move. That question turns a vague ambition into a target a tutor can be held to, and it usually reveals that only one of the four marks needs work.

faqs.question: My son is strong at algebra but scored 3 on investigating patterns. Why?
faqs.answer: Because criterion B asks for five moves and algebra fluency only covers part of one. The student has to select a technique, find a pattern, describe it, state it as a general rule, verify the rule beyond the given cases, and justify why it holds. Strong manipulators usually describe the pattern correctly and then stall at converting the description into an expression in n, or treat the rule as proved because it worked for the three rows in the table. Both are teachable in a short block: three worked justifications across different branches, and most students produce a fourth unaided on their own task.

faqs.question: Is criterion C just a mark for neat presentation?
faqs.answer: No. Criterion C rewards correct mathematical notation and terminology, coherent lines of reasoning, appropriate representation, and a conclusion that answers the question asked. A correct answer with undefined variables, inconsistent units and an unlabelled graph loses real marks from a teacher who agrees the mathematics is right. The fixes are a finite set of habits: define variables, carry units through the working, use the equals sign to mean equality, label both axes with quantity and unit, and finish with a sentence. Correct every instance for three sessions and the fourth marked task usually comes back with far fewer annotations on it.

faqs.question: What changes when a Dubai school moves my daughter into the extended route?
faqs.answer: Pace, mostly, and consolidation time. Extended adds algebraic and trigonometric content for students heading towards higher-level Diploma mathematics, and extended sets tend to meet a topic once, assess it and move on. Set placement is usually decided on criterion A, because knowing and understanding is easiest to measure in a class test, so a predictable pattern follows: a student with a 7 on A and a 4 on B is moved up and then exposed on investigating patterns, where harder content makes harder patterns to justify. If that is your report profile, buy investigation work rather than more content.

faqs.question: How do I know whether the tutoring is actually working after six weeks?
faqs.answer: Read the file and ask three questions. Has the target criterion scored higher on a comparable task, marked by the school rather than by us? Has the notation correction count on returned tasks fallen? Is your child now attempting the final, unfamiliar part of each task instead of leaving it blank? Three noes mean the plan is wrong, and the right response is to change it or stop. We build the file for exactly this audit: every marked task dated, with the criterion written on it and one line recording what the next task had to show. Nothing in it predicts a grade.

faqs.question: Do you supply worksheets, or work from my child's school tasks?
faqs.answer: The school's tasks, wherever they exist. A worksheet proves a tutor was busy; a marked school task proves the student did something different in front of a teacher who did not know a tutor was involved. School tasks also carry the task-specific clarification sheet, which states what the marker was looking for, so the work stays aligned to the exact wording your child is assessed against. Where there is no current task, practice material is written for the session or drawn from your child's own school resources. We do not redistribute board syllabus documents, past papers or mark schemes; those are linked at source.

faqs.question: Can a tutor help with a Middle Years maths investigation without breaking the rules?
faqs.answer: Yes, within a clear boundary. A tutor may teach the content, explain the descriptor, ask the questions a marker would ask, correct notation on completed work and coach the process. A tutor may not supply the conjecture, provide the general rule, dictate the justification or hand over sentences that end up in a submission. Every assessed word is the student's. We state this aloud in the first session with the parent present, because the alternative exposes the student to a malpractice finding, which is a far worse outcome than a middling mark. Where a school asks for a declaration of assistance, declare the tutoring plainly.

faqs.question: Does my child's school enter students for the on-screen mathematics examination at the end of MYP 5?
faqs.answer: That is a school decision and the only reliable answer comes from your programme coordinator. Some Dubai schools enter MYP 5 candidates for the end-of-programme on-screen examination; others close the programme with internal assessment alone. Ask directly, because it changes the final year from criterion coaching into examination technique. Where a student is entered, the gap is almost always timing rather than mathematics: five years of untimed, redraftable tasks do not prepare anyone to produce reasoning on screen against a clock. Preparation rehearses conditions, including typing mathematical notation, which is slower than handwriting for everybody.

faqs.question: When should we start if the set decision for next year is made in the spring?
faqs.answer: The term before the decision, not after it. Dubai schools generally discuss set placement and the Year 10 route around the second reporting point, using evidence gathered in the preceding months. A parent asking in March what September will look like still has time to produce marked tasks that show a different picture; one asking in August is responding to a decision already made. If the decision is close, a short block against one criterion is usually better value than starting a weekly pattern, because it targets the evidence the school will actually read.

faqs.question: How do lessons work around the Dubai school run and Ramadan?
faqs.answer: Sessions are online on Gulf Standard Time, and the realistic start is dictated by the bus rather than the calendar: 4.30pm works in Al Barsha South, closer to 5pm in Nad Al Sheba and Meydan, and later still for parents returning from Jebel Ali. During Ramadan school days shorten and families routinely move to a post-Iftar slot, so the practical plan is to front-load content teaching into the weeks before and keep notation and consolidation work for the shorter days. Booking that shift in advance is the difference between losing the month and using it.

faqs.question: Why is a 32-mark total not just a percentage?
faqs.answer: Because the school applies grade boundaries to the total rather than dividing it. That is why a student can gain two criterion marks and stay on the same grade, or gain one and move up. It also means improvement is not linear: a total sitting just under a boundary is the cheapest grade movement in the subject, and a total sitting just above one is the most expensive. Your programme coordinator can tell you where the current total sits. Asking that before buying anything reframes the purchase from a general ambition into a specific number of marks on a named criterion.

faqs.question: Do tutors in Dubai need a permit, and should I check?
faqs.answer: Yes, and yes. Individuals providing private lessons in the UAE need a private tuition work permit from the Ministry of Human Resources and Emiratisation, introduced under Ministerial Resolution No. 710 of 2023. It is granted free of charge for two years, and eligible applicants include registered school teachers, government and private sector employees, unemployed residents, university students and school students aged 15 to 18. Anyone tutoring without one is subject to fines and penalties under the applicable laws; no fine schedule is published, so treat any quoted amount with caution. Ask a prospective tutor directly whether they hold the permit.

faqs.question: What if no suitable Middle Years maths specialist is free in our slot?
faqs.answer: We say so. The honest options are a different slot with the right specialist, a different tutor profile in your slot, or a short wait, and we will tell you which we think is better for the criterion you are targeting. What we will not do is fill the slot with a generalist and let you discover the mismatch at the next reporting point. Online delivery means the pool is wide rather than limited to one community, so a genuine blank is rare, but it happens most often at 5pm on weekdays, which is when every family in Dubai wants a session.

faqs.question: Can one tutor cover both mathematics and sciences for the same student?
faqs.answer: Sometimes, and it is worth asking rather than assuming. The criteria differ by subject group, and a tutor fluent in mathematics criterion B is not automatically fluent in the sciences equivalent, where the investigation is practical rather than numerical. Where a student needs both, the usual arrangement is one specialist each with a shared evidence file, so the family reads one document rather than two. Where the overlap is genuine, a single tutor across both is simpler to schedule and cheaper to run. The deciding factor is which criterion is holding each grade down, not convenience.

intro.heading: Why Middle Years tutoring is a budgeting problem before it is a teaching problem
paragraphs: An IB MYP online tutor in Dubai will be quoted to you somewhere between AED 45 and AED 650 an hour, and both ends of that range are real. EdFlik advertises online tutoring from AED 45 to 65 an hour and Tutopiya from roughly AED 33 to 52; Unitors publishes IGCSE tuition from AED 150 and IB tuition from AED 200; TutorChase quotes AED 270; BartyED lists a premium tier at AED 650. Bestimate's Dubai rate table for 2026 puts in-home one-to-one at AED 180 to 350 and specialist exam-level tutoring at AED 200 to 450 and above. Those figures were read in October 2026 and belong to the companies that published them, not to us.

The spread is not noise. It is the market pricing four different products under one word. At the bottom you are buying a university student who has seen the subject. In the middle you are buying a qualified subject teacher who knows the specification. At the top you are buying someone who has marked the thing your child is about to sit. For the Diploma, the top of that range is often defensible. For the Middle Years Programme it frequently is not, and knowing why is the single most useful thing a Dubai parent can learn before paying anybody.

The reason is that the Middle Years Programme is not examined in the way the money assumes. There is no terminal paper in MYP 1 through MYP 4. Every subject group is marked against four criteria, each on a nought-to-eight scale, by the child's own teacher, against task-specific descriptors written for that unit. A tutor's value therefore comes from reading those descriptors accurately and teaching the student to hit them. That is a skill, and it is not the same skill as drilling past papers. It is also cheaper to buy than exam-board specialism, because the person who has it does not need to be an examiner.

So the honest shape of a Middle Years budget looks nothing like a Diploma budget. It is lighter per hour, longer in duration, and lumpy: MYP 3 and MYP 5 cost more than MYP 1 and MYP 2, the Personal Project year adds a block that has nothing to do with any subject, and the mandatory UAE subjects every Dubai private school must teach create a second bill that almost no family plans for. A family that spends AED 300 an hour for two years without noticing any of this will have paid more and moved less than a family that spent AED 180 in the right terms.

This page prices all of that. There is a rate table split by tier with the publisher of each figure named. There is a year-by-year table across MYP 1 to MYP 5. There is a table that prices tutoring by criterion rather than by hour, because a criterion is the unit the school actually reports on. There is a side-by-side of what else the same Dubai evening could buy. And there is a plain account of what the mandatory Arabic, Islamic Education and Social Studies requirement does to a Middle Years timetable and to a household's spend.

One structural note, stated up front because it changes what you are reading. Tuition for UAE families is delivered online, one-to-one, over live video. IB Gram does not send a tutor to a Dubai address; home visits are a service we run only in India. That is not a limitation we are apologising for in this context, it is a line item: travel is the largest single cost inside an in-home hourly rate, and removing it is why the online column in every table below is lower than the in-home one.

Tutoring here is descriptor work: what the task sheet is asking for, in what form, at what band.
programmes.countryNote: Dubai's Middle Years cohort is unusual in that a large share of it will leave the programme at sixteen for International GCSE or A Level rather than continuing to the Diploma. That makes MYP 4 and MYP 5 a decision point with a price attached, and it is why this page treats MYP 5 as the most expensive year in the sequence rather than the last cheap one.

programmes.name: Diploma Programme
programmes.description: Six subjects at Higher or Standard Level, three core components, external examinations in a May session for UAE schools, and Internal Assessments that carry real weight in every subject. This is where examiner-level specialism genuinely changes the mark, and where the AED 200-450 specialist band in the table below starts to look like value rather than markup. It is also where hours per subject rise sharply.
programmes.countryNote: A Dubai family planning across both programmes should expect the per-hour rate to roughly double at the MYP-to-DP boundary. Budgeting the Middle Years at a specialist rate therefore borrows from the years where that rate is actually needed. The pattern that works is lighter, steadier support through MYP 1-4, a concentrated block in MYP 5, then specialist rates from DP1.

programmes.name: Career-related Programme
programmes.description: A smaller sixteen-plus route combining DP courses with a career-related study, a reflective project, personal and professional skills, service learning and a language-development component. Few Dubai schools offer it and the subject-level tutoring demand is correspondingly thin, but the DP courses inside it are assessed exactly as they are in the full Diploma, so the rate card is the Diploma's.
programmes.countryNote: For a Dubai MYP 5 student weighing sixteen-plus options, the Career-related Programme is worth naming because it is the route most often left out of the conversation. Ask your school's IB coordinator whether it is offered on site; it rarely is, and the answer changes whether the Personal Project year should be treated as a bridge or an endpoint.

dubai/ib-myp-online-tutor.subjectsIntro: Middle Years tutoring money does not divide evenly across the eight subject groups. Some respond quickly to criterion coaching, some need subject content first, and two or three are usually left alone until MYP 4. The notes below say which is which, from a Dubai timetable's point of view.

subjects.name: Mathematics (Standard and Extended)
subjects.description: Criteria A-D cover knowing and understanding, investigating patterns, communicating, and applying maths in real-life contexts. Dubai students usually hold A and lose C and D: the investigation is done and the generalisation is never stated, or the answer is right and never interpreted. That gap is cheap to close and is where the first few paid hours should go.

subjects.name: Sciences (Biology, Chemistry, Physics, integrated)
subjects.description: Criterion B is the expensive one: formulating a testable hypothesis with scientific reasoning, selecting variables, and designing a method someone else could follow. Marks go missing in the method and the evaluation, not in the content. A tutor who teaches experimental design rather than revising the topic moves criterion B faster than any amount of content revision.

subjects.name: Individuals and Societies
subjects.description: Four criteria reward knowing, investigating, communicating and thinking critically. Dubai students often arrive strong on recall and weak on source evaluation, because the previous curriculum rewarded the first. The fix is a sequence of short, marked source exercises, which is one of the cheapest things a tutor can run well over a shared screen.

subjects.name: Language and Literature (English)
subjects.description: Analysing, organising, producing text and using language, each 0-8. The characteristic loss is criterion A: the student retells the plot instead of analysing the writer's choices. Marked paragraph work with the descriptor visible beside it is the standard remedy, and it is why English tutoring usually shows movement before maths does.

subjects.name: Language Acquisition (French, Spanish, Arabic B, German)
subjects.description: Comprehension of spoken and written text plus communication and use of language. Phase placement matters more than year group here, and a mismatched phase is the most common invisible cause of a stuck grade in Dubai schools with large mid-year intakes. Confirm the phase before buying any hours.

subjects.name: Design
subjects.description: Inquiring and analysing, developing ideas, creating the solution, evaluating. The design cycle is where marks are lost: students build first and document afterwards, which caps criterion B permanently. One session on the cycle itself usually returns more than three on the software.

subjects.name: Arts (visual, music, drama)
subjects.description: Knowing and understanding, developing skills, thinking creatively, responding. The process journal carries the marks, not the final piece, and a Dubai student who treats it as a sketchbook rather than evidence of thinking loses two criteria at once. Tutoring here is journal discipline more than technique.

subjects.name: Physical and Health Education
subjects.description: Assessed against knowing, planning for performance, applying and performing, and reflecting on performance. Written components exist and are frequently ignored until a report lands. Rarely worth paid hours on its own, but worth knowing about when a composite grade drops for reasons nobody can explain.

subjects.name: Interdisciplinary units
subjects.levels: MYP 1-5, at least one per year
subjects.description: A separate reported strand assessing disciplinary grounding, synthesis and reflection across two subject groups. Because no single teacher owns it, it is the most commonly neglected mark on a Dubai Middle Years report. Half an hour of explicit synthesis practice before each unit deadline is unusually good value.

subjects.name: Personal Project
subjects.description: Planning, applying skills, reflecting, marked against criteria with a process journal and a report. A tutor may teach project management, questioning and self-assessment against the criteria, and may comment on the student's own draft. A tutor may not supply content for assessed work. Budget it as its own block, not as an extra inside a subject.

dubai/ib-myp-online-tutor.regionsIntro: Where a Dubai family lives does not change the published rate card, but it changes two things that cost money: how late a session has to start, and how many local tutors would realistically take the booking. The notes below are about scheduling economics rather than geography.

regions.name: Jumeirah and Umm Suqeim
regions.note: Short school runs and early finishes make a 4pm start realistic here, which is the cheapest slot in the week because it competes with nothing. Families in these communities are also the most likely to be choosing between the Middle Years Programme and a British-track Year 10, so tutoring often doubles as decision support.

regions.name: Dubai Marina and Jumeirah Lakes Towers
regions.note: Apartment living and two working parents push sessions to 6.30pm or later, and an in-home tutor crossing Sheikh Zayed Road at that hour prices the journey into the fee. Online removes that line entirely, which is why the per-hour gap between formats is widest in this cluster.

regions.name: Arabian Ranches, Dubai Hills and Mudon
regions.note: Villa communities with long bus runs; many Middle Years students are not home before 4.30pm. The practical consequence is that one 60-minute slot works and two back-to-back do not, so the budget should buy frequency across the term rather than length on the day.

regions.name: Mirdif, Al Warqa and Al Qusais
regions.note: A dense mix of British, Indian and IB-continuum schools inside a few kilometres, which means siblings are often on different curricula and different reporting calendars. Families here benefit most from the criterion-priced approach, because one tutor can cover two children without pretending the two programmes are the same.

regions.name: Al Barsha and Emirates Hills
regions.note: Home to several full IB-continuum schools, so Middle Years demand is concentrated and specific: the same unit planner comes up repeatedly. That is useful. A tutor who has already read the task sheet your child was handed needs fewer diagnostic hours, and diagnostic hours are the ones parents resent paying for.

regions.name: Dubai Silicon Oasis and Academic City
regions.note: Proximity to the universities keeps the budget tier well supplied with postgraduate tutors, which is why the AED 45-150 band is genuinely available in this part of Dubai. It is also why asking about permit status matters here more than anywhere else in the emirate.

regions.name: Downtown Dubai and Business Bay
regions.note: Mostly apartments, mostly later sessions, and a high rate of mid-year arrivals from other systems. For a new MYP 2 or MYP 3 student the first spend should be a phase and placement check in Language Acquisition, not subject revision, because a wrong phase wastes every hour that follows.

regions.name: The Springs, The Meadows and Jumeirah Park
regions.note: Established family communities where a weekly fixed slot survives the whole term, which is the single biggest driver of value in Middle Years tutoring. Consistency beats intensity here: the same hour every Tuesday for twelve weeks outperforms a block of six hours in the week before a deadline.

schoolClusters.city: Al Barsha, Emirates Hills and Dubai Hills
schoolClusters.note: The densest concentration of full IB-continuum provision in Dubai, where students run Primary Years into Middle Years into the Diploma inside one school. Tutoring requests from this cluster arrive with the unit planner attached, which shortens diagnosis and lowers the number of paid hours needed before teaching starts.

schoolClusters.city: Mirdif, Al Warqa and Dubai Silicon Oasis
schoolClusters.note: A mixed-curriculum belt where IB-continuum schools sit alongside British and Indian-curriculum neighbours. Middle Years students here often have siblings on a different reporting cycle, so families tend to buy by criterion and by deadline rather than by subject across the household.

schoolClusters.city: Dubai Marina, JLT and Al Sufouh
schoolClusters.note: Apartment communities with later session times and a high share of relocating families. The Middle Years questions that come from this cluster are about placement and transition more than content: which phase, which subject group, and whether a mid-year arrival should be sitting Standard or Extended mathematics.

dubai/ib-myp-online-tutor.modesIntro: Three ways of buying Middle Years support, priced differently and suited to different problems. The right one depends on which year your child is in and whether the issue is content, criteria or deadlines.

modes.title: Weekly criterion coaching
modes.description: One 60-minute session a week on the same day across a term, working from the live unit planner and the task sheet rather than a fixed syllabus. The agenda is set by whichever criterion is being assessed next. This is the mode that suits MYP 1 to MYP 3, where the issue is almost never content knowledge and almost always what the descriptor wants.
bullets: Same slot weekly, which protects the habit and the price
Agenda driven by the next assessed task, not a generic scheme
Written feedback against the criterion letter after each session
Lowest cost per band moved across MYP 1-3

modes.title: Deadline blocks
modes.description: A short concentrated run of three to five sessions timed to a specific assessed task, an interdisciplinary unit or a Personal Project checkpoint. Families use this when the term is otherwise under control and one piece of work is not. It costs more per hour of attention than a weekly slot but less in total, and it is the honest answer for households that cannot hold a fixed weekly time.
bullets: Booked against a dated school deadline, then stopped
Works for interdisciplinary units nobody has been revising for

No open-ended commitment once the task is submitted

modes.title: Transition support at the MYP boundaries
modes.description: A defined block at either end of the programme: Year 6 into MYP 1, or MYP 5 into the Diploma, International GCSE or A Level. The work is placement, not revision. For an arriving student it establishes the right language phase and the right mathematics route; for a leaving student it closes the specific gaps the next system assumes are already there.

Language Acquisition phase checked before any hours are bought

sections.heading: What an IB MYP online tutor in Dubai costs, with every figure attributed
paragraphs: Published market rates for Middle Years tutoring in Dubai run from about AED 33 an hour at the bottom of the online platform tier to AED 650 an hour at the premium end, with the broad middle sitting between AED 150 and AED 300. Every figure in the table below was read from the provider's own public page in October 2026. None of them is an IB Gram price, and none of them should be read as a quote. We publish them because three of the six best-ranking pages for this search publish no price at all, and the two that do quote in US dollars, a currency no Dubai family pays tuition in.

Read the table by tier rather than by number. The budget tier is a real product and it is the right product for some Middle Years work: a capable postgraduate who can sit with a student through a maths investigation does not need to be an examiner. The qualified tier buys someone who has taught the subject group and can read a task-specific descriptor cold. The specialist tier buys exam-board depth, which the Middle Years Programme does not externally examine until the end, and which is therefore usually worth deferring until the Diploma.

What the table deliberately does not contain is an IB Gram rate card. Middle Years quotes depend on the subject group, the year, the number of sessions and whether the work is weekly or a deadline block, and a single number on a landing page would be a fiction. The free trial lesson, which is one per family and carries no card requirement, exists so that the first conversation is about the diagnosis rather than the invoice. Everything else is agreed in writing before a second session is booked.

sections.heading: Five years, not five sessions: what each MYP year actually costs
paragraphs: The Middle Years Programme runs five years, and a family that budgets it as one is nearly always surprised twice: once in MYP 3, when the criteria stop being forgiving, and once in MYP 5, when the Personal Project and the sixteen-plus decision arrive in the same term. The table below spreads the spend across the sequence using the mid-market qualified rate, because that is the tier most Dubai Middle Years families end up on, and because using the specialist rate across five years produces a number nobody should pay.

The pattern that falls out of it is worth stating plainly. MYP 1 and MYP 2 are cheap years in which small amounts of the right support prevent expensive years later; the work is written stamina, note-taking and learning what a descriptor is. MYP 3 and MYP 4 are the content years, where subject knowledge starts to carry real weight and where a weekly slot in one or two subject groups is the standard shape. MYP 5 is the most expensive year in the programme, and it is the one families routinely under-budget because it looks like the end rather than the pivot.

Two caveats about reading the monthly column. First, it assumes one subject group, not three; a household running maths and sciences together is doubling or tripling it. Second, it assumes a term of consistent weekly sessions rather than a panic block, which costs the same per hour and less in total. Bestimate's own monthly estimates for weekly one-hour sessions in Dubai, read in October 2026, run AED 240-600 at the budget tier, AED 600-1,200 mid-tier and AED 1,000-2,000 and above for specialist exam-year support, which brackets the figures below.

sections.heading: Buying by criterion rather than by hour
paragraphs: An hour is a unit of selling. A criterion is the unit the school reports on. Every Middle Years subject group is marked against four criteria, each on a nought-to-eight scale, and the grade your child brings home is a conversion of those totals rather than an average of test scores. If you buy hours, you cannot tell whether the money worked. If you buy against a criterion, you can: the next marked task either moves a band or it does not, and the task sheet names which criterion it was.

This reframing is the cheapest improvement available to a Dubai Middle Years family, and it costs nothing. Before booking, ask the school which criteria the next assessed task covers. Then brief the tutor on that criterion and nothing else. The table below gives the shape across the four letters as they appear in most subject groups, with the characteristic Dubai failure and a realistic number of sessions to move one band. The letters carry different names in different subject groups; the structure holds.

Confirm the criterion letters and the current grade boundaries with your child's subject teacher or the school's IB coordinator, because task-specific descriptors are written by the school and bands are set against the programme's published conversion. We are describing the mechanism, not publishing your school's figures. That distinction matters for the same reason the rate table names its sources: a number without a date and an owner is worth less than no number at all.

sections.heading: Eight subject groups, one timetable, and where a tight budget should go first
paragraphs: Dubai Middle Years students carry eight subject groups plus interdisciplinary units plus the mandatory UAE subjects their school is required to teach. No family can tutor all of that and none should try. The question is not which subject is weakest but which subject's criteria respond fastest to coaching, because a band gained in six weeks changes the student's confidence and a band gained in six months does not.

The honest ranking is roughly this. Language and Literature moves first, because criterion A analysis is teachable in marked paragraphs and the feedback loop is a week long. Mathematics moves next, because criteria C and D are structural and the content is usually already there. Sciences take longer because criterion B is a design skill rather than a knowledge gap. Individuals and Societies sits with Sciences. Design, Arts and Physical and Health Education rarely justify paid hours in isolation, though they routinely drag a composite report down and are worth one session to diagnose.

Interdisciplinary units deserve a line of their own. They are separately reported, they are owned by no single teacher, and they are the mark most commonly left to chance in a Dubai Middle Years report. Thirty minutes of explicit synthesis practice before each unit deadline is one of the highest-return half-hours a family can buy in the whole programme, and almost nobody buys it because nobody tells parents the strand exists. Ask the school when the next interdisciplinary unit is assessed and which two subject groups it draws on; both facts are usually on the unit planner and neither tends to reach the parent.

sections.heading: What else the same Dubai evening could buy
paragraphs: Tutoring is bought against alternatives, and most Dubai families compare it against nothing. The table below sets one-to-one online support beside the other things that occupy a Middle Years student's weekday evening and a household's monthly outgoings, using figures published by the providers themselves and read in October 2026. The point is not that one is better. It is that AED 800 a month is a choice between things, and the choice should be made with the numbers visible.

The context number that belongs in this conversation is school fees. KHDA confirmed on 22 May 2026 that there would be no increase in private school fees in Dubai for the 2026-27 academic year, under the emirate's second economic incentives package. For a Middle Years family that is a genuinely useful planning fact: the largest education line in the household budget is flat for a year, which is the year to decide whether a weekly tutoring slot is affordable on a stable base rather than a rising one.

The second context number is the market's own shape. Dubai had 387,441 private school students across 227 private schools in 2024-25, offering seventeen different curricula, with UK-curriculum schools accounting for 37% of enrolment, Indian 26%, US 14% and the International Baccalaureate 7%. The Middle Years cohort is therefore a minority inside a very large market, which is precisely why local in-home tutor supply for MYP-specific criterion work is thinner than it is for International GCSE, and why the online pool matters more here than the neighbourhood pool.

sections.heading: Gulf Standard Time, the school run, and the cost of a badly placed slot
paragraphs: The least discussed driver of Middle Years tutoring cost in Dubai is the clock. A session at 4pm competes with nothing and tends to be available at the lower end of whatever tier you are buying. A session at 7.30pm competes with every working parent in the emirate, and the price follows the scarcity. If your child can be at a desk by 4.15pm two days a week, you are shopping in a cheaper market than a family that can only do 8pm, for exactly the same teaching.

Villa communities with long bus routes and apartment households with two commutes end up at the expensive end of the evening by default. There are two ways out of it that cost nothing. The first is the weekend: Saturday mornings are the most underused hours in the Dubai tutoring week and the easiest slot to hold for a whole term. The second is the split session: two 45-minute slots a week outperform one 90-minute slot for criterion work, because the feedback loop closes twice.

Online delivery also widens the tutor pool across time zones, which is where availability stops being a local supply problem. A Middle Years sciences specialist working from India or the United Kingdom can take a 5pm Gulf Standard Time booking without travelling, which is the mechanism behind the gap between the online and in-home columns in the rate table. Ramadan shifts the whole pattern: sessions move to late morning or after Iftar, and families who plan that in advance keep their slot rather than losing the term.

sections.heading: The Personal Project year is a separate budget line
paragraphs: In MYP 5 every student completes the Personal Project: a self-directed piece of work with a process journal and a report, assessed against its own criteria and reported separately from any subject group. It is the single most common reason a Dubai family who had never bought tutoring suddenly needs some, and it is also the piece of work where the boundary between help and malpractice is narrowest.

What a tutor may legitimately do is teachable and specific. They may help the student choose a goal that is achievable in the time available. They may teach project management, research method, note-taking and referencing. They may ask the questions that make a vague goal measurable. They may read the student's own draft and give feedback against the criteria, and they may teach the student to self-assess against those criteria. They may coach the oral presentation and the reflection.

What a tutor must never do is supply any part of the assessed work. Not a paragraph of the report, not an entry in the process journal, not a product the student then presents as their own. The IB's academic honesty rules make that an expulsion risk for the student and it is not a service we sell at any price. One competitor in this market advertises completed Internal Assessments for a four-figure sum; that is not a cheaper version of tutoring, it is a different and much more expensive mistake. Budget the Personal Project as three to five sessions of process coaching, spread across the checkpoints the school sets.

sections.heading: The second bill: Arabic, Islamic Education and Social Studies
paragraphs: Every Dubai private school must teach Arabic, Islamic Education and Social or Moral Studies regardless of which international curriculum it is licensed to deliver, and KHDA's published requirements had to be implemented by the start of the 2025-26 academic year, or April 2026 for schools whose year begins in April. For a Middle Years family this is not a footnote. It is three subjects that sit outside the eight subject groups, are reported on, and are the most common source of a tutoring bill that was never budgeted.

The organisational rules are specific and they explain why finding help is harder than it looks. KHDA requires separate classes for Arabs and non-Arabs in Arabic as a first language, Islamic Education and Social Studies, and states that combined classes for both groups are strictly prohibited because the curriculum expectations and language of instruction differ. Standard Arabic is required as the main language of instruction for Islamic Education for Arabs and for Arabic as a first language; Arabic is the primary language for Social Studies for Arab students; non-Arabs are taught Islamic Education and Moral, Social and Cultural studies in the school's licensed-curriculum language.

Two further constraints matter for anyone buying support. Schools are required to ensure that all teachers of Islamic Education and Arabic have appropriate KHDA approval to teach those subjects, and for the mandatory UAE subjects the use of any different or additional content without prior permission from the Ministry of Education is strictly prohibited. In practice that means tutoring in these subjects is school-material work: a tutor supports the student with the content the school is required to use, rather than importing a parallel scheme. KHDA calculates mandatory-subject instructional time on a 40-minute lesson unit, allows schools to vary lesson length provided the weekly total is met, and advises that any mandatory subject lesson should be at least 25 minutes.

sections.heading: Is the money working? What to check at six weeks
paragraphs: Six weeks is roughly six sessions, and it is long enough to tell. The check is not whether your child says the tutor is nice, and it is not whether the homework is done. It is whether a marked task has moved a criterion band, and if it has not, whether you can see what the tutor was working on and why it should have. Either answer is useful. The one unacceptable state is not knowing.

Four things should exist by week six. A written diagnosis from the first session that names criteria rather than topics. Session notes that reference the criterion letter and the task. At least two marked pieces of the student's own work with the descriptor visible beside the feedback. And a stated next step that is specific enough to be wrong. If all four exist and nothing has moved, the diagnosis was probably wrong and the fix is a different subject group or a different criterion, not more hours.

If none of the four exist, you are paying for company rather than teaching, and that is true at AED 45 an hour and at AED 650 an hour. This is also the point at which a Dubai family should ask the question nobody asks at the start: is the tutor legally permitted to teach privately here? Individuals providing private lessons in the UAE need a MoHRE private tuition work permit under Ministerial Resolution No. 710 of 2023. The permit is granted free of charge for two years, the official route is MoHRE's own private tutor licensing service with a two-working-day completion time, and those operating without one are subject to fines and penalties under the applicable laws. No fine schedule is published, so nobody should be quoting you an amount.
bullets: A written diagnosis naming criteria, produced after the first session
Session notes that reference the criterion letter and the assessed task
Two or more marked pieces of the student's own work with feedback against the descriptor
A next step specific enough that you could tell if it failed
A straight answer about the tutor's MoHRE private tuition work permit

sections.heading: How these lessons actually run, and what we will not claim
paragraphs: Sessions are one-to-one, live, over video, on a shared screen with a writing surface both people can use. The student works and the tutor watches them work, which is the part that cannot be replaced by a recording or a worksheet. Scheduling is on Gulf Standard Time against your child's own school calendar, and the material is your child's own unit planner, task sheet and marked work. IB Gram does not make home visits in Dubai or anywhere else in the UAE; in-home tuition is a service we run only in India, and this page's comparison tables exist so that the trade is visible rather than buried.

There are things this page will not tell you, and the omissions are deliberate. We do not publish an IB exam or results date, because the IB's own site blocks automated verification and a date on a landing page that turns out to be wrong is worse than no date. Confirm every IB session date with your school's IB coordinator or on ibo.org. We do not hold KHDA, ADEK, SPEA, Ministry of Education, MoHRE, IB or Cambridge accreditation, approval or partnership, and we do not describe ourselves as if we did; a KHDA Educational Services Permit is a specific document issued to training institutes with premises in Dubai, and we do not operate premises in the UAE.

We also make no promises about any grade, publish no satisfaction percentages, and show no star rating we cannot evidence with real, dated, attributable reviews. What we will commit to is narrower and checkable: a diagnosis in writing, work against the criterion the school is about to assess, feedback on your child's own drafts, and a straight answer when no specialist is available for a niche subject group rather than a match made to fill a slot. If a Middle Years subject has no suitable tutor free in the window you need, we will say so, say when that changes, and not take the booking in the meantime.

process.title: Send the report and the task sheet
process.description: Not a description of the problem: the actual documents. A Middle Years report with criterion marks and the task sheet for the next assessed piece tell a tutor more in five minutes than a half-hour phone call. If the school publishes the unit planner, send that too.

process.title: Take the trial lesson
process.description: One lesson at no charge per family, with no card required to book it. It is a diagnostic rather than a sample lesson: the tutor works the student through a task and reports which criteria are actually costing marks, which is frequently not the subject the parent named.

process.title: Agree the scope and the price in writing
process.description: Session length, number of sessions, which criterion is being targeted, cancellation terms and whether VAT applies to the quoted figure. Put all five in a message before the second session. A quote that cannot survive being written down is not a quote.

process.title: Hold one fixed slot across the term
process.description: Consistency outperforms intensity in the Middle Years, because criterion work needs a feedback loop rather than a cram. Pick the earliest hour your household can actually sustain, which is usually cheaper as well as better attended, and defend it against everything short of exams.

process.title: Review at six weeks against the criteria
process.description: Read the marked work, not the invoice. Has a criterion band moved, and if not, does the tutor's own reasoning explain why? Change the target or the tutor at that point rather than at the end of the year, when the term you paid for is already gone.

process.title: Rescope at each MYP boundary
process.description: What worked in MYP 2 is wrong for MYP 4, and MYP 5 needs its own plan for the Personal Project and the sixteen-plus decision. Treat each boundary as a fresh diagnosis rather than a continuation, and expect the budget shape to change with it.

whyPoints.title: Prices with owners and dates attached
whyPoints.description: Every AED figure on this page names the provider that published it and the month it was read. Three of the six best-ranking competitor pages for this search publish no price at all, and the two that do quote in US dollars. A number without a source is not information.

whyPoints.title: Criterion-led, not topic-led
whyPoints.description: Middle Years grades come from four criteria marked nought to eight against task-specific descriptors, so that is what sessions target. Buying topic revision when the loss is in criterion B or D is the most common way Dubai families waste tutoring money without noticing.

whyPoints.title: Delivery stated plainly
whyPoints.description: Lessons are one-to-one over live video on Gulf Standard Time. IB Gram does not send tutors to UAE addresses; home visits are a service we run only in India. You are told that before you book, not after, and the cost consequence is in the tables above.

whyPoints.title: Academic honesty as a boundary, not a disclaimer
whyPoints.description: A tutor teaches, questions and gives feedback on the student's own draft. Assessed work stays the student's own, which on the Personal Project is the difference between support and an expulsion risk. We say where the line is rather than leaving it to be discovered.

whyPoints.title: Availability disclosed, including when it is bad
whyPoints.description: If no suitable tutor is free for a niche Middle Years subject group in your window, we say so and say when that changes. Filling a slot with whoever is available costs a family a term and is the failure mode nobody in this market admits to.

whyPoints.title: Regulator facts cited, never borrowed as credentials
whyPoints.description: KHDA, MoHRE and Ministry of Education requirements are described with their source so a parent can check them. We hold no approval, accreditation or partnership from any of them and operate no premises in the UAE, which is why none of this page claims otherwise.

faqs.question: How much does an IB MYP online tutor in Dubai charge per hour?
faqs.answer: Published market rates in Dubai span roughly AED 33 to AED 650 an hour, and Middle Years work usually sits in the AED 150 to AED 300 band. Tutopiya lists from AED 33-52 and EdFlik from AED 45-65 at the platform end; Unitors lists IB tuition from AED 200; TutorChase lists AED 270; BartyED lists AED 650 at the premium end. All read October 2026, all theirs rather than ours. Middle Years tutoring rarely needs the specialist tier, because MYP 1 to MYP 4 carry no external examination. Our own quote depends on subject group, year and session count, and is agreed in writing after the trial lesson.

faqs.question: Is it cheaper to start Middle Years tutoring in MYP 2 or wait until MYP 5?
faqs.answer: Starting earlier is cheaper in total and almost always cheaper per band moved. MYP 1 and MYP 2 problems are mechanical: no system for eight task sheets, weak written stamina, no idea what a descriptor is. Those take a handful of sessions. The same student in MYP 5 is carrying four years of the same habits into the Personal Project and the sixteen-plus decision at once, which is why MYP 5 is the most expensive year in the programme. Waiting does not avoid the spend; it concentrates it into the year with the least room to absorb it.

faqs.question: How many tutoring hours does one MYP criterion realistically need?
faqs.answer: It depends on the letter. Criterion A, knowing and understanding, is usually the student's strongest and often needs nothing. Criterion C, communicating, typically moves a band in two or three sessions because the problem is form rather than knowledge. Criterion B, investigating, takes three or four, since designing an inquiry is a skill rather than a fact. Criterion D, thinking critically, is the slowest at three to five, because evaluation has to be built as a habit. Those are working estimates across subject groups, not guarantees, and the band your school awards depends on its own task-specific descriptors.

faqs.question: Which MYP subject group gives the best return on tutoring spend?
faqs.answer: Language and Literature, in most cases. Criterion A analysis is teachable in marked paragraphs, the feedback loop is a week long, and movement shows on the next assessed task rather than next term. Mathematics is second, because the content is usually already present and the loss sits in communication and interpretation. Sciences and Individuals and Societies take a term, since the weak criterion is a design or evaluation skill. Design, Arts and Physical and Health Education rarely justify paid hours alone, though one diagnostic session is worth buying when a composite grade drops without explanation.

faqs.question: Do I pay more for a tutor who has read my child's school unit plans?
faqs.answer: No, and you should expect it as standard rather than as a premium. Working from the live unit planner and task sheet is what makes Middle Years tutoring effective, because the descriptors are task-specific and written by the school. What reading them does change is the number of paid hours you need: a tutor who already has the document spends the first session teaching rather than diagnosing. Send the report, the task sheet and the unit planner before the trial lesson. It is the cheapest thing you can do to lower the total bill.

faqs.question: Does the Personal Project year cost more in tutoring than MYP 4?
faqs.answer: Usually yes, for three reasons that stack in the same year. The Personal Project is a separate assessed strand needing its own process coaching, typically three to five sessions across the school's checkpoints. Subject groups are simultaneously at their heaviest. And the sixteen-plus decision between continuing to the Diploma or moving to International GCSE or A Level often needs its own diagnostic work. Budget MYP 5 as the peak year of the programme rather than its wind-down. A tutor may coach process, method and self-assessment, but may never supply any part of the assessed work itself.

faqs.question: What does eAssessment preparation add to a Dubai family's tutoring budget?
faqs.answer: Only some Dubai schools enter students for end-of-programme eAssessment, so the first step costs nothing: ask your school's IB coordinator whether your child is being entered, and for which subject groups. Where it applies, it introduces on-screen examinations and ePortfolio requirements that differ in format from everything the student has done for four years, and format practice is the spend. Expect a short block rather than a term, concentrated in the months before the window. Where the school does not enter students, the programme remains internally assessed and no separate preparation budget is needed.

faqs.question: Do we have to pay separately for Arabic and Islamic Education support?
faqs.answer: If you need it, yes, and it is the most commonly unbudgeted line in a Dubai Middle Years household. All Dubai private schools must teach Arabic, Islamic Education and Social or Moral Studies whatever their licensed curriculum, under KHDA requirements implemented from the start of 2025-26. These sit outside the eight subject groups and are reported separately. KHDA also requires separate classes for Arabs and non-Arabs in Arabic as a first language, Islamic Education and Social Studies, and prohibits combined classes, so support has to match the right stream and work from the school's own prescribed material.

faqs.question: Is a 45-minute online session cheaper per criterion than a 90-minute one?
faqs.answer: Two 45-minute sessions a week usually outperform one 90-minute session at the same total cost, for criterion work specifically. The reason is the feedback loop: the student attempts something, gets it marked against the descriptor, revises it and attempts again. That cycle closes twice in two short sessions and once in one long one. Ninety-minute sessions earn their place for investigations, Personal Project work and anything needing a long run at one document. For weekly descriptor coaching in MYP 1 to MYP 3, split the time.

faqs.question: Why does a 7pm slot in Dubai cost more than a 4pm one?
faqs.answer: Scarcity, not quality. Every working parent in the emirate wants the same two hours of the evening, so the late slots fill first and clear at the top of whatever tier you are buying. A 4.15pm start competes with almost nothing. The two cheapest moves available to a Dubai household are therefore the earliest sustainable weekday hour and Saturday morning, which is the most underused window in the Dubai tutoring week. Online delivery also removes travel from the equation entirely, which is why the online column in our rate table sits below the in-home one.

faqs.question: Can two siblings in different MYP years share one tutoring budget?
faqs.answer: They can share a tutor and a weekly rhythm, but not a session. Criterion coaching is descriptor work on one student's own task sheet, and two children in MYP 2 and MYP 4 are working to different descriptors in different subject groups. What does work across a household is sequencing: one sibling on a weekly slot while the other runs deadline blocks, then swapping as the terms demand. Families in mixed-curriculum neighbourhoods like Mirdif and Al Warqa often run this pattern, because one tutor can hold both children's calendars without pretending the programmes are the same.

faqs.question: Does the Dubai 2026-27 fee freeze change what tutoring should cost?
faqs.answer: It does not change tutoring rates, but it changes the planning. KHDA confirmed on 22 May 2026 that private school fees in Dubai would not increase for the 2026-27 academic year, under the emirate's second economic incentives package. For a Middle Years family that means the largest education line in the household budget is flat for a year, which makes it a sensible year to commit to a steady weekly slot rather than panic blocks. It is also useful context for judging a quote: a tutoring bill is being set against a stable fee base, not a rising one.

faqs.question: Is a tuition centre group class in Dubai better value than one-to-one online?
faqs.answer: Per head, a group of two to four costs roughly a third to a half of the one-to-one rate, which is real money. Per criterion, it is usually slower, because descriptor work depends on one student's own task sheet and a group has to share attention. Groups suit content revision and exam-style drilling. They suit Middle Years criterion coaching badly. A centre also adds travel at the Dubai hours when travel is slowest, and a centre with premises needs a different permission from an individual tutor, which is worth asking about before paying.

faqs.question: What should I put in writing before paying a Dubai Middle Years tutor?
faqs.answer: Five things, in one message, before the second session. The session length and the rate for it. The number of sessions you are committing to. Which criterion or criteria the work is targeting, named by letter. The cancellation and rescheduling terms. And whether the quoted figure includes VAT. Ask separately whether the tutor holds a MoHRE private tuition work permit, which individuals providing private lessons in the UAE require under Ministerial Resolution No. 710 of 2023 and which is granted free of charge for two years. A quote that cannot survive being written down is not a quote.

faqs.question: How do I tell whether MYP tutoring is actually worth the money yet?
faqs.answer: Check at six weeks, and check the marked work rather than the invoice. Four things should exist: a written diagnosis naming criteria rather than topics, session notes referencing the criterion letter and the assessed task, at least two marked pieces of your child's own work with feedback against the descriptor, and a next step specific enough that you could tell if it failed. If all four exist and nothing has moved, the target was wrong and should change. If none exist, you are paying for company rather than teaching, at any hourly rate.

dubai/ib-myp-online-tutor.closingHeading: Start with the diagnosis, then decide what to spend
dubai/ib-myp-online-tutor.closingBody: The useful order is diagnosis, then budget, then hours. Send your child's Middle Years report, the task sheet for the next assessed piece and the unit planner if the school publishes it. Take the trial lesson, which is one per family and needs no card, and read what comes back: which criteria are actually costing marks, in which subject groups, and what it would take to move them. Then set a figure against the year your child is in rather than against the whole programme. Lessons run one-to-one over live video on Gulf Standard Time, and the terms go in writing before a second session is booked.
