sections.heading: Criterion C in four sessions: the fix that moves a flat five
paragraphs: A student sitting on five out of eight for Criterion C across three reporting cycles has almost never got a language problem. They have got a task-reading problem. The pattern is consistent enough to be diagnostic: the Spanish is accurate, the paragraph is well formed, the content answers the text rather than the question, and the format asked for in the prompt has been ignored. A blog post, an email to a teacher and a speech to a class are three different registers, and Criterion C notices.

The first session is spent reading prompts without writing any Spanish at all. The student highlights the command, the text type, the audience and the number of ideas required. Most students discover they have been reading only the topic. The second session introduces a planning frame: three ideas, one connective each, one register marker, one piece of evidence from the source. The third session runs a timed response to the frame. The fourth marks that response against the Criterion C strands aloud, so the student hears what a six and a seven sound like.

This is slow work and it is dull for the first fortnight. It also tends to be the only intervention that moves Criterion C, because adding vocabulary to a student who is answering the wrong question just produces a better-dressed wrong answer. The side effect is useful: the same planning frame works in MYP Arabic, in MYP Language and Literature, and later in the DP individual oral, because all four reward a planned response over a fluent ramble.

Progress here is visible without waiting for a report card. A parent can read the first unplanned response and the fourth planned one side by side and see the difference in structure even without reading Spanish. That is deliberate. Evidence a parent can check beats a tutor's assurance that things are going well.
bullets: Session one: read prompts, write nothing, highlight command, text type and audience
Session two: build a three-idea planning frame with register markers
Session three: timed response using the frame
Session four: mark that response aloud against the Criterion C strands
The frame transfers to MYP Arabic and to the DP individual oral

sections.heading: MYP eAssessment and Spanish: an ePortfolio, not an on-screen exam
paragraphs: Schools that choose to register for the IB MYP certificate put MYP 5 students through eAssessment at the end of the programme. This catches Dubai families by surprise because it is not universal: plenty of Dubai IB continuum schools run MYP to MYP 5 and then move students straight into the Diploma without any external MYP assessment at all. Ask your MYP coordinator which route your school takes, because it changes what MYP 5 Spanish is building towards.

Where a school does register, Language Acquisition is assessed through an ePortfolio rather than a two-hour on-screen examination. That distinction matters. The on-screen examinations sit in Language and Literature, Individuals and Societies, Mathematics, Sciences and interdisciplinary learning. Language Acquisition, Arts, Design and Physical and Health Education are portfolio subjects, externally moderated against the same four criteria the student has been marked on all year.

A portfolio is a kinder format for a nervous student and a harsher one for a disorganised one. There is no single exam day to peak for, but there is a body of work assembled over months, and a task that was rushed in October cannot be unrushed in April. The tutoring implication is that MYP 5 Spanish support should start in the autumn term, not in the spring. Work that is already strong is what gets selected; work produced under deadline panic usually is not.

Confirm every date and requirement with your school's MYP coordinator and against the IB's own published guidance. The IB's site is the authority on eAssessment registration and deadlines, and school-level internal deadlines for portfolio work typically sit well ahead of anything the IB publishes. We do not publish IB session or results dates on these pages because they could not be verified from the IB directly.

sections.heading: From MYP 5 Spanish into the Diploma: which door your phase opens
paragraphs: The phase a student finishes MYP 5 in largely decides their Diploma Spanish options, and in Dubai this conversation happens too late more often than not. Option blocks for DP1 are usually set in the spring of MYP 5, by which point a Phase 2 student hoping for Spanish B SL has no runway. Starting the conversation in MYP 4 gives a full year to move a phase, which is realistic; moving a phase in a term is not.

The three routes behave differently. Spanish ab initio SL assumes little or no prior knowledge and works from prescribed themes with a tightly bounded grammar list, which makes it predictable and makes it a sensible choice for a student protecting marks in a science-heavy diploma. Spanish B SL assumes genuine prior learning and asks for writing to a text type under timed conditions. Spanish B HL adds two literary works and expects nuance rather than accuracy alone.

A fourth route exists for bilingual students: Spanish A: Language and Literature, which is a literature course taught in Spanish and nothing like Language Acquisition. Dubai has enough Spanish-speaking families that this comes up, and a student who has coasted through MYP Spanish at Phase 6 is often better served by Spanish A than by an HL B course that will bore them. The school has to offer it, which depends on numbers.

The table below maps the routes against the phase a student is likely arriving from, what changes, and what has to be closed during MYP 5. Treat the gap column as the work, not the warning: every one of these is a term or two of structured sessions rather than a change of plan.

sections.heading: Arabic, Islamic Education and Social Studies alongside Spanish in a Dubai school week
paragraphs: Every private school in Dubai teaches Arabic, Islamic Education and Social and Moral Studies regardless of the international curriculum it is licensed for, and KHDA's published requirements had to be in place by the start of the 2025-26 academic year. For an MYP student taking Spanish, this is not background information. It is the reason the option block is tight and the reason a second additional language often cannot be fitted in.

KHDA's guidance is specific about how these subjects run. Schools must organise separate classes for Arabs and non-Arabs in Arabic as a first language, Islamic Education and Social Studies, and combined classes for both groups are not permitted, because the curriculum expectations and the language of instruction differ. Standard Arabic is required as the main language of instruction for Islamic Education for Arabs and for Arabic as a first language. Instructional time is calculated on a forty-minute lesson unit, and KHDA advises that any mandatory-subject lesson runs at least twenty-five minutes.

The practical effect on a Dubai MYP timetable is that a student is already carrying Arabic as an additional language alongside Spanish, with both marked on the same four Language Acquisition criteria. Families who treat these as two unrelated problems end up paying for two sets of sessions. Families who treat the criteria as the shared object get more out of one. A Criterion C planning frame built in Spanish works in Arabic, because the criterion is identical.

One constraint worth knowing if you are considering extra Arabic support: for the mandatory UAE subjects, using different or additional content without prior permission from the Ministry of Education is not allowed, and schools must ensure Arabic and Islamic Education teachers hold the appropriate KHDA approval to teach those subjects. Tutoring around those subjects therefore works best as support for the school's own material rather than as a parallel course.

sections.heading: What MYP Spanish tutoring costs in the Dubai market
paragraphs: Nobody in this corner of the market publishes a price, which is odd given it is the first question every parent asks. Of the competitor pages examined for this project, three published no figure at all and two quoted in US dollars, a currency Dubai families do not transact in. The figures below are the market's, gathered from providers' own published rates and from a Dubai tutoring-cost survey, and they are not IB Gram's price list.

Two things move the number more than anything else. The first is scarcity: MYP Spanish is a smaller pool than MYP Maths, and a tutor who genuinely knows Language Acquisition phase descriptors sits in the specialist band rather than the general-languages band. The second is travel. An in-home rate in Dubai is partly a mileage charge, and the further out the community, the more of the hour you are paying for the drive rather than the teaching.

A useful piece of context when you are weighing the monthly figure: KHDA confirmed in May 2026 that private school fees in Dubai would not rise for the 2026-27 academic year, under an economic incentives package the emirate valued at AED 1.5 billion. School costs are flat this year. Tutoring is the discretionary line, which makes it worth asking what a given rate buys in marked work rather than in contact minutes alone.

For IB Gram's own arrangement, the honest answer is that the first lesson is a free trial and the rate is quoted after it, because a Phase 5 student preparing a Spanish B HL route and a Phase 1 student six weeks into the language are different pieces of work. Ask for the rate in writing, ask whether marking between sessions is included, and ask what happens if the match is wrong. Those three answers tell you more than a headline figure.

sections.heading: Fitting a Spanish session into a Dubai school week, including Ramadan
paragraphs: The scheduling reality in Dubai is that a weekday session before 5pm is usually fiction. School buses from the Al Barsha and Nad Al Sheba clusters routinely deliver students home between 4 and 4.45pm, and a student who walks in at 4.30 is not ready to analyse an unseen Spanish text at 4.35. Our Dubai MYP sessions overwhelmingly sit between 5.30pm and 7.30pm Gulf Standard Time, with a second peak on Saturday mornings.

Ramadan changes the shape of the week rather than cancelling it. School days shorten, energy in the late afternoon drops, and families reorganise around iftar. Sessions that normally sit at 6pm move either earlier, into the newly free early afternoon, or later, after iftar, and in our experience the post-iftar slot works better for language work because the student is alert. Plan the shift a fortnight ahead rather than week by week, because the good slots go quickly.

The other fixed point in a Dubai MYP year is the internal assessment calendar. Schools stack Language Acquisition tasks into defined assessment weeks, and the weeks before them are when tutoring earns its keep. A parent who knows those dates in September can book an intensive block around them instead of discovering a Criterion C task three days out. Ask for the assessment calendar at the first parents' evening; most Dubai IB schools publish one.

Two smaller things save a lot of friction. Travel is common in this city, and a tutor working over live video can hold the slot while a family is in Spain, London or Kerala, which an in-home arrangement cannot. And a sixty-minute session that moves by a day costs nobody a commute, so rescheduling around a school trip or a sports fixture is a message rather than a negotiation.

process.title: Tell us the phase, or tell us you do not know
process.description: A short form: MYP year, school, which phase the report card names, and what the four criterion scores were last cycle. If you do not know the phase, say so. Roughly half of Dubai families who contact us about MYP Spanish do not, and the diagnostic exists for exactly that reason.

process.title: A free trial lesson spent on placement
process.description: Sixty minutes with a Spanish specialist, structured as four short tasks, one per criterion, including a recorded ninety-second interaction. You get a written note placing the evidence against the phase descriptors. No payment, and no obligation to continue if the tutor is not the right fit.

process.title: Agree the focus criterion and the cadence
process.description: Weekly, twice weekly for a fixed block, or a short diagnostic only. One criterion is named as the focus for the first month, because four at once moves none of them. The tutor asks for the school's unit plan and assessment calendar so sessions sit alongside the course rather than beside it.

process.title: Marked work between sessions, strand by strand
process.description: One piece of the student's own written or recorded work is marked each week against the named criterion, with strand-level comments in the same language the school report uses. It comes back before the next session. This is the evidence trail a parent reads instead of taking a progress report on trust.

process.title: Review at six weeks and change something
process.description: Six weeks in, we look at the first marked task and the most recent one together and decide one of three things: keep going on the same criterion, switch focus, or change tutor. Asking for a different tutor is a normal request and not a complaint. The alternative is a term of polite drift.

whyPoints.title: Marking in the school's own language
whyPoints.description: Feedback names the criterion and the strand, so it lines up with the Dubai MYP report card instead of running parallel to it. A parent can hold the tutor's comment and the teacher's comment side by side and see whether they agree, which is a more useful test of a tutor than any claim on a website.

whyPoints.title: Phase placement checked, not assumed
whyPoints.description: The trial lesson tests against the phase descriptors rather than accepting the set a student was put in during week one of term. Where the evidence suggests a mismatch, you get a written note you can take to the MYP coordinator. Where it confirms the placement, you have saved yourself a doubt.

whyPoints.title: A specialist, not the nearest Spanish speaker
whyPoints.description: Because lessons run online, the pool is Spanish teachers who know MYP Language Acquisition rather than Spanish speakers within a twenty-minute drive of your community. For a subject as thinly staffed as MYP Spanish in Dubai, that difference is the whole argument.

whyPoints.title: Clear limits on coursework
whyPoints.description: A tutor teaches, questions and gives feedback on work the student has produced. For the MYP Personal Project and for any assessed Spanish task, the student writes every word themselves. We say this plainly because parts of this market do not, and because an IB academic-honesty finding follows the student, not the tutor.

whyPoints.title: Scheduling that survives a Dubai year
whyPoints.description: Slots sit in the 5.30pm to 7.30pm window that a Dubai school run actually allows, shift for Ramadan, and hold through family travel. Rescheduling is a message, not a renegotiated commute, because nobody is driving anywhere.

whyPoints.title: Sourced figures, including the ones that are not ours
whyPoints.description: Every AED band on this page is attributed to whoever published it and dated to when it was read. Regulatory points are attributed to KHDA, u.ae or MoHRE. Where a fact could not be verified, including IB session dates, it is left off the page rather than guessed at.

faqs.question: What does an IB MYP Spanish tutor in Dubai actually mark?
faqs.answer: Four criteria, each out of eight. Criterion A is comprehending spoken and visual text, Criterion B is comprehending written and visual text, Criterion C is communicating in response to spoken, written and visual text, and Criterion D is using language in spoken and written form. Every assessed task in MYP Spanish is tagged to one or two of them, and the thirty-two marks convert to a one-to-seven grade using your school's own boundaries. A tutor who marks generally rather than by criterion cannot tell you which of the four is holding the grade down, which is the only diagnostic information that matters.

faqs.question: Which MYP Spanish phase is my child in, and who decides it?
faqs.answer: The school decides, usually in the first fortnight of term, often from one short written task and a conversation. Language Acquisition runs on six phases rather than year groups, so an MYP 4 student can legitimately sit in Phase 2 and an MYP 2 student in Phase 4. The weakness of the method is that it happens once and is rarely revisited. A four-task diagnostic, one per criterion, including a recorded interaction, gives you evidence against the published phase descriptors that you can take to the MYP coordinator as a basis for a conversation.

faqs.question: Is MYP Spanish assessed by an on-screen examination or by a portfolio?
faqs.answer: Where a Dubai school registers its MYP 5 students for IB MYP eAssessment, Language Acquisition is a portfolio subject, externally moderated against the same four criteria used all year. The two-hour on-screen examinations sit in Language and Literature, Individuals and Societies, Mathematics, Sciences and interdisciplinary learning. Many Dubai IB continuum schools do not register for eAssessment at all and move students straight from MYP 5 into the Diploma. Ask your MYP coordinator which route your school takes, because it changes what the final MYP year is building towards.

faqs.question: Why has my child's Criterion C score been stuck on five for a year?
faqs.answer: Almost always because they are answering the text rather than the prompt. Criterion C is a response task: it asks for an interpretation or an opinion, in a named text type, for a named audience. A student who writes an accurate paragraph summarising the source has produced good Spanish and a mid-band response. The fix takes about four sessions and starts with reading prompts without writing any Spanish, highlighting the command, the text type, the audience and the number of ideas required. Adding vocabulary to this problem produces a better-dressed wrong answer.

faqs.question: My child joined an IB school in Dubai from a British curriculum with no Spanish at all. What happens?
faqs.answer: They start at Phase 1 regardless of year group, which is the system working as intended rather than a setback. The realistic timeline is two terms of consistent work to be comfortable at Phase 2, and the limiting factor is usually listening stamina rather than grammar. Twenty minutes of Spanish audio a week moves Criterion A faster than any other single habit. If the Diploma plan involves Spanish, the honest route from Phase 1 is ab initio at SL, and that is worth settling in MYP 4 rather than discovering in MYP 5.

faqs.question: How many Spanish sessions a week does an MYP 4 student need?
faqs.answer: One a week is the normal starting point, with a named focus criterion for the first month and a piece of marked work returned between sessions. Two a week makes sense in a fixed block of four to six weeks around an internal assessment window or a portfolio deadline, and then stops. More than two a week for a single Language Acquisition course is rarely productive, because language gains come from frequent short exposure between lessons rather than from longer lessons. What the student does on the other six days matters more than the second session.

faqs.question: Can a tutor help with a Spanish-themed MYP Personal Project?
faqs.answer: A tutor can question the goal, help the student plan the process, discuss sources and read what the student has produced against the criteria. The student writes every word of the report and the process journal themselves. We state that boundary plainly because parts of this market do not, and because an academic-honesty finding under IB rules follows the student rather than the tutor. If a provider offers to produce the project or the report for you, that is the clearest signal available to walk away.

faqs.question: Does online tutoring really work for Spanish pronunciation and speaking?
faqs.answer: For speaking it has a specific advantage: a session over live video can record a ninety-second interaction, play it back, and mark it against the Criterion D strands while the student listens. Few in-home sessions do that, and almost no classroom does. Pronunciation work benefits from the replay more than from physical proximity. The honest limitation is that a poor connection ruins a listening task, so we ask Dubai families to use a wired or strong Wi-Fi connection and headphones rather than a laptop microphone across a room.

faqs.question: Where do MYP Spanish lessons actually take place for a Dubai family?
faqs.answer: No. IB Gram does not offer home visits in Dubai or anywhere else in the UAE; home visits are a service we run only in India. UAE lessons are one-to-one over live video, scheduled on Gulf Standard Time. For MYP Spanish specifically the trade is a good one: you get a tutor who knows Language Acquisition phase descriptors rather than whichever Spanish speaker can reach your community by 5pm, and the slot survives school trips, family travel and a changed bus time without anyone recalculating a drive.

faqs.question: What do Spanish tutors charge per hour in Dubai?
faqs.answer: Market rates read in October 2026 run roughly AED 45-150 for budget online tutors, AED 150-300 for a qualified subject tutor online, AED 180-500 for an in-home visit with travel included, and AED 200-450 or more for an IB specialist; one premium provider publishes AED 650. Those are other providers' published figures, not ours. MYP Spanish sits in the specialist band more often than general-languages tutoring does, because the pool of tutors who know the phase descriptors is small. IB Gram quotes after the free trial lesson.

faqs.question: Do Arabic and Islamic Education leave room for Spanish in a Dubai timetable?
faqs.answer: They tighten it. Arabic, Islamic Education and Social and Moral Studies are required in every Dubai private school whatever curriculum it is licensed for, and KHDA required its arrangements to be in place from the start of the 2025-26 academic year. Most MYP students therefore carry Arabic as an additional language alongside Spanish, with both marked on the same four Language Acquisition criteria. That overlap is useful: a Criterion C planning frame built in Spanish transfers directly to Arabic, so one set of sessions can move two grades.

faqs.question: How do Spanish sessions work during Ramadan in Dubai?
faqs.answer: School days shorten and the late afternoon becomes a poor time for language work, so sessions move either into the newly free early afternoon or to after iftar. In our experience post-iftar slots suit Language Acquisition better, because the student is alert and the household is settled. Book the shift about two weeks ahead rather than week by week; the good post-iftar slots fill fast across the Gulf. Because lessons are online, the change is a calendar edit rather than a renegotiated journey for anyone.

faqs.question: Will my child be taught by a tutor based in the UAE?
faqs.answer: Sometimes, and we tell you which before the trial. MYP Spanish is a thin pool in the UAE, so for some phases the right specialist is based elsewhere and teaches your child over live video on Gulf Standard Time. We would rather disclose that than conceal it behind a local number. Where we cannot staff a request well, we say so instead of assigning a general Spanish speaker to a criterion-referenced course, and you are told before any payment rather than after a disappointing first month.

faqs.question: What do I get in writing after the first six weeks?
faqs.answer: Six marked pieces of your child's own work, each tagged to the criterion that was the focus, with strand-level comments in the same vocabulary your school's report card uses. Plus the baseline recording from the trial lesson and a later one for comparison. At the six-week review we decide one of three things together: continue on the same criterion, switch focus, or change tutor. Asking for a different tutor is a normal request. Progress you can read beats a reassurance you cannot check.

faqs.question: Does a Spanish tutor teaching a Dubai MYP student need a MoHRE permit?
faqs.answer: Yes. Private tuition in the UAE is covered by a MoHRE private tutor work permit introduced under Ministerial Resolution No. 710 of 2023, and u.ae states that individuals offering private tutoring without a permit from MoHRE are subject to fines and penalties under the applicable laws. The permit is granted free of charge for two years, and eligible applicants include registered school teachers, government and private-sector employees, unemployed residents, university students and school students aged 15 to 18. Apply through MoHRE's own private tutor licensing service, which lists a two-working-day completion time.

dubai/ib-myp-spanish-tutor.closingHeading: Start with a diagnostic, not a subscription
dubai/ib-myp-spanish-tutor.closingBody: If your child's MYP Spanish grade has been flat for three reporting cycles, the useful first step is not more lessons. It is finding out which of the four criteria is holding the grade down and whether the phase placement fits the evidence. That is what the free trial lesson does: four short tasks, one per criterion, a recorded interaction, and a written note you can take to the MYP coordinator. If weekly sessions follow, they start with one named criterion and marked work you can read. If they do not, you still have the note. Tell us the MYP year, the school and last cycle's four scores, and we will match a Spanish specialist for the trial.

intro.heading: Standard does not mean lower, and it does not mean easier
paragraphs: The single most common misunderstanding we meet from Dubai families is that a standard-route placement caps what a child can achieve. It does not. Standard and extended are two routes through the same Middle Years mathematics framework. Both are assessed against the same four criteria, each marked from 0 to 8, and both convert to a subject grade on the same scale. A standard-route student can be awarded a 7. What differs is the additional content the extended route carries and the pace at which it is delivered.

What standard does mean is that the time extended spends on extra algebra and trigonometry is spent instead on consolidation. For most students that is the better arrangement, because the four branches of the framework are revisited every year and a topic half-secured in Year 8 becomes a liability in Year 10. The students who struggle on the standard route are not the ones who find mathematics hard; they are the ones whose earlier fluency gaps were never closed, because the standard course assumes them just as firmly as the extended one does.

The second misunderstanding is about where the standard route leads. It is the natural feed into Applications and Interpretation at Diploma level, which is a serious course involving modelling, statistics and technology rather than a soft option. It does not automatically close off Analysis and Approaches, but taking higher-level Analysis and Approaches from a standard-route Middle Years background requires a bridging plan and the honest time to execute it, usually over the summer before the Diploma begins. That decision is cheap to act on in Year 10 and expensive in Year 12.

Now the search phrase. Families type home tutor because that is the ordinary way to describe one-to-one help. The honest answer is that IB Gram does not arrange home visits in Dubai; home tutoring is a service we offer only in India. Visiting tutors in this city publish hourly rates of roughly AED 180 to AED 350 according to the Bestimate rate survey, with individual listings to AED 500, and a real share of that figure is driving rather than teaching. We deliver the same one-to-one work over live video, and the reason is the tutor pool rather than the price.

That matters more on the standard route than people expect. A standard-route student's marks usually hinge on two things: whether the unfamiliar-context question at the end of each task is attempted, and whether a pattern is pushed as far as a general rule. Recognising those two habits from a glance at marked work is a skill built by seeing hundreds of standard-route tasks, and the person who has done that is not necessarily the person who can reach Jumeirah Golf Estates by five o'clock on a Tuesday.

So the page that follows is about the mathematics. The standard course branch by branch. Criterion A and the question students skip. Pattern work at standard depth, where difference tables do most of the heavy lifting. Proportional reasoning, which quietly underpins half the course. The end-of-programme on-screen examination. The Diploma bridge. Then the practical matter of how a session is spent, minute by minute, and what we will not claim.

dubai/ib-myp-standard-mathematics-home-t.programmesIntro: Three courses matter to a standard-route family: the Middle Years course itself, the Diploma mathematics it leads into, and the International GCSE alternative some Dubai schools switch to at Year 10. Here is how each treats the same mathematics.

programmes.name: Middle Years Programme, standard mathematics
programmes.description: The standard framework covers number, algebra, geometry and trigonometry, and statistics and probability across five years, with assessment against knowing and understanding, investigating patterns, communicating, and applying mathematics in real-life contexts. Tasks are untimed, redraftable in some schools, and marked against descriptors the school adapts for each piece of work. Depth rather than breadth separates it from extended: the branches are the same, the ceiling within each is lower, and the consolidation time is greater.
programmes.countryNote: Dubai schools place students into routes at different points, commonly at the end of Year 9 and occasionally mid-Year 10, and the placement is usually decided on criterion A evidence from class tests. Ask your child's department when the decision is made, what evidence it uses, and whether movement between routes is possible later, because the answer varies by school rather than by programme rule.

programmes.name: Diploma Applications and Interpretation
programmes.description: The Diploma course the standard route feeds most naturally. It extends modelling, statistics, probability and technology use, and it expects fluency with the proportional reasoning and data handling the standard Middle Years course builds. The internal assessment is a single mathematical exploration written by the student. Students arriving from a secure standard route generally find the transition manageable; those arriving with unresolved fluency gaps find the exploration difficult, because it requires choosing and defending a method unaided.
programmes.countryNote: UAE and overseas universities publish mathematics requirements per course, and some engineering and economics programmes specify Analysis and Approaches or a particular level. Read the requirements for two target courses while your child is in Year 10, because that is when a bridging plan from the standard route is still inexpensive to build.

programmes.name: Diploma Analysis and Approaches
programmes.description: The algebra, proof and pattern-heavy Diploma route. Reachable from the standard Middle Years course with preparation, not by default. The gap is concentrated in algebraic manipulation, function work and formal reasoning, which the extended route has already rehearsed. A student who completes the standard route with high criterion B marks and strong algebra is a reasonable candidate; one whose strength sits in computation and modelling will find higher level hard going without a bridge.
programmes.countryNote: The bridging work is a defined list rather than a vague ambition: algebraic fractions, function notation and transformations, harder factorisation, trigonometric identities and formal generalisation. Taught deliberately, it is a summer's work of perhaps fifteen to twenty sessions. Discovered in the first term of Year 12, it becomes a crisis that competes with five other subjects.

programmes.name: International GCSE mathematics
programmes.description: Where a Dubai school leaves the programme at Year 10, mathematics becomes a timed terminal examination with a tiered entry, and the standard-route student's profile changes meaning. Untimed criterion tasks have trained thinking time; a terminal paper rewards recognition and pace. The content overlap is substantial, so the retraining is about question triage, marks per minute and knowing when to abandon a question, rather than about new mathematics.
programmes.countryNote: Cambridge examines International GCSE in June and November series and allocates every centre to one of six administrative zones, warning that the correct zone timetable must be used. Pearson examines in May or June and November. For the March 2027 Cambridge series, final entries were due 27 November 2026 against an exam period of 3 February to 4 March 2027, which shows how far ahead entry decisions sit.

dubai/ib-myp-standard-mathematics-home-t.subjectsIntro: A standard-route request works best when it names the topic. These are the areas Dubai families bring most often, described by what the standard course expects and where the marks go.

subjects.name: Proportional reasoning
subjects.description: Ratio, direct and inverse proportion, scale, percentage change, unit conversion and compound measures. The quiet spine of the standard course: weak proportional reasoning shows up later as failure in trigonometry, similar shapes, grouped data and modelling tasks. When a student is losing marks across apparently unrelated topics, this is the first thing we test.

subjects.name: Linear sequences and the nth term
subjects.description: Difference tables, generalising to an expression in n, and reversing the process from rule to terms. The standard course's main vehicle for criterion B, and the step where most standard-route students stall. Fluency here is the difference between a middle-band investigation mark and an upper-band one, and it is drilled rather than discussed.

subjects.name: Quadratic patterns and second differences
subjects.description: Recognising a constant second difference, building a quadratic rule, and verifying it beyond the given cases. Standard tasks often present these in geometric contexts such as growing shapes, which is also where the justification mark lives: explaining why each new layer adds what it adds.

subjects.name: Right-angled trigonometry
subjects.description: Pythagoras and the three ratios in two and simple three-dimensional contexts. Losses cluster in identifying the correct side relative to the angle and in leaving answers unrounded or wrongly rounded for the context. The standard course rarely asks for non-right-angled work, which is one of the clearest route differences.

subjects.name: Circle properties and angle reasoning
subjects.description: Angle facts, parallel lines, polygons and the circle theorems the standard course includes. The characteristic standard-route loss is a correct numerical answer with no property named, which costs communication marks the student had the knowledge to earn. Every step naming its reason is the habit being built.

subjects.name: Grouped data, averages and spread
subjects.description: Frequency tables, estimated means, cumulative frequency, quartiles and comparison of distributions. This branch carries most standard-route modelling tasks, and the recurring gap is a competent calculation followed by a comparison that never mentions spread or the limitations of the sample.

subjects.name: Probability and tree diagrams
subjects.description: Single and combined events, tree diagrams, relative frequency and simple conditional reasoning. Errors are usually structural rather than arithmetic: branches drawn without replacement considered, or probabilities read off a tree without multiplying along the path. Drawing the structure before computing is the fix.

subjects.name: Straight-line graphs and simple functions
subjects.description: Gradient, intercept, the equation of a line, interpreting a graph in context and reading values from it. Standard tasks frequently ask what the gradient means in the situation, which is a criterion D question wearing a graph. Students who answer with a number rather than a rate lose the mark.

subjects.name: Perimeter, area, surface area and volume
subjects.description: Compound shapes, circles, prisms, cylinders and conversions between units of area and volume. The standard course returns here every year and the error is almost always the unit conversion rather than the formula, particularly between square and cubic measures, which is why we check it as a fluency item rather than a topic.

subjects.name: Unfamiliar-context questions
subjects.levels: The final part of most standard tasks
subjects.description: Criterion A at the upper bands asks for the procedure applied in an unfamiliar situation, and standard-route students routinely leave that part blank. It is a confidence habit rather than a knowledge gap: the mathematics required is the same, dressed differently. Three sessions of deliberate attempts at unfamiliar framing change the pattern.

sections.heading: Standard against extended: the comparison a Dubai report does not give you
paragraphs: Schools communicate route placement in a line of text and leave families to work out the consequences. The consequences are specific and they are worth setting out properly, because they drive both the tutoring plan and a Diploma decision two years later. Both routes sit inside one framework and share the four criteria, the 0 to 8 scales and the subject grade range. Neither route is reported differently to a university. The report says 5 or 6 or 7 with no annotation of which course produced it.

The real differences are three. Content: the extended route carries additional algebra, function work and trigonometry aimed at higher-level Diploma mathematics. Pace: extended sets meet topics once and move on, while standard sets return to them. Expectation at the upper bands: an extended task's unfamiliar-context question is harder than a standard one's, which matters for criterion A at the top of the scale.

Those differences cut both ways. A student placed in extended on the strength of fast, accurate computation can be exposed on criterion B, where harder content produces harder patterns to justify, and can end up with a lower subject grade than they would have earned on the standard route. A student placed on the standard route who intends to study higher-level Analysis and Approaches has a real gap to bridge, and the bridge is a defined list of topics rather than a vague extra effort.

Use it in a conversation with your child's department rather than instead of one: schools differ on when placement happens, what evidence it uses and whether movement is possible later, and those three answers are specific to your school.

sections.heading: The four branches at standard depth, and what each task asks
paragraphs: The standard course covers number, algebra, geometry and trigonometry, and statistics and probability, every year, at rising depth. What changes between Year 7 and Year 11 is not the list but the demand inside each item, and that is why a parent asking what is my child studying gets a less useful answer than one asking what does my child never secure. The branches lean on each other: proportional reasoning underpins trigonometry and similar shapes, and algebraic fluency underpins every pattern task.

Each branch also has a characteristic task type and a characteristic loss. Number work appears inside contexts, so the loss is interpretation. Algebra appears inside pattern tasks, so the loss is generalisation. Geometry appears in reasoning chains, so the loss is the unnamed property. Statistics appears inside modelling, so the loss is the evaluation. That mapping is stable enough across marked Dubai standard-route tasks that we use it to diagnose before meeting the student.

What the standard course does not do is go beyond right-angled trigonometry, heavy algebraic manipulation or formal function work. Families sometimes arrive worried that a standard-route child is missing content needed for the Diploma, and for Applications and Interpretation that worry is misplaced: the standard course is built to feed it. The worry becomes real only when a higher-level Analysis and Approaches ambition enters the picture.

The table below sets out the four branches at standard depth with the task type each generates and the loss to look for in marked work. Read the final column first if you have a report in front of you, because the pattern in the teacher's comments usually matches one row rather than all four.

sections.heading: The question standard-route students leave blank
paragraphs: Open any marked standard-route task and look at the final part. In a large share of the work we read, it is blank or abandoned halfway. That final part is usually where criterion A reaches its upper bands, because the descriptor asks for the procedure applied in an unfamiliar situation rather than a repeat of the practised one. The mathematics needed is almost always content the student already holds. What is missing is the willingness to begin without recognising the question type.

This is a teachable habit and it responds quickly. The method is to spend part of every session on deliberately unfamiliar framing of familiar mathematics: the same proportional reasoning inside a tariff, a recipe, a map scale and a currency conversion; the same Pythagoras inside a ladder, a screen diagonal, a shipping crate. Students who have met four dressings of one idea stop looking for the recognisable version and start looking for the structure.

The second move is explicit permission to start badly. Standard-route students frequently have a history of being right, and an unfamiliar question threatens that. Writing down what is known, labelling a diagram, and attempting a plausible first step earns marks even when the attempt is incomplete, while a blank space earns nothing. Saying that aloud, once, with the parent present, changes behaviour more often than any amount of content revision.

There is a diagnostic benefit too. A student who attempts the final part and goes wrong tells you exactly where the understanding stops, which is information. A student who leaves it blank tells you nothing, and the next few sessions are spent guessing. Families who ask their child to attempt every final part for a fortnight, however badly, usually arrive at a first session with a far better brief than one built on a placement test.

sections.heading: Pattern work at standard depth: difference tables do the heavy lifting
paragraphs: Criterion B on the standard route is built almost entirely on sequences, and the practical skill is the difference table. A student who can take a sequence, build first differences, recognise a constant difference and convert it into an expression in n has the core of the criterion. Add second differences and a constant second difference for quadratic patterns and the standard course's pattern work is largely covered. These are mechanical skills, and the market's reluctance to drill them is one reason so many standard-route students sit mid-band on this criterion.

The two directions matter equally. Given terms, produce the rule. Given the rule, produce the terms and check. Students who have only practised the first direction cannot verify their own work, which is exactly what the descriptor asks for at the next band: testing the rule on cases beyond those given. Verification is cheap once the reverse direction is fluent and almost impossible when it is not.

Justification is the band above and the one most often skipped. At Middle Years level it does not require formal proof; it requires a reason tied to the structure of the problem. If the pattern counts the perimeter of a growing arrangement of tiles, the justification explains why each additional tile adds two to the perimeter rather than four. Dubai schools frequently set these in geometric contexts precisely because the structure is visible, which makes them the easiest justifications to learn on.

A short block does this work well: three or four sessions on difference tables in both directions, two on verification and justification with the student writing, and a fifth against a real task if one is due. After that, the skill carries. It is also the single piece of standard-route coaching most likely to move a subject grade, because criterion B has the widest mark range in the subject and the lowest typical starting point.

sections.heading: Proportional reasoning: the fluency everything else leans on
paragraphs: When a standard-route student is losing marks in apparently unrelated topics, the first thing to test is proportional reasoning. Ratio, direct and inverse proportion, scale, percentage change and unit conversion are not a topic in the standard course so much as a load-bearing wall. Similar shapes depend on it. Trigonometric ratios depend on it. Grouped-data estimation depends on it. Compound measures are it. A student with shaky proportional reasoning appears to have five weaknesses and has one.

The giveaway in marked work is inconsistency: a correct percentage increase followed by an incorrect reverse percentage; a correct scale drawing followed by an area scaled linearly instead of by the square of the factor; a correct speed calculation with the units mismatched. Teachers often mark these as careless. They are not careless; they are a single underlying model that has never been secured, and no amount of care fixes a missing model.

The fix is a short intensive rather than a year of weekly sessions, and it is one of the few places where drilling is the right answer. Four to six sessions on multiplicative reasoning across contexts, with the student writing the reasoning rather than the answer, generally closes it. The test afterwards is a cold re-attempt of a topic set from two years earlier, which is why we ask for old marked work as well as recent work at the start.

This is also where the standard route differs most usefully from the extended one. Standard sets have the consolidation time to secure proportional reasoning properly if the gap is identified; extended sets rarely do, because the scheme of work is moving. A Dubai family whose child was placed on the standard route and who uses that consolidation time deliberately is in a better position at the end of Year 11 than one whose child was pushed up and never caught up.

Five apparent weaknesses are often this one gap

Four to six sessions, then a cold re-test of an older topic set

sections.heading: The end of MYP 5: on-screen mathematics for standard candidates
paragraphs: Some Dubai schools enter MYP 5 students for the end-of-programme on-screen mathematics examination and some close the programme with internal assessment alone, so the first question is for your school's programme coordinator rather than for a tutoring site. Where a standard-route student is entered, the examination is set at the level appropriate to the route, and the content is not the difficulty. The clock is.

Five years of untimed, often redraftable tasks build habits that work against a fixed-duration paper. Students over-plan the first question, write prose where a line of working would do, and leave the final part unattempted for the same reason they leave it blank on coursework. Preparation therefore rehearses conditions: a real clock, the stimulus read on screen, planning kept to a minute or two on paper, and deliberate practice at attempting rather than perfecting.

There is a typing dimension as well. Mathematical notation entered through an equation tool is slower than handwriting for everyone, and for a student meeting the tool for the first time in the room it is much slower. Where the school uses a particular interface, practising in it is worth more than another hour of content revision. Standard-route students are rarely short of mathematics by this point; they are short of fluency in producing it under the conditions the assessment imposes.

On dates, this project publishes no specific International Baccalaureate session or results date, because none could be confirmed from the organisation's own site during research. Treat the May session as the one Dubai schools sit and get your windows from the school's coordinator or the board's own published pages. Cambridge and Pearson dates can be read from their own sites, and for the Cambridge March 2027 series final entries were due on 27 November 2026, which is a useful illustration of how early entry decisions are made.

sections.heading: Home visits, online lessons and what the difference buys a standard-route student
paragraphs: To be plain about the search phrase: IB Gram does not arrange home visits in Dubai, and home tutoring is a service we offer only in India. The published market figures for a visiting tutor in this city are AED 180 to AED 350 an hour from the Bestimate rate survey, with individual listings to AED 500 and in-home monthly packages advertised at AED 1,599 to AED 1,799 for four two-hour sessions. Those belong to the providers and surveys that published them, read in October 2026.

The case for video on a standard-route brief is not that it is cheaper, although removing the drive does remove a cost. It is that the two things which move standard-route marks, pushing a pattern to a justified rule and attempting the unfamiliar final question, are recognised instantly by someone who has read hundreds of these tasks and only slowly by a generalist. Restricting the search to tutors who can reach your community inside the evening window selects for geography over that recognition.

Online delivery also fits the specific mechanics of this work. The student writes on a shared whiteboard while the tutor annotates in a second colour, so a difference table can be corrected line by line as it is built. The session is recorded, which matters for a route whose recurring job is retrieval: a student can redo the same task mid-week without a second live session. Paper in a living room produces none of that, and the parent sees the outcome rather than the process.

What stays the same either way is the boundary on assessed work and the honesty about availability. A tutor teaches, questions, annotates and coaches process; the student writes every assessed word. Where no suitable specialist is free in the slot a family needs, we say so and offer a different time, a different profile or a wait, rather than filling it with whoever is available and letting the mismatch surface at the next reporting point.

sections.heading: What a standard-route session actually contains, minute by minute
paragraphs: Families almost never get told how an hour is spent, so here is the shape we use for standard-route work. The first five to eight minutes are retrieval on an older topic, chosen from the file rather than at random: a reverse percentage, a unit conversion, one nth-term question. This is the mechanism that stops the yearly revisiting of the four branches from producing new gaps, and it is the part most tutors drop when time is short. It should be the last thing dropped.

The next twenty-five minutes or so work the current unit or the current task with the student writing. Not the tutor demonstrating: the student writing, on the shared whiteboard, with the tutor annotating. This is slower and it is the only arrangement that reveals where the reasoning actually breaks. A tutor who writes the solution while the student watches produces a session that felt productive and a marked task that looks the same as last term's.

Then ten to fifteen minutes on the weakest criterion specifically. On the standard route that is usually either pushing a pattern through to a justified rule, or writing an evaluation paragraph on a completed modelling task, or naming the property at each step of a geometry chain. One of those three, chosen in advance, not improvised. The final five minutes set the next task requirement in writing: what the next piece of marked work has to show.

That structure also makes the session auditable. A parent reading the session note can see what was retrieved, what was worked, which criterion was targeted and what the next marked task should demonstrate. Over a term the notes form a record you can take to a parent-teacher meeting, which is more useful than a general impression that maths is going better, and more honest than a prediction nobody can stand behind.

sections.heading: The boundary on assessed work, and the claims we will not make
paragraphs: A standard-route investigation or modelling task carries assessment weight, so the boundary is stated at the start and in front of the student. A tutor may teach content, explain a descriptor, ask the questions a marker would ask, annotate completed work and coach the process of investigating or modelling. A tutor may not supply the conjecture, the general rule, the justification or any sentence that ends up in a submission. Every assessed word is the student's own.

That boundary is a genuine differentiator in this market rather than a formality. The competitor set for these searches includes operators selling finished internal assessments at published prices, which exposes a student to a malpractice finding far worse than a middling mark. If a provider offers to produce assessed work, end the conversation. Where a school asks for a declaration of assistance, declare the tutoring plainly, because declared teaching is ordinary and undeclared authorship is not.

We also do not host board material. Syllabus documents, past papers, mark schemes and subject guides belong to the International Baccalaureate, Cambridge and Pearson, and we link to their own pages rather than distributing copies. Practice material is written for the session or drawn from your child's own school resources, which has the advantage of matching the task-specific wording the student is marked against.

Finally, the claims we avoid. IB Gram holds no approval, accreditation, licence or partnership from any regulator, examination board, school or school group, and occupies no UAE office. We promise no grade and publish no statistic about our own students without the sample size, date and method attached. Private tutors in the UAE need a private tuition work permit from the Ministry of Human Resources and Emiratisation under Ministerial Resolution No. 710 of 2023, granted free of charge for two years; those without one are subject to fines and penalties under the applicable laws, and no fine schedule has been published.

faqs.question: Does being on the standard route cap the grade my child can get?
faqs.answer: No. Both routes are assessed against the same four criteria, each marked from 0 to 8, and both convert to a subject grade on the same 1 to 7 scale. A standard-route student can be awarded a 7, and the report carries no annotation telling a university which route produced it. What differs is the additional content the extended route covers and the pace it moves at. The practical consequence is about Diploma route choice rather than the Middle Years grade: higher-level Analysis and Approaches from a standard background needs a bridging plan built deliberately.

faqs.question: My child was put on the standard route and is still getting 4s. Why?
faqs.answer: Usually because the standard course assumes the same earlier fluencies as the extended one. The commonest culprit is proportional reasoning: ratio, reverse percentages, scale factors and unit conversion as a single model rather than four topics. A student missing that model shows what looks like five separate weaknesses, and teachers often mark them as carelessness. The second commonest is pattern work stopping at description. Both are diagnosable from marked tasks in minutes, and both respond to a four to six session intensive rather than a year of general weekly teaching.

faqs.question: What exactly is a difference table and why does it matter so much?
faqs.answer: It is the standard route's main tool for criterion B. Write the sequence, write the gaps between consecutive terms, and look at what those gaps do. A constant first difference means a linear rule; a constant second difference means a quadratic one. From there the student builds an expression in n. The skill has to run in both directions, because the next band up asks for the rule to be verified on cases beyond those given, and verification is only possible if the student can generate terms from a rule. Three or four sessions usually makes it fluent.

faqs.question: Why does my daughter leave the last part of every maths task blank?
faqs.answer: Because the last part is normally where criterion A reaches its upper bands by asking for a familiar procedure in an unfamiliar situation, and students with a history of being right would rather write nothing than write something wrong. The mathematics required is usually content she already holds. Two things change it: meeting the same idea in four different dressings until she looks for structure rather than recognition, and explicit permission to start badly. A wrong attempt earns marks and shows where understanding stops; a blank space earns nothing and hides the diagnosis.

faqs.question: Does the standard route close off engineering or medicine at university?
faqs.answer: Not by itself, but check rather than assume. Universities publish mathematics requirements per course, and some engineering and economics programmes specify Analysis and Approaches or a particular level, while many accept Applications and Interpretation. The practical move is to read the requirements for two target courses while your child is in Year 10, when a bridging plan is still cheap to build. Tutoring is not required for university admission and anyone implying otherwise is selling urgency. What is required is the right subject choice, made with the published requirement in front of you.

faqs.question: How long does a bridge from standard route to higher-level Analysis and Approaches take?
faqs.answer: It is a defined list rather than an open-ended effort, which is what makes it manageable. The gap sits in algebraic fractions, function notation and transformations, harder factorisation, trigonometric identities and formal generalisation. Taught deliberately, that is roughly fifteen to twenty sessions, which fits into a summer between MYP 5 and the Diploma if it is planned in Year 10 or early Year 11. Discovered in the first term of Year 12, the same work has to compete with five other Diploma subjects and the extended essay, which is why the timing matters more than the content.

faqs.question: Can a student move from the standard route to extended mid-programme?
faqs.answer: That depends on your school rather than on a programme rule, and it is worth asking the department three specific questions: when placement decisions are made, what evidence they use, and whether upward movement has happened in practice. Most Dubai schools decide at the end of a year on class-test evidence, which is largely criterion A. Downward movement tends to be easier than upward. If the aim is to move up, the useful preparation is strong criterion B work rather than more computation practice, because investigation marks are what distinguish a student who will cope with extended pace.

faqs.question: Which topics should a Year 10 standard-route student secure first?
faqs.answer: Proportional reasoning, nth-term work and unit conversion, in that order, before anything in the current unit. All three are load-bearing: trigonometric ratios, similar shapes and grouped-data estimation all lean on proportional reasoning, criterion B leans on nth-term fluency, and area and volume questions fail on square and cubic conversions rather than on formulas. Securing them takes four to six sessions and makes the rest of Year 10 cheaper. Working the current unit while those three remain shaky produces sessions that feel productive and marked tasks that do not change.

faqs.question: What does a good evaluation paragraph look like on a standard modelling task?
faqs.answer: Three short moves. Name the model chosen and why it suited the situation. State what the result means in the context, as a rate or a quantity with units rather than a bare number. Then say what limits the conclusion: an assumption made, a sample that was small or unrepresentative, or a simplification in the model. Two or three sentences is enough. The most common omission on Dubai standard-route tasks is this paragraph missing altogether, with the work stopping at the computation, and writing evaluations on already-completed tasks for two sessions usually makes it automatic.

faqs.question: Is a visiting tutor better for a child who will not concentrate on a screen?
faqs.answer: It is a fair argument and worth weighing honestly, particularly for younger students. IB Gram does not arrange home visits in Dubai; that service runs only in India, and published visiting rates here are AED 180 to AED 350 with listings to AED 500. What we would say for video on a standard-route brief is that the student writes on a shared whiteboard while the tutor annotates, so attention is visible rather than assumed, and the session is recorded for a mid-week repeat. For an eleven-year-old, two 45-minute sessions usually beat one long one in either format.

faqs.question: How should the recording of a session be used during the week?
faqs.answer: For a repeat, not a rewatch. Passive review of a recording achieves very little. What works on the standard route is redoing the same task from a blank page two or three days later, using the recording only when stuck, then comparing. That converts one live session into two pieces of practice and feeds the retrieval slot at the start of the next session. Families in communities with late school runs, where a second weekly session is not realistic, get most of the value here, and it costs nothing beyond the student's own twenty minutes.

faqs.question: Will my child sit an on-screen maths examination at the end of Year 11?
faqs.answer: Ask your school's programme coordinator, because it is a school decision rather than an automatic one. Some Dubai schools enter MYP 5 candidates for the end-of-programme on-screen examination and others close the programme with internal assessment. Where a standard-route student is entered, the paper is set at the route's level and the difficulty is the clock rather than the content: five years of untimed tasks do not train pace. Preparation rehearses conditions and the equation tool, which is slower than handwriting for everybody and much slower on first acquaintance.

faqs.question: Do you teach the UAE mandatory subjects alongside standard maths?
faqs.answer: They are a separate stream and worth understanding when you plan the week. Arabic, Islamic Education and Social or Moral Studies are mandatory in every Dubai private school whatever the licensed curriculum, with the Knowledge and Human Development Authority requiring separate classes for Arab and non-Arab students in several of them and instructional time calculated against a 40-minute lesson unit. That stream generates homework, which is why a single reliable maths slot outperforms two optimistic ones. For the mandatory subjects, schools may not use different or additional content without Ministry of Education permission.

faqs.question: What should I ask a prospective standard-route maths tutor in the first call?
faqs.answer: Four questions. Which criterion do you think is holding the grade down, and what in the marked work tells you that? What will the student be doing for most of the hour, writing or watching? What should appear on the next school-marked task if this is working? And do you hold the Ministry of Human Resources and Emiratisation private tuition permit, which is free and valid for two years? A tutor who answers the first three specifically is working from evidence. One who answers only in reassurance is working from a script.

faqs.question: Is it worth starting in Year 7 or should we wait until the route is decided?
faqs.answer: Year 7 is worth a short intervention rather than a standing commitment. The useful work at that age is the format shift and basic fluency: learning that reasoning carries marks, that variables get defined, and that fractions and negative numbers need to be automatic rather than calculator-dependent. Three or four sessions does it for many students. A weekly slot from Year 7 to Year 11 is rarely good value on the standard route, because spending should be lumpy: light early, heavier in the set-decision year, heavier again in the final year.

Lessons run online, one-to-one, over live video on Gulf Standard Time, with the student holding the pen.

dubai/ib-myp-standard-mathematics-tutor.tutorsIntro: The tutors listed here teach the standard route through the Middle Years mathematics framework: the full four branches at the depth the standard course requires, aimed at security rather than extension. Each quotes against a named target before the first paid session.

intro.heading: The number first, then the arithmetic behind it
paragraphs: Three of the six highest-ranking pages for tutoring searches in this market publish no price at all, and the two that do quote in US dollars, a currency no Dubai family pays in. So this page starts with dirhams. Rate surveys and provider pages read in October 2026 put budget online tutoring at AED 33 to AED 65 an hour, qualified subject tutors online at AED 150 to AED 300, in-home one-to-one visits at AED 180 to AED 350 with individual listings reaching AED 500, and specialist International Baccalaureate or Cambridge tutors at AED 200 to AED 450 and above. One named provider publishes AED 650. Monthly packages advertised in this market include AED 799 for eight online sessions and AED 1,599 to AED 1,799 for four two-hour in-home sessions.

Those are market rates and they belong to the providers and surveys that published them, not to us. IB Gram does not publish a price list on these pages, because a number quoted next to sourced competitor figures invites a comparison that is not like for like: our model is a free trial lesson, then a quote for a named target against a named tutor. What this page can do honestly is show you which band a standard-route Middle Years maths request falls into and what makes the quote move inside it.

The second half of the question is the one nobody answers: how many hours. A rate is useless without a quantity, and a provider happy to tell you AED 220 an hour and unwilling to estimate the number of sessions is selling you an open-ended commitment. For standard-route Middle Years mathematics the realistic answers are narrow. A habit fix on notation is three or four sessions. An investigation or modelling block is three to five against a deadline. An inherited gap in fractions or proportional reasoning is four to six. A full year of weekly consolidation in MYP 4 or 5 is twenty-eight to thirty-two sessions once assessment weeks and travel are deducted.

The standard route itself is widely misunderstood as the cheaper problem. It is not. Standard covers the same four branches of the framework as extended, to the depth the standard course specifies, and it is the route into Applications and Interpretation at Diploma level, which is a serious mathematics course. What differs is pace and the additional content extended carries. Where standard-route students are quoted less, it is usually because the tutor pool is wider, not because the teaching is easier.

Dubai gives this conversation an unusual backdrop. The Knowledge and Human Development Authority confirmed in May 2026 that private school fees in the emirate would not rise for the 2026-27 academic year, under a Dubai economic incentives package valued at AED 1.5 billion within a AED 2.5 billion total. In a city with 227 private schools and 387,441 private school pupils in 2024-25, a frozen fee line changes where the discretionary education budget goes, and tutoring is the usual beneficiary. That is worth knowing before a provider tells you demand has pushed rates up.

The rest of this page is the arithmetic: the rate bands and what each buys, the five variables that move a quote in this emirate, the yearly totals for three plan shapes, what the standard route actually covers, where families here waste money, and what to put in writing before paying anyone. Lessons themselves are online, one-to-one, over live video; IB Gram does not arrange home visits in Dubai, and home tutoring is a service we offer only in India.

dubai/ib-myp-standard-mathematics-tutor.programmesIntro: What a family pays across the school years depends on which stage the support sits in, because the hours each stage needs differ sharply. Here is the sequence a Dubai standard-route student travels, costed in hours rather than promises.

programmes.name: Primary Years Programme
programmes.description: Tutoring demand in the primary years is low and should be. Primary mathematics is reported in commentary rather than criterion marks, and most apparent gaps at this stage close without paid help. Where support is genuinely useful it is short and specific: a handful of sessions on fractions, negative numbers or multiplicative reasoning, which are the three fluencies Year 7 assumes from day one and the three most likely to resurface expensively in Year 9.
programmes.countryNote: Dubai families often buy primary tutoring as insurance ahead of a competitive secondary admission, which is a different purchase from fixing a gap. If the aim is an entrance assessment, ask the target school what it tests and for how long, because a general weekly slot across Year 5 is an expensive way to prepare for a 45-minute paper.

programmes.name: Middle Years Programme, standard route
programmes.description: Five years, four branches, four criteria marked 0 to 8 each. Spending is lumpy rather than even: Years 7 and 8 need occasional habit work, Year 9 is the year most families start because set decisions are made on it, and Years 10 and 11 carry the heaviest load because the standard route consolidates everything and the Diploma choice follows. A family that buys evenly across five years overspends; one that buys at Year 9 and Year 11 usually does not.
programmes.countryNote: In Dubai the decision to stay in the programme at Year 10 rather than move to International GCSE also changes the bill. Criterion coaching is bought in blocks against task deadlines; examination technique is bought in a sustained run of timed practice. Ask the school which route Year 10 takes before committing to a two-year plan.

programmes.name: Diploma Programme mathematics
programmes.description: The standard route through Middle Years mathematics leads naturally to Applications and Interpretation, at standard or higher level. Diploma tutoring is the most expensive stage in the whole continuum because the specialist pool is thinner and the exploration carries assessment weight, which is why the cheapest thing a Year 10 family can do is close the standard-route gaps now rather than pay Diploma rates to close them later.
programmes.countryNote: Published specialist bands in Dubai sit at AED 200 to AED 450 and above for International Baccalaureate work, with one provider at AED 650, so a Diploma year of weekly support is a materially larger commitment than a Middle Years one. Course requirements for UAE and overseas universities are published per programme; read two target courses before the route is fixed.

programmes.name: International GCSE, the Year 10 alternative
programmes.description: Where a Dubai school switches at Year 10, mathematics becomes a timed terminal examination and the tutoring economics change. Published rates for International GCSE support start lower than Diploma work, with one agency publishing from AED 150, and the hours needed are more predictable because past-paper practice is measurable. The cost risk here is buying teaching when the student needs timing practice.
programmes.countryNote: Cambridge runs International GCSE in June and November series with six administrative timetable zones, and Pearson in May or June and November. Private candidate entry carries its own fee paid to the centre, which belongs in the family budget and is not something a tutoring provider charges or controls.

dubai/ib-myp-standard-mathematics-tutor.subjectsIntro: Quotes move with what is being bought, so it helps to name the piece of work. These are the standard-route Middle Years mathematics requests we price most often in Dubai, and what each usually takes.

subjects.name: Number fluency repair
subjects.description: Fractions, negative numbers, proportional reasoning. Diagnosed from marked work rather than a placement test, and typically four to six sessions as a standalone intensive. Left alone, it reappears in Year 9 simultaneous equations and in Year 11 modelling, where it costs considerably more to fix because two other things have to be unpicked first.

subjects.name: Criterion C notation and reasoning
subjects.description: The cheapest grade movement available on the standard route: three or four sessions correcting every notation slip on the student's own work. Defined variables, carried units, labelled axes, a stated conclusion. Priced as a short block rather than a weekly commitment, because once the habit is installed, it holds.

subjects.name: Investigating patterns blocks
subjects.description: Three to five sessions against a specific task deadline. The student brings the task sheet and clarification and writes every assessed word. Priced per block because the work is bounded; a weekly open-ended slot for investigation coaching is a way of paying for sessions in weeks with no task to coach.

subjects.name: Real-life modelling and evaluation
subjects.description: Two to three sessions in most cases, because the missing piece is usually the evaluation paragraph rather than the mathematics. Dubai schools often set these tasks on local data such as tariffs or journey times, so the work is practical and finishes quickly once the student knows what the final paragraph must contain.

subjects.name: MYP 4 standard consolidation
subjects.description: The heaviest single year for standard-route spending, usually a weekly slot across two or three terms. Quadratics, trigonometry, circle properties and compound measures all land in this year, and the standard course covers them to a depth that the Diploma Applications and Interpretation route then assumes.

subjects.name: MYP 5 retrieval and exit assessment
subjects.description: Mostly retrieval across five years rather than new content, plus format work where the school enters candidates for the end-of-programme on-screen examination. Priced as a term-long run rather than a year, because the useful window is the one before the final assessments.

subjects.name: Standard or extended route advice
subjects.description: Often a single session rather than a plan. A specialist reads the four criterion marks and the marked tasks and gives an honest view on whether the extended route is survivable for this student, and what it would cost in weekly hours to make it so. Families who buy this one session frequently save a year of misdirected support.

subjects.name: Mid-year transfer mapping
subjects.description: For students arriving in Dubai from another curriculum. Four to six sessions comparing what has been covered against the school's current unit and the four branches, then teaching only the real gaps. Cheaper than a weekly slot and considerably cheaper than discovering the gaps in a Year 10 assessment.

subjects.description: One or two sessions on the exact permitted device and, where the school collects tasks digitally, on the equation editor. Low cost, disproportionate return: mangled typeset notation loses criterion C marks that the student has entirely earned mathematically.

subjects.description: Common in Dubai, and worth asking about explicitly. Two students in different programme years cannot share a session usefully, but they can share a diagnostic review and one evidence file, and staggered slots on the same evening are easier for a family to protect than two separate commitments.

sections.heading: The Dubai rate bands, and what each one buys a standard-route student
paragraphs: The usable way to read tutoring prices in this emirate is by band rather than by brand. There are five bands in the market and they are separated by what the hour contains, not by marketing. At the bottom, budget online platforms publish from AED 33 to AED 65 an hour; the model is scheduled sessions with material supplied by the platform and, in several cases, a rotating tutor. In the middle, qualified subject tutors online publish from AED 150 to AED 300; one agency states from AED 150 for International GCSE and from AED 200 for International Baccalaureate work.

Above that, specialists in International Baccalaureate and Cambridge subjects are quoted at AED 200 to AED 450 and beyond, with one UK agency publishing AED 270 and a premium named provider at AED 650. In-home visits sit across the middle and upper bands at AED 180 to AED 350 per the Bestimate rate survey, with individual listings to AED 500, because the drive is inside the rate. Monthly packaging appears in two shapes: AED 799 for eight online sessions, and AED 1,599 to AED 1,799 for four two-hour in-home sessions.

For a standard-route Middle Years request the honest guidance is that the middle band does most of the work. A tutor who knows the framework, reads criterion descriptors fluently and has marked investigation tasks is the requirement; an examiner-level specialist is rarely necessary before the Diploma. Where a standard-route family is quoted at the top of the market, ask what specifically in the brief requires it. Where a family is tempted by the bottom band, ask who the tutor will be next month, because continuity is what a criterion-marked subject rewards.

The table sets the bands against what each delivers for a standard-route student.
