sections.heading: The teacher-of-your-own-child problem
paragraphs: A recurring suggestion in Dubai parent networks is to engage your child's own subject teacher privately, on the reasoning that nobody knows the pupil or the course better. It is the arrangement to avoid, for rule-based reasons and for a practical one that families find more persuasive.

On the rules: the private tuition permit carries a code of conduct that bars serving pupils affiliated with the tutor's own school, and in Abu Dhabi ADEK's professional-ethics rules for private and charter school staff prohibit teachers from providing paid private tutoring to pupils enrolled at their own school. Those rules are press-reported, so verify the current wording with the authority or the school rather than relying on a summary, including this one.

On the practice: the person who set your child's assessment is not the person best placed to show them how an external examiner reads an answer. Internal marking develops its own habits, generous in some places and severe in others, and a candidate coached by their own marker can become excellent at satisfying that marker specifically. The session that moves a Diploma grade is usually the one that introduces an unfamiliar, external reading of the same script.

There is also a conflict nobody discusses comfortably. A teacher who is paid by a family holds a position in relation to that family's child inside school as well as outside it, and both parties feel the awkwardness the first time an internal grade disappoints. The cleanest arrangement is a specialist who has no role in the pupil's school at all.
bullets: The permit's code of conduct bars pupils affiliated with the tutor's school
ADEK ethics rules bar Abu Dhabi school staff from tutoring their own pupils
Internal marking habits are not an external examiner's habits
Verify the current wording with the authority or the school directly

sections.heading: Why there is no Dubai address to visit, and what that changes
paragraphs: IB Gram has no premises, office or centre in the UAE, and no page on this site will suggest otherwise. Two competitor pages examined for this project show a UAE footer address on a page about a different emirate, and two route UAE parents to a non-UAE phone number as the conversion path. Both are trust failures, and an address a business does not occupy is a misrepresentation.

The operating consequence is that teaching for UAE families is delivered one-to-one over live video on Gulf Standard Time, and that in-home visiting is available only in India. A parent who wants a person in the room should hire locally, and should do so with the verification questions above in hand rather than on a recommendation alone.

What the model buys is the thing that is actually scarce in Dubai. A Higher Level Chemistry specialist, or a tutor who has supervised an Economics commentary portfolio, is rare within any single community and considerably less rare across a national pool. A family in Dubai South chooses from the same specialists as a family in Al Barsha, and neither pays for a drive.

What it costs is the things presence provides, and they are worth naming rather than dismissing. A tutor in the room reads a pupil's body language more fully than a camera does. For younger children, physical presence helps with attention. For a pupil with specific access requirements, in-person support may be the right answer, and a family in that position should hire locally and pay the premium without apology.

sections.heading: Replacement, cancellation and the three things that actually go wrong
paragraphs: Over a two-year Diploma, three failures account for almost every unhappy tutoring arrangement in this market, and none of them is about teaching quality. Knowing them in advance is how a family writes an agreement that survives them.

The first is departure. Dubai's population moves, and a tutor leaving the country in March of DP2 is a genuine and common event. A family contracting directly with an individual has no remedy and starts the search in the worst month of the year. The protection is not a longer contract; it is knowing in advance who, if anyone, is responsible for finding a replacement.

The second is the quiet mismatch. The sessions happen, everyone is pleasant, and nothing moves. This is why a review instrument agreed in advance matters so much: without one, the arrangement continues on goodwill until the mock arrives. With one, the four-week review either shows a changed pattern of lost marks or it does not, and the conversation is about evidence rather than about anyone's feelings.

The third is the boundary failure, and it usually arrives at 10pm the night before a coursework deadline. A candidate under pressure asks for more than feedback, and a tutor who wants to be helpful supplies a paragraph. The consequence falls on the candidate and can extend to the loss of a Diploma. The protection is to have agreed the boundary in writing at the start, so that the answer in the moment is a reference to something already settled rather than a judgement made at 10pm.

process.title: Ask the permit question first
process.description: Of any individual tutor, from any source, including one a platform introduced: do you hold a current private tuition work permit, under which category, and when does it expire. It is free to obtain and takes two working days, so there is no legitimate reason for the answer to be complicated.

process.description: Not what are your qualifications, which anyone can answer, but a question only someone who has taught the level can answer in a sentence. The subject entries above give one for each. A general answer about exam technique is itself the answer.

process.description: A full session with the proposed specialist, at no cost and with no card required. Use it to test the two things that matter: whether they can diagnose from a marked script, and whether they are clear about where their role stops on assessed work.

process.description: Session length, minimum block, whether coursework support is inside the figure, written records, cancellation terms, replacement obligation and the tax position. Six lines. A provider unwilling to put them in writing has told you how a dispute would go.

process.description: Which piece of school-marked work the four-week review will measure, and exactly what will and will not be provided on coursework. Both settled before the first session, so that neither is being decided under pressure later.

faqs.question: Is it legal for a Dubai family to hire a private IB tutor?
faqs.answer: Yes, provided the tutor holds the right permit. Private tuition in the UAE runs on a work permit introduced by Ministerial Resolution No. 710 of 2023, granted free of charge for two years through the Ministry of Human Resources and Emiratisation. Individuals offering private tutoring without one are subject to fines and penalties outlined in the applicable laws. The obligation sits on the tutor rather than the family, but a parent engaging an unpermitted tutor is building a two-year arrangement on an unlawful footing, which is a poor foundation whatever the teaching is like.

faqs.question: How long does a UAE private tuition work permit last and what does it cost?
faqs.answer: It is granted free of charge for two years. The Ministry of Human Resources and Emiratisation lists the service as Issuance of a New Work Permit for Private Tutor Licensing, with no fees and a two-working-day completion time, applied for through the ministry's smart app, website and e-services system. Because it costs nothing and takes two days, a tutor without one has either not looked into it or has decided not to, and both answers are informative. Ask for the expiry date rather than simply whether they hold one.

faqs.question: Who is eligible to apply for the private tutor permit in the UAE?
faqs.answer: The published eligibility list is wide: teachers registered in government or private schools, employees in the government and private sectors, unemployed individuals, university students, and school pupils aged 15 to 18. That breadth tells you the resolution was written to regularise an existing informal market rather than to restrict tutoring to professionals. It also means the permit says nothing about expertise. A permitted tutor may be a Diploma examiner or a first-year undergraduate, and establishing which is a separate question entirely.

faqs.question: Can the same permit be used for online lessons as for in-person ones?
faqs.answer: The permit regularises private tuition as an activity rather than a venue, so the sensible assumption is that it covers the work however it is delivered, and the Ministry of Human Resources and Emiratisation is the authority to confirm that with directly. What a parent can rely on is simpler: ask the individual whether their current permit covers the arrangement you are proposing, and take the answer in writing. Any provider telling you the question does not apply to online teaching is guessing on your behalf about something they could check.

faqs.question: Can a tutoring centre be opened on a private tutor permit in Dubai?
faqs.answer: No. An operation with premises and staff in Dubai is a different legal animal and requires a KHDA Educational Services Permit for a training institute, obtained after initial approval, with a maximum of six months to complete the permit and licence steps and annual renewal requested at least 30 days before expiry. The personal permit covers an individual providing private tuition. The two are routinely conflated in marketing, and a platform describing itself as holding a KHDA permit when it has no premises is describing something it cannot hold.

faqs.question: Are there fines for using a tutor without a permit, and how much?
faqs.answer: The published position is that individuals offering private tutoring without a permit are subject to fines and penalties outlined in the applicable laws. No fine schedule has been published. Press reporting on the regime stated explicitly that the ministry did not specify the fine amounts or detail the penalties, and a figure circulating online could not be verified. For that reason no amount appears on this page, and any provider quoting you a specific number is repeating something unchecked. The absence of a published figure is not an absence of consequence.

faqs.question: Can a 15-year-old be paid to tutor in the UAE?
faqs.answer: School pupils aged 15 to 18 are explicitly listed among those eligible to apply for the private tuition work permit, which surprises most parents reading the rules for the first time. Whether that is a suitable arrangement for your child is a separate judgement from whether it is lawful. For primary numeracy or middle-years content practice, a capable older pupil can be genuinely effective and inexpensive. For a Higher Level Diploma subject, buying a tutor one or two years ahead of the candidate purchases reassurance rather than marks.

faqs.question: How can I check whether an IB tutor is permitted to teach in the UAE?
faqs.answer: Ask the individual directly: do you hold a current private tuition work permit, under which eligibility category, and what is the expiry date. A tutor operating properly answers in one line. A platform cannot hold the permit on an individual's behalf, so a reply along the lines of all our tutors are fully licensed is not an answer to the question you asked. Ask the same question regardless of how the introduction was made, including through a recommendation from another parent in your community.

faqs.question: Why should I avoid hiring my child's own subject teacher privately?
faqs.answer: Two reasons. The permit carries a code of conduct that bars serving pupils affiliated with the tutor's own school, and in Abu Dhabi ADEK's professional-ethics rules prohibit private and charter school staff from paid private tutoring of pupils enrolled at their own school. Those rules are press-reported, so verify the current wording with the authority or the school. The practical reason is stronger: the person who set the assessment is not the person best placed to show a candidate how an unfamiliar external examiner reads the same answer.

faqs.question: Who employs the tutor, and who is accountable if the arrangement fails?
faqs.answer: It depends entirely on the model, and this is the question families most often skip. Contracting directly with an independent tutor means there is no third party, which keeps the rate lower and leaves verification, record-keeping and replacement with you. Contracting through a platform means a named contact is responsible for changing a match that is not working. A tuition centre is accountable for the service but will usually offer a different class rather than a different teacher. Establish which arrangement you are in before the first payment.

faqs.question: What should a Dubai tutoring agreement actually say?
faqs.answer: Six things, in writing, before the first session. Whether the rate is per sixty minutes or per session. Whether a minimum block applies. Whether coursework support is inside the figure or billed separately. What the cancellation terms are, including for a prepared session. Who is responsible for finding a replacement if the tutor becomes unavailable. And exactly what will and will not be provided on assessed work. Everything that later becomes a dispute in this market is one of those six left unstated.

faqs.question: What happens if the first private tutor turns out to be the wrong match?
faqs.answer: With a platform arrangement, a named contact changes the match and the four-week review exists precisely to surface the problem early rather than at the mock. Contracting directly, the family starts the search again, which in February or March of the Diploma second year is a genuinely difficult position. Either way the protection is the same: agree in advance which piece of school-marked work the review will measure, so that a mismatch shows up as evidence rather than as a slowly growing suspicion that nobody wants to raise.

faqs.question: What personal information should a tutoring enquiry form ask about a child?
faqs.answer: As little as answers the question. Subject, level, target grade and one piece of marked work is enough to give an honest response. UAE data protection sits under Federal Decree-Law No. 45 of 2021, and the standard a parent should expect is a clear statement of what is collected, why, how long it is kept and how to have it deleted, with a privacy link on the same page as the form. A tutoring enquiry does not need a photograph of your child, and it is reasonable to ask what happens to a marked script after the diagnosis.

faqs.question: Does a private tutor cost more than a tuition centre in Dubai?
faqs.answer: Per hour, one-to-one is more expensive than a group class in a centre, and that is the clearest genuine saving available in this market. Published one-to-one rates run from AED 45 at the budget online end to AED 650 for a named premium provider, with qualified subject teachers at AED 150 to AED 300 and specialists at AED 200 to AED 450 or above. A centre group class undercuts all of those. What it cannot offer is a diagnosis of one candidate's specific fault, which is what a Diploma family is usually paying for.

faqs.question: Why does IB Gram not have a Dubai office or centre to visit?
faqs.answer: Because it has none, and saying otherwise would be a misrepresentation. Two competitor pages examined for this project display a UAE address on a page about a different emirate, and two route UAE parents to a non-UAE phone number. IB Gram operates no premises in the UAE, holds no KHDA institute permit, and delivers teaching one-to-one over live video on Gulf Standard Time. In-home visiting is a service offered only in India. A family who wants someone physically present should hire locally, using the verification questions on this page.

dubai/ib-private-tutor.closingBody: If you are hiring an IB private tutor in Dubai, two questions do most of the work and cost nothing to ask: whether the individual holds a current private tuition work permit with its expiry date, and one subject-specific question only someone who has taught that level can answer in a sentence. Ask them of anyone, from any source, including us. The trial lesson that follows here is a full diagnostic session over live video on Gulf Standard Time, with no card required and nothing to cancel, and it is the right place to test whether the proposed specialist can read a marked script and is clear about where their role stops.

dubai/ib-pyp-english-tutor.tutorsIntro: The tutors below teach primary English, which means they can tell a decoding problem from a comprehension problem in ten minutes with a book and a few questions. Sessions run short, work on one strand at a time, and leave a note naming what was practised and what to read at home.

intro.heading: Four problems that look the same from the kitchen table
paragraphs: A Dubai parent who says their child needs help with English is usually describing one of four things, and they are not variations of each other. The child may be unable to turn letters reliably into sounds, which is decoding. They may decode accurately and understand very little, which is comprehension. They may understand the sentences and not know enough words to understand the passage, which is vocabulary breadth. Or they may follow everything and be unable to get any of it onto paper, which is written output. Each needs different teaching, and buying the wrong one is the most common waste in primary tutoring.

Telling them apart is the first job of an IB PYP English tutor in Dubai, and it takes about ten minutes with a book that is slightly too hard and a handful of well-chosen questions. A child who reads a page aloud flawlessly and then cannot say what happened has a comprehension problem, not a reading problem, and a term of extra reading practice will not touch it. A child who stumbles over every third word has a decoding problem, and asking them inference questions is pointless until that is fixed. Parents can run both tests themselves, for free, and this page explains how.

The programme itself makes the diagnosis harder than it should be, because it produces no marks. PYP language is organised into three strands, oral, written and visual, each described across four phases rather than year groups, and reports describe what a child can do rather than scoring it. A Dubai report saying your daughter is beginning to make inferences from text could describe a child slightly behind or comfortably on track, and the sentence reads identically either way. So parents arrive at a tutoring conversation with a worry and no data.

Dubai adds a specific complication that deserves its own section rather than a footnote. A large share of children in the emirate's private schools are learning in English while speaking one or two other languages at home, and the UK curriculum alone accounts for 37% of Dubai private school enrolment according to the Dubai Media Office, with Indian curriculum schools at 26% and US at 14%. A child whose spoken English is fluent and conversational can still have a vocabulary gap that only appears in a reading passage about an unfamiliar topic. That is a normal, well-understood pattern, and it is routinely misread as a reading difficulty.

There is also a strand almost nobody tutors and the programme genuinely assesses: viewing and presenting, which covers interpreting images, film, diagrams and multimodal texts, and presenting ideas in those forms. Dubai children do a surprising amount of it at school and almost none of it at home, and it is one of the few places where a parent can help quickly without any specialist knowledge. What follows is the detail on all three strands, the four comprehension question types and their characteristic failures, the English as an additional language picture, and what a session with a seven-year-old actually contains. Lessons are one-to-one on live video; IB Gram does not send tutors to homes in Dubai.

dubai/ib-pyp-english-tutor.programmesIntro: Language expectations in the PYP are described by phase rather than age, so a Dubai classroom often contains children across two phases. These are the stages we work with and what each one is really being assessed on.

programmes.name: PYP language, early phases
programmes.description: Oral language dominates: listening, following instructions, retelling, building spoken vocabulary. Written language begins with letter-sound correspondence, then simple sentences. Visual language starts with reading pictures, which sounds trivial and is the foundation of inference. Most worries at this stage describe a normal developmental range.
programmes.countryNote: Dubai foundation classes draw children from very different language backgrounds, so the spread within one Year 1 room is wide. A parent concerned here should ask the class teacher whether their child is behind the class or behind the phase, because those are different answers with different implications.

programmes.name: PYP language, middle phases
programmes.description: The years when reading shifts from learning to read to reading to learn, and the gap between decoding and comprehension becomes visible. Writing moves from sentences to structured paragraphs. This is where most genuine primary English problems surface and where targeted teaching does the most work.
programmes.countryNote: The classic Dubai referral is a Year 3 or 4 child whose early reading was strong and whose comprehension has stalled. It is almost always vocabulary breadth or inference rather than decoding, and the parent has usually been buying more reading practice for a year.

programmes.name: PYP language, final phase
programmes.description: Inference, author's purpose, summarising, comparing texts, and writing at length with control over structure and register. The Exhibition in the final year asks children to research, write and present, which puts all three strands under pressure at once.
programmes.countryNote: Dubai families often start spending here because of the step into the Middle Years Programme or a British Year 7. The highest-value work at this point is inference and written structure, both of which carry forward directly into criterion-marked work.

programmes.name: MYP Language and Literature
programmes.description: Four criteria marked 0 to 8, analysis of literary and non-literary texts, and a requirement to write reasoning down rather than simply answer. Comprehension gaps left from primary become criterion-level weaknesses here, which is the honest case for working on inference in Year 5 or 6.
programmes.countryNote: In Dubai continuum schools the Year 7 intake mixes children from several primary systems, and teachers spend the autumn finding gaps. Children who arrive able to infer and to structure a paragraph are rarely the ones needing paid support in Year 8.

dubai/ib-pyp-english-tutor.subjectsIntro: Primary English is not one subject. These are the areas we work on, with what each is actually assessing and the characteristic way children fail at it.

subjects.name: Phonics and decoding
subjects.description: Turning letters into sounds reliably, including digraphs, split vowels and multi-syllable words. A child who hesitates on every third word is spending all their attention here and has none left for meaning. Fixable, with a systematic method and daily short practice, and the gains are quick.

subjects.name: Reading fluency and expression
subjects.description: Reading at a pace that leaves room for thinking, with phrasing that tracks punctuation. Fluency is the bridge between decoding and comprehension, and a monotone reader usually has not noticed that punctuation carries meaning. One or two sessions plus reading aloud at home makes a visible difference.

subjects.name: Reading comprehension: retrieval
subjects.description: Finding information stated directly in the text. The easiest question type and still a source of lost ground, because children answer from memory rather than going back to the page. The single most useful habit a tutor installs at primary age is underlining where the answer came from.

subjects.name: Reading comprehension: inference
subjects.description: Working out what the text implies but does not state. The hardest strand to teach and the most valuable, because every later system assesses it heavily. Children fail here by guessing from their own experience rather than from evidence in the passage.

subjects.name: Vocabulary breadth
subjects.description: Knowing enough words to make sense of an unfamiliar passage. For Dubai's many children learning in English alongside other home languages, this is frequently the real gap behind an apparent reading problem. It responds to wide reading and explicit word teaching rather than to comprehension drills.

subjects.name: Writing structure and paragraphing
subjects.description: Organising ideas so a reader can follow them: an opening that does a job, paragraphs with a single focus, an ending that is not just stopping. The most common primary writing problem in Dubai, and far more teachable than families expect.

subjects.name: Sentence construction and grammar
subjects.description: Varying sentence length, using subordination, and controlling tense. Children who write one long sentence joined by repeated connectives are usually unaware there is an alternative, and showing them two versions of their own sentence is often enough.

subjects.name: Spelling and handwriting stamina
subjects.description: Spelling patterns rather than word lists, and the physical ability to write for twenty minutes without the hand failing. Stamina is routinely mistaken for a writing problem: a child with good ideas whose hand gives out at line six looks like a weak writer.

subjects.name: Oral language: speaking and listening
subjects.description: Explaining, questioning, retelling in sequence and listening for detail. Assessed throughout the programme, often inside units of inquiry, and almost never practised deliberately at home. Retelling a story in order is a free and surprisingly effective exercise.

subjects.name: Viewing and presenting
subjects.description: Interpreting images, film, diagrams and multimodal texts, and presenting ideas in those forms. A genuine PYP strand that almost no tutoring addresses. Asking a child what a photograph is not showing is one of the best inference exercises available and costs nothing.

dubai/ib-pyp-english-tutor.regionsIntro: What a primary English session should address varies with what happens at home, and in Dubai that varies a great deal between communities. These notes cover the patterns we see and the practical constraints on building a reading routine.

regions.name: Jumeirah, Al Safa and Umm Suqeim
regions.note: Mixed home languages and strong school provision, with Dubai Public Library operating community branches within reach of these neighbourhoods. The pattern here is usually inference rather than decoding, and a weekly library visit does more for vocabulary breadth than an extra paid session.

regions.name: Al Mankhool and Bur Dubai
regions.note: Dense, long-settled and multilingual, with a community library branch nearby. Children here are often confident speakers of two or three languages and still short on the written vocabulary a reading passage assumes, which is a vocabulary problem rather than a reading one.

regions.name: Al Qusais, Al Twar and Al Nahda
regions.note: Many households where English is the school language and not the home one, and where older siblings do much of the reading support. The useful intervention is often explicit word teaching rather than comprehension exercises, plus reading aloud to an adult who asks why questions.

regions.name: Mirdif and Al Warqa
regions.note: Longer school runs that push the session window past five o'clock, which matters for a child under nine. Short sessions twice a week work better here than a weekend hour, and online delivery is what makes that length economic at all.

regions.name: Dubai Marina, JLT and Palm Jumeirah
regions.note: High mobility, with children arriving mid-year from several different systems. A child who has changed curriculum twice often has gaps that look random and are not: ask which phase the new school places them in rather than comparing to the old year group.

regions.name: Dubai Hills, Al Barsha and Emirates Hills
regions.note: Dense IB continuum provision and families who read the school's reporting closely. Parents here most often ask for inference and written structure in Years 5 and 6, which is the right request and the highest-value primary English work available.

regions.name: Mudon, Town Square and Dubailand
regions.note: Younger families with several children close in age, so reading time at home competes with everything. A ten-minute bedtime routine done every night beats a thirty-minute session twice a week, and it is free, which makes it the first thing we ask about.

regions.name: Dubai South and The Sustainable City
regions.note: Longer distances and a thinner local tutor supply, which is where an in-home arrangement becomes expensive and fragile. One-to-one live video costs the same here as anywhere in the emirate, and a 25-minute slot is viable because nobody travelled.

schoolClusters.city: Western Dubai IB continuum provision
schoolClusters.note: Students we support in these communities usually attend schools with well-developed PYP language practice and clear phase-based reporting, so the diagnosis often starts from the school's own observation. Our work there is most often inference and written structure in the final two primary years.

schoolClusters.city: Eastern and southern Dubai primary provision
schoolClusters.note: A wider curriculum mix and more children moving between systems during primary. Students we support from these areas more often need vocabulary breadth and the language of questions rather than reading skill, because changing system changes the wording before it changes the content.

sections.heading: The two tests a Dubai parent can run tonight for nothing
paragraphs: Before paying anybody, run two tests. The first separates decoding from comprehension. Choose a book slightly harder than your child's usual level, have them read a page aloud, and count the words they stumble on. More than about one word in twenty and attention is going on decoding, which means comprehension questions are premature. Fewer than that, and the problem is somewhere else. Then ask three questions about the page: one with the answer stated directly, one requiring inference, one about what a specific word means in that sentence.

The pattern of answers tells you which of the four problems you have. A child who answers the direct question and fails the inference question has an inference gap, which is the most common Year 3 to Year 5 referral in Dubai and needs explicit teaching rather than more reading. A child who fails the vocabulary question and then gets the inference question right once the word is explained has a vocabulary breadth gap, which is built by wide reading and word teaching and does not need comprehension drills at all.

The second test separates understanding from written output. Ask the child to tell you about something that happened at school, then ask them to write the same thing. If the spoken version is detailed and the written version is three short sentences, the ideas are there and the problem is output: handwriting stamina, spelling anxiety or no sense of structure. All three are teachable and none of them is a reading problem. Parents who run these two tests before the first conversation arrive with better information than most paid assessments produce.

sections.heading: The three language strands, and the one nobody tutors
paragraphs: PYP language is organised into three strands rather than the reading-and-writing pair most parents expect. Oral language covers listening and speaking. Written language covers reading and writing. Visual language covers viewing and presenting: interpreting images, film, diagrams and multimodal texts, and presenting ideas in those forms. All three are assessed across four phases, and Dubai schools report against them in descriptive rather than numerical terms.

The practical consequence is that a tutoring conversation about English is usually a conversation about half of one strand. Reading comprehension and writing matter enormously and they are not the whole assessment. A child who cannot retell a sequence of events aloud has an oral language gap that will show up in their writing, because writing is the harder version of the same skill. A child who cannot say what a diagram is telling them is weak in visual language, which appears across science, mathematics and social studies as much as in English.

Visual language is the most neglected and the easiest for a parent to help with. Looking at a photograph and asking what is happening just outside the frame, or what the photographer chose not to show, is an inference exercise with no reading load at all. It works with children who resist books, it works in any home language, and it transfers directly to inference in text. We use it deliberately in early sessions with reluctant readers, because it establishes that the child can infer before anyone asks them to do it on a page.

sections.heading: Decoding against comprehension: two problems that look identical
paragraphs: The most expensive misdiagnosis in primary English is treating a comprehension problem as a reading problem. A child who reads aloud accurately and fluently and then cannot answer a question about the paragraph does not need more reading practice. They are already reading. What they need is explicit teaching in what to do with a text: go back to the page, find the evidence, work out what is implied rather than stated. That is a different lesson entirely and it is usually a short one.

The reverse misdiagnosis is less common and more damaging. A child who is still spending most of their attention on turning letters into sounds has nothing left for meaning, and asking them inference questions produces failure that looks like stupidity to a seven-year-old. The right sequence is decoding to automaticity first, then fluency, then comprehension. Skipping to comprehension because it feels more intellectually respectable is a reliable way to damage a child's belief that they can read.

There is a third case specific to multilingual Dubai households and worth naming separately. A child may decode well, comprehend well in familiar contexts, and fail on a passage about an unfamiliar topic purely because they do not know enough of the words. This is a vocabulary breadth problem, not a comprehension problem, and the treatment is wide reading plus explicit teaching of word families rather than comprehension exercises. Comprehension drills on a passage the child cannot vocabulary their way through teach nothing except frustration.

sections.heading: The four comprehension question types, and the characteristic failure of each
paragraphs: Comprehension questions in primary English come in four broad types, and children fail each one in a predictable way. Knowing which type your child misses turns a vague worry into a specific lesson. Retrieval asks for information stated in the text. Inference asks what the text implies. Vocabulary in context asks what a word means here. And the fourth group, covering author's purpose, summary and comparison, asks about the text as a made thing.

The failures are consistent. Retrieval is failed by answering from memory instead of returning to the page, which is a habit and takes one or two sessions to fix. Inference is failed by substituting the child's own experience for textual evidence: asked why a character is nervous, they say because she has a test, when the passage says nothing of the kind. Vocabulary in context is failed by offering a general definition rather than the meaning in that sentence. And the fourth group is failed by retelling the plot in answer to a question about why the author did something.

This is also where Dubai's examination-light primary context shows. Children who have never been asked to point at the words that justify an answer do not develop the habit, and the first system that demands it is usually Middle Years Language and Literature with its criterion marking, or a Year 7 British curriculum classroom. Installing the habit at primary age is cheap: the instruction is simply to underline where the answer came from before writing anything. Children resist it for about three sessions and then do it automatically.

sections.heading: Writing: structure, sentence variety and the output problem
paragraphs: Primary writing problems in Dubai concentrate in three places, and only one of them is about ideas. The first is structure: an opening that does no work, paragraphs with no single focus, and an ending that simply stops. The second is sentence construction: one very long sentence joined by repeated connectives, because nobody has shown the child there is an alternative. The third is physical, and it is the most consistently misread.

Handwriting stamina matters more than families expect. A child with excellent ideas whose hand gives out at line six produces a short, deteriorating piece that looks like weak writing, and is not. The test is simple: compare the first two lines with the last two. If the quality falls off a cliff rather than being uniformly weak, the problem is stamina, and the treatment is shorter writing bursts, better grip and position, and typing where the school permits it. Teaching more structure to a child whose hand is failing fixes nothing.

The structure work itself is unusually teachable. Showing a child two versions of their own sentence, one long and one split into three, produces an immediate preference and a lasting habit. Giving them a topic sentence frame for a paragraph produces coherent paragraphs within a session. The caution is that the writing must stay theirs: a tutor who improves a child's piece has improved one piece. A tutor who asks what this paragraph is about, and lets the child answer, has taught a paragraph. We write nothing for a child, which at primary age is a pedagogical point before it is an integrity one.

sections.heading: Learning in English while speaking something else at home
paragraphs: This deserves a section rather than a footnote because it describes a large share of Dubai primary children and because it is so often misread. UK curriculum schools account for 37% of Dubai private school enrolment, Indian curriculum 26% and US 14%, according to the Dubai Media Office, and a great many children in all of them speak one or two other languages at home. A child in that position frequently has fluent conversational English, accurate decoding, and a vocabulary gap that appears only in a reading passage about an unfamiliar subject.

The distinction that matters is between conversational fluency and academic language. Playground English arrives quickly. The language of a geography passage, a science explanation or a comprehension question takes considerably longer, because it uses words nobody says at home in any language. A Year 4 child who cannot answer questions about a passage on erosion may understand erosion perfectly and not know the words deposition, sediment or gradually. That is a vocabulary problem with a clear treatment and no implication at all about ability.

Three things help and one does not. Wide reading at a level where the child meets a few unknown words per page helps most. Explicit teaching of word families, prefixes and suffixes helps second. Reading aloud to an adult who asks why questions helps third. What does not help is comprehension drills on passages the child cannot get through vocabulary-wise, which is what most purchased worksheets provide. Alongside this, Arabic, Islamic Education and Social Studies are mandatory in all Dubai private schools whatever the licensed curriculum, per KHDA's guidelines, and a well-established body of evidence finds that maintaining home languages supports rather than hinders English.

sections.heading: How PYP English is assessed when there is no test
paragraphs: The PYP produces no examinations and no percentages at primary age, which makes it genuinely hard for a Dubai parent to know whether to act. Assessment is continuous and descriptive: guided reading records, marked written pieces across subjects rather than only in English lessons, observation of discussion, and periodic reading assessments whose results schools report in different ways. Progression is described against four phases rather than year groups, so a child can be in Year 4 and working in the phase that spans Years 3 to 5.

The way to get something actionable out of that is to ask narrow questions at the parent meeting. Which phase is my child working in for reading, and which for writing, because they are often different. What specifically does she do when a comprehension question goes wrong. Is the writing issue structure, sentence construction or stamina. A teacher who sees your child every day can answer all three quickly, and those answers are a better diagnosis than any paid assessment, because they rest on months of observation.

Some Dubai schools also use external reading assessments or Cambridge Primary Checkpoint, which Cambridge International runs in March, May and October. Where a school uses one, it is a useful external reading in a programme that otherwise offers none, and worth asking about rather than worrying about. It is diagnostic rather than high-stakes, no tutoring is required to sit it, and a provider telling you otherwise is manufacturing urgency about a process that is not a gate.

sections.heading: The Exhibition, the Middle Years step, and the line a tutor stays behind
paragraphs: In the final primary year, the Exhibition asks children to research a topic, write about it and present it, which puts all three language strands under pressure at the same time. It is the first piece of extended independent work most PYP children do, and it is a reasonable place for a family to want help. It is also the first place where the line matters: a tutor may teach note-taking, paragraph structure and how to present to an audience, and may not write, redraft or produce any part of the child's work.

That boundary is easier to hold at primary age than parents expect, because the useful teaching is generic. How to take notes without copying whole sentences. How to turn four notes into a paragraph with one focus. How to look at an audience rather than read a slide. All of it can be taught on a completely different topic from the child's own, and the child then applies it to their Exhibition alone. We work that way deliberately, and we would be wary of any provider offering to help with the actual piece.

The step into Middle Years Language and Literature is where primary English spending either pays off or does not, and the list of what carries forward is short. Inference supported by quoted evidence. A paragraph with a single focus and a topic sentence that does a job. Enough vocabulary to read an unfamiliar passage. The habit of underlining where an answer came from. That is four things, all teachable in a six to ten session block in Year 5 or 6, and all worth more than a general sense that the child is a confident reader.

sections.heading: How lessons run, what the market charges, and what we will not claim
paragraphs: Lessons are one-to-one on live video, timed to Gulf Standard Time. IB Gram does not run home visits in Dubai or anywhere in the UAE; visiting tutors are a service we operate only in India. For primary English the honest trade is this: a very young or very reluctant child often does better with an adult physically present, and the Dubai market serves that at AED 180 to AED 350 per hour in-home according to Bestimate's rate survey. Against that, online delivery makes a 25-minute session economically viable, which for a seven-year-old is the correct length, and lets us match on primary training rather than on who lives nearby.

On price generally, the published market as we read it in October 2026: Tutopiya from roughly AED 33 to AED 52 per hour and EdFlik from AED 45 to AED 65 at the budget end; Unitors from AED 150 for IGCSE and AED 200 for IB; TutorChase at AED 270 for specialist support; Bestimate reporting AED 200 to AED 450 and above for specialist exam-year help; BartyED advertising AED 650 for premium named tutors. Those are other providers' published figures with their reading date attached, not IB Gram prices. We publish a free first lesson and a structure rather than a single rate, because primary English and Diploma English are not the same purchase.

What we will not claim. No regulator or examination board endorses IB Gram: KHDA is responsible for enhancing and overseeing the quality of private education in Dubai per the UAE government's own information service, and that is a fact about KHDA, not a credential of ours. We hold no permit, accreditation or partnership from KHDA, ADEK, SPEA, the Ministry of Education, the IB, Cambridge or Pearson. Private tutors in the UAE need the MoHRE private tuition work permit introduced by Ministerial Resolution No. 710 of 2023, granted free of charge for two years; tutoring without one carries fines and penalties under the applicable laws, and since no fine schedule is published we quote no amount.

process.title: Run the two free tests first
process.description: A slightly hard page read aloud, with words-misread counted, then three questions: one direct, one inference, one about a word in context. Then compare a spoken account with a written one. Fifteen minutes, no cost, and it tells you which of four problems you have before anybody quotes you anything.

process.title: Ask the class teacher two narrow questions
process.description: Which phase is my child working in for reading and which for writing, and what specifically goes wrong when a comprehension question is missed. A teacher who sees your child daily answers both quickly, and those answers beat any paid assessment because they rest on months of observation.

process.title: Free 25-minute first lesson
process.description: Short, because that is what a primary child can use, and free with no card details taken. The tutor confirms or corrects the diagnosis and tells you plainly which strand to work on. If the answer is a reading routine and no paid block, we will say so and you keep the written diagnosis.

process.title: Buy one strand with an end condition
process.description: Not a term of English. One strand, an agreed number of sessions, and a stated signal that means it is done: inference answers quoting evidence without being reminded, or paragraphs with a single focus. The number, the strand and the end condition go in writing before anything is paid.

process.title: Ten minutes of reading every day
process.description: Every session sets reading aloud or a short writing burst, because vocabulary breadth and stamina are built by repetition and repetition is free. Families who do the ten minutes need fewer paid sessions, which is the opposite of how most packages are designed to work.

process.title: Stop at the end condition
process.description: When the agreed signal appears the block ends and we say so. If a different strand surfaces in a later year, start a short block then. No rolling commitment, no minimum term, and we would rather you returned for a targeted Year 6 block than paid continuously from Year 2.

whyPoints.title: Diagnosis before teaching
whyPoints.description: Decoding, comprehension strategy, vocabulary breadth and written output look identical from the kitchen table and need completely different lessons. The first session establishes which one you have, and we would rather lose the booking than sell a block aimed at the wrong problem.

whyPoints.title: All three strands, including the neglected one
whyPoints.description: Oral language and visual language are assessed in the programme and almost never tutored. Asking a child what a photograph is not showing is one of the best inference exercises available, works with children who resist books, and costs nothing at all.

whyPoints.title: Evidence underlined before an answer is written
whyPoints.description: The single most valuable habit at primary age, because every later system rewards it and Middle Years criterion marking depends on it. Children resist it for about three sessions and then do it automatically for the rest of their schooling.

whyPoints.title: The child writes every word
whyPoints.description: A tutor who improves a child's piece has improved one piece. A tutor who asks what this paragraph is about, and waits, has taught a paragraph. At primary age that is a teaching principle before it is an integrity rule, and it is also what we hold to on Exhibition work.

whyPoints.title: Short sessions, priced as short sessions
whyPoints.description: Twenty-five minutes twice a week beats a bought hour for a seven-year-old, and online delivery makes the format economic because nobody has driven across Dubai to deliver it. Most providers avoid it for administrative reasons rather than educational ones.

whyPoints.title: No claims we cannot support
whyPoints.description: No regulator endorses IB Gram and we claim none. No grade promises, no reading-age guarantees, no statistics without a source. Where this page states a regulatory or market fact it names the authority or the provider, and every AED figure carries the date we read it.

faqs.question: My son reads a page aloud perfectly and then cannot tell me what happened - what is that?
faqs.answer: A comprehension problem, not a reading problem, and the distinction decides what you should buy. He is already decoding well, so more reading practice will not touch it. What he needs is explicit teaching in what to do with a text: return to the page rather than answering from memory, find the words that justify an answer, and work out what is implied rather than stated. That is a short, specific course of teaching, usually four to six sessions, and it is one of the most reliably effective things in primary English.

faqs.question: What are the three PYP language strands, and which one does the school report on least?
faqs.answer: Oral language, which is listening and speaking; written language, which is reading and writing; and visual language, which is viewing and presenting. Reports usually say most about written language because it generates the most visible evidence, and least about visual language, which is assessed through unit tasks rather than reported separately. That is a gap worth knowing about, because interpreting images and diagrams is an inference skill that transfers straight into reading, and it is the easiest strand for a parent to support at home.

faqs.question: What is viewing and presenting, and why has nobody mentioned it to us before?
faqs.answer: It is the visual language strand: interpreting images, film, diagrams, maps and multimodal texts, and communicating ideas in those forms. Nobody mentions it because tutoring markets organise themselves around reading and writing, and because it rarely appears as its own line on a report. It is genuinely useful. Looking at a photograph and asking what is happening just outside the frame is an inference exercise with no reading load, which makes it the best available starting point for a child who resists books.

faqs.question: How do I tell a real reading difficulty from English simply being our second language?
faqs.answer: Test whether the problem moves when a word is explained. If your child fails a comprehension question, then answers it correctly once you define the unfamiliar word, the issue is vocabulary breadth rather than reading skill. That is extremely common in Dubai, where conversational English arrives quickly and academic language takes much longer, and it is treated by wide reading and explicit word teaching rather than comprehension exercises. If the failure persists after the vocabulary is cleared, the problem is comprehension strategy and needs different teaching.

faqs.question: Her reading age came back above her year group, so why is the writing so weak?
faqs.answer: Because reading and writing are separate strands and most children are stronger at one. A reading-age measure says nothing about structure, sentence variety or handwriting stamina. Run one test: compare the first two lines of a piece with the last two. If quality falls off a cliff rather than being uniformly weak, the problem is physical stamina, and the fix is shorter writing bursts and better position rather than more teaching. If it is uniformly weak, it is structure, which is unusually teachable and often moves within a few sessions.

faqs.question: Does the PYP actually teach phonics, or should we be doing that at home?
faqs.answer: Dubai PYP schools teach early reading, and most use a systematic approach to letter-sound work in the early phases, though the specific scheme varies between schools. The thing to ask is which scheme your school uses, because mixing two different systems at home and school genuinely confuses a five-year-old. Once you know, ten minutes a day of reading aloud using that approach is the highest-value unpaid thing a parent can do, and it is what we would recommend before any paid block at that age.

faqs.question: Which comprehension question type do primary children here lose most ground on?
faqs.answer: Inference, by a clear margin, and the failure is specific: children substitute their own experience for evidence in the passage. Asked why a character is nervous, they offer a reason from their own life rather than from the text. The treatment is a rule applied without exception, that every answer must quote a word or phrase from the page, and it takes four to six sessions to become automatic. Author's purpose questions are harder still but appear less often at primary age.

faqs.question: How much reading at home actually makes a difference?
faqs.answer: Ten minutes a day, every day, at a level where the child meets a few unknown words per page. Frequency matters more than duration, and a short bedtime routine done nightly beats a long weekend session by a wide margin. The quality lever is cheap too: an adult who occasionally asks why rather than what turns reading time into inference practice. For vocabulary breadth, which is the most common underlying gap in Dubai, nothing a tutor does competes with this.

faqs.question: Should I correct every spelling mistake in my child's writing?
faqs.answer: No, and doing so often makes the output problem worse. A child who expects every word to be marked writes shorter pieces using only words they are sure of, which shrinks their vocabulary on paper. The usual approach is to let a first draft run, then pick two or three spelling patterns rather than individual words to work on. Patterns transfer; corrected words do not. If spelling anxiety is visibly limiting what gets written, that is the problem to treat first.

faqs.question: How is PYP English assessed if there is no test at the end?
faqs.answer: Continuously and descriptively: guided reading records, written pieces marked across subjects rather than only in English lessons, observation during discussion, and periodic reading assessments reported in various ways by different schools. Progression is described against four phases rather than year groups, so a child may be in Year 4 and working in a phase spanning several years. To get something actionable, ask which phase your child is in for reading and which for writing, because they are frequently different.

faqs.question: We speak two languages at home and school is adding Arabic - will English suffer?
faqs.answer: The evidence does not support that worry, and maintaining home languages is generally found to support rather than hinder English literacy because the underlying skills transfer. Arabic, Islamic Education and Social Studies are in any case mandatory in all Dubai private schools regardless of the licensed curriculum, per KHDA's guidelines, so it is not an optional addition. The genuine constraint is time rather than interference: more compulsory subjects means less timetable space, which is a scheduling fact worth counting when planning any session.

faqs.question: What does a session with a seven-year-old actually contain?
faqs.answer: Twenty-five minutes, one strand, and a clear task at the end. A typical decoding session is five minutes of sound and pattern work, ten minutes reading aloud from a book at the right level with the tutor correcting precisely, five minutes on the same patterns in writing, and a book and a target set for home. A comprehension session is one short passage, three questions, and the evidence underlined for each. Nothing in it is a lecture, because a seven-year-old cannot use one.

faqs.question: At what point does a writing problem need a specialist rather than a tutor?
faqs.answer: When the pattern is persistent and disproportionate: a child with strong spoken language, adequate reading and writing that stays severely limited despite teaching, or spelling that is phonetically wild rather than merely inaccurate, or handwriting that remains painful after explicit work on grip and position. Those patterns warrant a conversation with the school's inclusion team and possibly an educational psychology assessment. We will say so rather than sell sessions, because a tutor working around an unidentified difficulty wastes a family's money and a child's confidence.

faqs.question: What changes when my daughter moves into MYP Language and Literature?
faqs.answer: Four criteria marked 0 to 8 replace descriptive reporting, texts become literary and non-literary rather than mostly narrative, and reasoning has to be written down rather than simply arrived at. The habits that carry over are specific: inference supported by quoted evidence, paragraphs with a single focus and a topic sentence that does a job, enough vocabulary to read an unfamiliar passage, and the habit of pointing at the page. A targeted block in Year 5 or 6 aimed at those four is the best-timed English purchase in primary.

faqs.question: Can a tutor help with the Exhibition writing without crossing a line?
faqs.answer: Yes, if the teaching happens on a different topic. Note-taking without copying whole sentences, turning four notes into one focused paragraph, and presenting to an audience rather than reading slides are all generic skills, and we teach them on material unrelated to the child's own project. The child then applies them to the Exhibition alone. What nobody should do is write, redraft or produce any part of the actual work, and a provider offering to help with the piece itself is offering the wrong thing.

faqs.question: How many sessions before reading comprehension actually shifts?
faqs.answer: It depends which part is broken, which is why we agree an end condition before starting. The retrieval habit of returning to the page takes one or two sessions. Vocabulary in context takes about two. Inference with quoted evidence takes four to six and becomes automatic some weeks later. Author's purpose takes longer and is often better left until Year 6. If nothing has moved in four sessions on retrieval or vocabulary, something is wrong with the diagnosis and the honest response is to revisit it rather than to extend the block.

dubai/ib-pyp-english-tutor.closingHeading: Fifteen minutes of free testing beats a term of guessing
dubai/ib-pyp-english-tutor.closingBody: Before paying anyone, read a slightly hard page with your child and count the words they miss, then ask one direct question, one inference question and one about a word in that sentence. Then compare what they can tell you with what they can write. That tells you which of four problems you have. Bring it to the free 25-minute first lesson and the tutor will confirm or correct it and name the strand to work on, with no card details taken. Lessons run one-to-one on live video across the UAE, timed to Gulf Standard Time.

dubai/ib-pyp-exhibition-tutor.tutorsIntro: The tutors below have supervised culminating primary projects and know exactly where the boundary sits. They ask questions rather than supply answers, they will tell your child that a line of inquiry is unanswerable, and they will decline any request to produce part of the submission. Levels covered run from upper primary through to the MYP.

intro.heading: What the Exhibition actually assesses, and why that is not what parents worry about
paragraphs: The PYP Exhibition is the culminating project of the Primary Years Programme, carried out in the final primary year by children of roughly ten to twelve. Students, usually working in small groups, run an extended inquiry into a real issue, build it around a central idea and lines of inquiry, draw on every subject area rather than one, take some form of action, keep a record of their thinking as they go, and present the whole thing to the school community. Your school's PYP coordinator sets the exact format, and it varies more between Dubai schools than parents expect.

Here is the thing that surprises most families: the IB awards no mark for it. There is no external examiner, no grade boundary, no certificate. The Exhibition is organised and reported on internally, against learning outcomes and against the approaches to learning, which is why a parent can sit through a showcase evening feeling proud and still have no idea whether their child did well. The assessment is of the process, and the process happened over four months in a classroom you were not in.

That mismatch is where tutoring money goes wrong in this specific year. Parents see a presentation approaching and buy help with the presentation. The school is assessing research skill, self-management, collaboration, thinking and communication over the whole project, and a polished final talk built in the last fortnight demonstrates almost none of it. The talk is the visible tip. The marked part is the four months of decisions underneath, and most of those decisions were made badly in week two.

The failure modes are predictable enough to list. A central idea so broad that no evidence could ever answer it. A line of inquiry that is really a yes-or-no question. Three sources, all of them an adult's blog post, none of them named. Primary data collected from six friends and presented as a finding. A process journal written in one sitting the night before it was due. An action that was decided before the research and therefore unconnected to it. A group of four in which one child did everything and two did nothing. Every one of those is fixable in week two and nearly unfixable in week fourteen.

The other half of this page is the boundary, and it is written out in a table rather than gestured at. The Exhibition must be the student's own work. A tutor may teach how to narrow a question, how to judge a source, how to structure a talk and how to handle being asked something they did not prepare for. A tutor may not pick the topic, write any text, build any slide, collect any data or rehearse a script somebody else composed. A provider who will not say where that line sits is offering you a problem with your child's school, not a service.

Everything that follows is specific to Dubai: when schools here tend to launch the Exhibition and when they showcase it, what the mandatory Arabic and Islamic Education timetable does to the research weeks, where in the emirate a child can realistically carry out an action that is theirs rather than their parent's, and what Exhibition-year support costs in this market.

dubai/ib-pyp-exhibition-tutor.programmesIntro: The Exhibition is the first of four independent projects an IB student meets, and each one asks for the same thing at a higher level. Knowing what comes next changes what is worth building now.

programmes.name: Primary Years Programme and the Exhibition
programmes.ageRange: Ages 3-12 · Exhibition in the final primary year
programmes.description: The Exhibition sits at the end of the PYP as its culminating piece. Students take a real issue, frame it with a central idea and lines of inquiry, use the key concepts as lenses, gather their own evidence, act on what they found and present the result. It is transdisciplinary by design, so a strong project pulls in maths for the data, language for the writing, arts for the communication and social studies for the context.
programmes.countryNote: Dubai schools run the Exhibition on noticeably different calendars. Some launch straight after the winter break and showcase before the end of the second term; others start in the third term and finish close to the end of the year. Get the dates from your PYP coordinator in writing rather than from another parent, because a four-week difference in the launch date changes the whole support plan.

programmes.name: Middle Years Programme and the Personal Project
programmes.ageRange: Ages 11-16 · Project in the final MYP year
programmes.description: The MYP ends with an independent project assessed against criteria covering planning, applying skills, reflecting and the product itself. The structure is recognisably the Exhibition grown up: a goal the student sets, a process journal that evidences the work, a product or outcome, and a report. The step up is that it is individual rather than collaborative, and that the documentation of process carries explicit marks.
programmes.countryNote: Several Dubai schools run the full continuum, so the same child meets both projects in the same building with the same expectations about process journals. Families who treated the Exhibition as a presentation to be survived tend to meet the MYP project unprepared four years later, which is the most expensive version of this mistake available in the emirate.

programmes.name: Diploma Programme, the Extended Essay and TOK
programmes.description: The Diploma carries a 4,000-word independent research essay with a supervisor, plus a Theory of Knowledge exhibition and essay. Both demand exactly the skills the PYP Exhibition introduces: a question narrow enough to answer, sources judged rather than collected, a documented process and an argument the student can defend in a conversation. By this stage the academic-honesty rules carry real consequences, including for the student's diploma.
programmes.countryNote: Dubai's 2026-27 intake adds seven new private schools, three of them International Baccalaureate, which widens Diploma access across the emirate. For a current Exhibition-year family that is a long way off, and the only sensible preparation is the research habit being built this term rather than any Diploma content.

programmes.name: Career-related Programme and the Reflective Project
programmes.description: The IB's career-related route pairs Diploma courses with a career-related study and asks for a reflective project on an ethical dilemma arising from it. It is the least known of the four and it closes the same loop: an independent question, evidence gathered by the student, a documented process and a defensible conclusion. Worth knowing exists, because a child who enjoys the Exhibition's real-world framing sometimes fits this route better than the full Diploma.
programmes.countryNote: The Career-related Programme is offered by a small number of UAE schools and availability changes year to year, so it is a question for an open evening rather than an assumption. What matters now is that every route out of a Dubai IB primary school eventually asks for independent research, so the skill is not wasted whichever one your child takes.

dubai/ib-pyp-exhibition-tutor.subjectsIntro: The Exhibition is not one task. It is nine or ten separable skills, each of which can be taught, practised and tested on its own. These are the pieces, and what usually goes wrong inside each.

subjects.name: Central Idea and Lines of Inquiry
subjects.description: Writing a statement that is conceptual rather than factual, then breaking it into three or four questions that evidence could actually answer. Most projects fail here. 'Plastic is bad for the ocean' is a conclusion pretending to be a central idea, and no amount of later research rescues it. The teachable move is turning a yes-or-no question into a how or why question.

subjects.name: Key Concepts as Lenses
subjects.description: Using form, function, causation, change, connection, perspective and responsibility deliberately rather than decoratively. A child who picks causation and responsibility for the same inquiry gets two genuinely different sets of questions out of it. A child who lists all seven on a poster has used none of them, which a mentor spots immediately.

subjects.name: Research Methods for Ten- and Eleven-Year-Olds
subjects.description: Deciding what kind of evidence the question needs before looking for any. Some lines of inquiry need published facts, some need an expert's view, some need the student's own measurements and some need opinions from a defined group. Children default to typing the whole question into a search bar, which answers whichever version of it is most popular online.

subjects.name: Source Evaluation and Attribution
subjects.description: Asking who wrote this, when, and why, then recording the answer. At primary level this does not need a referencing system; it needs the habit of naming the source in the sentence. The commonest honesty problem in an Exhibition is not deliberate copying but an unattributed paragraph the child genuinely believes they wrote.

subjects.name: Primary Data: Surveys and Interviews
subjects.description: Writing a question that does not lead the answer, asking enough people for the answer to mean something, and reporting what was found rather than what was hoped. Six friends is not a survey. An interview with one informed adult, properly prepared and properly quoted, is worth more than forty rushed tick-boxes and is far easier to arrange.

subjects.name: The Process Journal
subjects.description: A running record of decisions, dead ends and changes of mind, kept as the project happens. It is the single most useful artefact in the whole Exhibition and the one most often faked the night before it is collected. A journal that records a line of inquiry being abandoned and why is stronger evidence of thinking than one that records only successes.

subjects.name: Action and Its Evidence
subjects.description: Doing something because of what the research found, then showing the link. Action chosen before the research is decoration. Action does not have to be a fundraiser or a beach clean; changing a household habit and measuring the result for three weeks is more defensible than a one-off event a parent organised.

subjects.name: The Presentation and the Question Session
subjects.description: Structuring a talk around the central idea, choosing which evidence to show and which to leave out, and surviving the part most children dread: an adult asking something that was not in the script. The fix is rehearsing unexpected questions, not rehearsing the script harder.

subjects.name: Collaboration and Group Roles
subjects.description: Most Exhibitions are group projects, and most group projects contain one child doing too much. Naming roles, agreeing deadlines between group members and raising a problem with the mentor early are all learnable. A child who learns to say 'we are behind and here is why' in week four has learned something worth more than the project.

subjects.name: Reflection and Self-Assessment
subjects.description: Saying what was learned about the topic and what was learned about working, separately and honestly. Reflection written to please an adult reads identically in every project a mentor sees. Reflection that names a mistake and what it changed is both rarer and exactly what the learner profile is asking for.

subjects.name: Academic Honesty at Primary Level
subjects.description: Understanding, at eleven, the difference between help and substitution. Being taught how to narrow a question is help. Having the question chosen for you is substitution. A child who can explain that distinction in their own words is better protected than one who has simply been told not to cheat.

dubai/ib-pyp-exhibition-tutor.regionsTitle: Where Dubai Exhibition-year families book from, and what action is realistic nearby
dubai/ib-pyp-exhibition-tutor.regionsIntro: The one part of the Exhibition that genuinely depends on where you live is the action. A ten-year-old can only act on what they can reach without a parent doing it for them, so geography matters more here than anywhere else in primary schooling.

regions.name: Jumeirah Village Circle
regions.note: Dense, mid-rise and full of shared amenity space, which makes building-level actions genuinely feasible: a recycling audit of one tower's bin room, a survey of residents on water use, a notice campaign in a lobby. All of it is within a child's own reach rather than their driver's.

regions.name: Dubai Hills Estate
regions.note: Parks, a long shaded walking loop and a community centre, so observational data is easy to gather: footfall counts at different times, shade mapping, tree and bird surveys. The risk here is a parent with a car making the action bigger than the child's actual contribution.

regions.name: Palm Jumeirah and Dubai Marina
regions.note: Coastal frontage puts marine and waste inquiries within walking distance, which is why half the Exhibition projects in these communities are about plastic. That popularity is itself the problem: a mentor has seen the generic version many times, and the narrow local question is what stands out.

regions.name: Al Quoz and Alserkal
regions.note: An unusual mix of light industry, warehouses and arts spaces inside one district. Projects on recycling chains, making and repair, or the working lives of people in the neighbourhood have access to real interview subjects a short distance away.

regions.name: Arabian Ranches and Mudon
regions.note: Villa communities with gardens and long compound walks, which suits inquiries on water consumption, composting, heat and shade, or household energy. Three weeks of daily readings from one villa makes a stronger dataset than a one-off event.

regions.name: Business Bay and Downtown Dubai
regions.note: High-rise living with little private outdoor space, so actions tend towards building management, transport and food waste. Interview access is unusually good here because so many families live and work in the same few towers.

regions.name: Discovery Gardens and The Gardens
regions.note: Older low-rise stock with shared courtyards and a genuinely mixed resident population, which makes survey work both easy and worth doing. A questionnaire translated into two languages is an achievable stretch for a capable eleven-year-old.

regions.name: Motor City and Dubai Sports City
regions.note: Sport-dominated communities where health, activity and heat are the natural inquiry territory. Clubs and academies nearby are usually willing to answer a child's written questions, which turns a vague health project into one with primary evidence.

schoolClusters.city: Al Barsha, Al Khail and Emirates Hills
schoolClusters.note: The largest concentration of IB continuum schools in Dubai, and the cluster where Exhibition showcases are biggest. Large cohorts mean tighter slots, shared display space and a firmer timeline, so a family that misses the week-two decisions has very little room to recover later in the term.

schoolClusters.city: Mirdif, Al Jaddaf and the southern communities
schoolClusters.note: Smaller year groups and more flexible showcase formats, which cuts both ways. There is more room for an unusual inquiry, and less structure holding a drifting project together, so self-management is the skill that decides the outcome in this cluster.

dubai/ib-pyp-exhibition-tutor.modesIntro: Exhibition support is bought in a short window and should be shaped to it. These are the four arrangements that make sense, and the one that does not is a weekly open-ended booking that runs past the showcase.

modes.title: The week-two intensive: two sessions on the question alone
modes.description: Two sessions in the first fortnight, spent entirely on narrowing the central idea and turning each line of inquiry into something evidence could answer. This is the highest-value purchase in the whole Exhibition year and the cheapest, because two sessions in January prevent eight in April. The output is a written question set your child can take to their mentor.
bullets: Scoped to the question and nothing else
Your child does the choosing; the tutor supplies objections
Ends with a question set the mentor can approve or redirect
Deliberately booked before any research has started

modes.title: Weekly 45 minutes through the research term
modes.description: A fixed slot across the middle of the project, where the tutor reviews what was done since last week, asks what the evidence actually showed, and teaches the next skill the project needs. The point of the regularity is self-management: a child who knows somebody will ask on Tuesday works on Monday, which is most of what the Exhibition is testing.
bullets: Same tutor, same weekday, in Gulf Standard Time

A short written note to the parent after each session

modes.title: Presentation rehearsal with unexpected questions
modes.description: Two or three sessions in the fortnight before the showcase, built around the part children fear: being asked something they did not prepare. The tutor asks awkward, fair questions, records the answers, plays them back and works on structure, pace and what to do when the answer is 'I do not know'. The script, if there is one, is the child's.
bullets: Recorded playback so the child hears themselves

Explicit practice at saying what the project did not establish

modes.title: A single diagnostic session for a project already in trouble
modes.description: Sometimes a family arrives in week ten with a project that has drifted. One session, with the process journal and whatever has been gathered, is usually enough to say what can still be rescued and what should be abandoned. The honest answer is sometimes that the inquiry cannot be saved and the right move is to tell the mentor, early, in the child's own words.
bullets: One session, one written assessment of what is salvageable
Priority is what the child can still do themselves in the time left
